rity. The Apostle says the same: You, my brothers, have been called to freedom; Be careful that this freedom does not serve as an occasion for you to live according to the flesh; but through charity be servants of one another. Let the Christian not say: I am free, I have been called to freedom; I was a servant, but I have been redeemed and made free by the same redemption; I will do what I want; no one opposes my will; I am free. But if, having that freedom, you sin, you are a servant of sin. Therefore, do not abuse freedom to sin freely, but use it to not sin. Your will will be free if it is good. You will be free if you are a servant: free from sin, a servant of righteousness, as the Apostle says: When you were servants of sin, you were free from justification; but now, freed from sin and converted into servants of God, you reap your fruit in sanctification and, finally, eternal life. To achieve this let us direct all our efforts. 9- The first freedom is to be free from crimes. Attend, brothers, attend, so that I may bring to your knowledge what this freedom consists of now and what it will consist of in the future. No matter how righteous you think one is in this life, and even if he is already worthy of this appellation, yet he is not exempt from sin. Saint John himself says it, whose gospel is this: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not with us. This could only be said by one who was free among the dead, and it can only be said of the one who did not know sin, of whom he quoted: Vos autem fratres in libertalem vocati estis; tantum ne libertatem in occasionem carnis detis, sed per charitatem servite invloem (Gal 5,13). Non ergo dicat christianus: Liber sum, ¡n libertatem vocatus sum: servus eram, sed redemptus sum, et ipsa redemptione liber effectus sum, faciam quod voló; nemo forbid me to volúntate mea, si liber sum. Sed si ista volúntate peccatum facis, servus es peccati. Noli ergo libértate abuti ad liberate peccandum, sed utere ad non peccandum. Erit enim voluntas tua libera, si fuerit pia. Eris liber, if you were servus; liber peccati, servus iustitiae: dicente Apostolo, Cum serví essetis peccati, liberi eratis iustitiae: nunc autem liberati a peccato, servi autem jacú Deo, habetis jructum vestrum in sanctificationem, finem vero vitam aeternam (Rom 6,20.22). Hoc conemur, id agamus. 9. Prima libertas est carere criminibus.

Intendite, fratres mei, intendite; Ne forte possim perducere vobis ad sensum et qualis moda sit, et qualisfutura sit ista libertas. Quemlibet valde iustum discourses in hac vita, quamvis iam sit dignus iusti vocabulo, non est tamen sine peccato: audi ipsum sanctum Ioannem, cuius et hoc Evangelium est, in Epístola sua dicentem. Si dixerimus, inquit, quia peccatum non habe-mus, nos tpsos decipimus, et veritas in nobis non est (1 lo 1,8). Solus hoc dicere potuit in mortuis liber, de solo dici potuit qui non noverat peccatum; from just saying potuit: etenim expertus est orrjnia se-
About the Gospel of Saint John

It could only be said that he passed through all things in the likeness of the sinless flesh. Only He could say: The prince of the world is coming and will find nothing in me. Anyone else, no matter how righteous he may seem to you, is not totally without sin. Not even Job himself, of whom God gave such testimony that the devil was envious of him, and asked for power to tempt him, emerging defeated in the temptation and he justified. He was not tested because God did not know that he deserved the crown, but so that men would have an example to imitate. Job himself says: Who is totally clean? Not even the child who has been on earth for a day. Certainly many have been called righteous without complaint, which means without crime, since in human matters no just complaint can be filed against someone who has no crime. Serious sin is a crime worthy of being exposed and condemned. God does not condemn certain sins nor does he justify and praise others: he praises none, he hates them all. Just as the doctor hates the sick person's illness and with cures tries to ward off the illness and relieve the sick, so God works in us with his grace to destroy sin and free man. But you will say, when is it destroyed? If it decreases, why is it not destroyed? It diminishes in the life of the proficient and is destroyed in the life of the perfect. 10. The first freedom is, therefore, not having crimes. Hence the apostle Saint Paul, when choosing those who were to ordain priests or deacons, or anyone else, for the government of the Church, did not say: "If anyone is without sin," because, if cundum similarinem sine sine (Hebrews 4:15). Solus dicere potuit, Ecce veniet princeps mundi, et in me nihil inveniet. Quemcumque alium licet iustum discusseris, non omnimodo est sine peccato. Nec qualis erat Iob, cui Dominus tale testimonium perhibebat, ut diabolus invideret, et postularet tentandum, tentans superaretur, ut ¡lie proveretur (Iob 1,2). Ideo autem ille probatus est, non quia latebat Deum coronandus, sed ut innotesceret hominibus imitandus. Etiam ipse Iob quid dicit? Quis enim mundus? Nec infans, cuius est unius diei vita super terram (ibid. 14,4 sec. 70). Sed plan multi iusti dicti sunt sine querela, quod intelligitur sine crimine: nulla enim querela iusta est de his in rebus humanis, qui non habent crime. Crimen autem est peccatum grave, aecusatione et damnatione dignissimum. Non ergo Deus quaedam peccata damnat, quaedam iustificat et laudat: nulla laudat, odit omnia.

Quomodo odit medicus aegritudinem aegroti, et id agit curando ut aegritudo pellatur, aeger levetur: sic Deus gratia sua hoc in nobis agit, ut peccatum consummatur, homo liberetur. Sed when you consume, are you interested? Si minuitur, quare non consumitur? Minuitur autem in vita proficientium, quod in vita consumitur perfectionum. 10. Prima est ergo libertas, carere criminibus. Ideo et apostolus I'aulus quando elegit ordinandos vel presbyteros vel deacons, et quicumque ordinandus est ad praeposituram Ecclesiae, non ait, Si quis sine peccato est; hoc enim si dicetet, omnis homo reptobaretur, nullus
About the Gospel of Saint John

had said this, all would be rejected and none ordained. But he said: If there is any who has no crime, such as murder, adultery, some filthiness of fornication, theft, fraud, sacrilege, and the like. When man begins to not have such crimes (the Christian should not have them), he begins to raise his head towards freedom; but this is an inchoate freedom, it is not perfect. Why, someone will say, is it not perfect freedom? For I see in my members another law that resists the law of my spirit, because I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I hate. The flesh, he says, has desires against the spirit, and the spirit has desires against the flesh, so that you do not do everything you want. On the one hand, freedom; on the other, slavery; It is not yet total, it is not yet pure, it is not yet full freedom, because we are not yet in eternity. In part we have illness, in part we receive freedom. All our sins were erased by baptism. Because all iniquity had disappeared, was there no weakness left? If none had remained we would be here without sin. Who will dare to say such a thing but the arrogant, the one unworthy of the mercy of the liberator, who wants to deceive himself and does not speak the truth? Because some weakness has remained in us, I dare say that because we serve God we are free; but because we serve sin we are still servants. For this reason the Apostle says what we had begun to say: I take pleasure in the law of God according to the inner man. Whence comes our delight in the law of God ordinaretur: sed ait, Si quis sine crimine est (1 Tim 3:10, et Tit 1:6), sicuti est homicidium, adulterium, aliqua immunditia fornicationis, furtum, fraus, sacrilegium, et caetera huiusmodi. Cum coeperit ea non habere homo (debet autem non habere omnis christianus homo), incipit caput erígete ad libertatem: sed ista inchoata est, non perfection libertas. Quare, inquit aliquis, isn't this perfect freedom? Quia "video aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentís meae: non enim quod voló ago, ait, sed quod odi illud fació" (Gal 5,17). "Caro, inquit, concupiscit adversus spiritum, et spiritus adversus carnem, ut non ea quae vultis illa faciatis." Ex parte libertas, ex parte servitus: nondum tota, nondumpura, nondum plena libertas, quia nondum aeternitas. Habemus enim ex parte infirmitatem, ex parte accepimus libertatem.

Quidquid peccatum est a nobis, antea deletum est in Baptism. Numquid quia deleta est tota iniquitas, nulla remansit infirmitas? Si non remansisset, sine peecato hic viveremus. Quis autem audeat hoc dicere nisi superbus, nisi misericordia liberatoris indignus, nisi qui seipsum vult decipere, et in quo veritas non est? Ergo ex eo quod remansit aliquid infirmitatis, audeo dicete, ex qua parte servimus Deo, liben sumus: ex qua jarte servimus legi peccati, adhuc servi sumus. Unde dicit Apostolus quod dicere coeperamus: Condelector legi Dei secundum interiorem hominem. Ecce unde liberi, unde condelectamur legi Dei: libertas enim delectat. Nam quamdiu timore facis quod iustum
About the Gospel of Saint John

freedom comes to us. For freedom delights us, and while you do justice with fear, God is not your delight. Do not fear punishment, love justice. Don't you still love justice? Fear punishment so that you come to love justice. 11. He already felt free in the upper part, when he said: I am pleased in the law of God according to the inner man. I delight in the law, I delight in what the law orders, I delight in justice itself. Vero I see in my members another law (it is the disease that had remained) that resists the law of my spirit and subjugates me to the law of sin, which is in my members. For this part he felt captivity, because justice was not complete. When you find delight in the law of God, you are not a captive, but a friend of the law, and you are free because you are a friend. What will we do about the disease that remains? Let us turn to Him who said; If the Son will set you free, then you will be truly free. Also the same Apostle who spoke came to Him, saying: "I am a wretched man, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Therefore, if the Son will free you, then you will be truly free." Finally, he concluded: "Meanwhile, I myself live subject by spirit to the law of God and by flesh to the law of sin." Myself, he says: we are not two, opposed to each other, coming from different principles; but: I myself serve the law of God by the spirit, and by the flesh the law of sin as long as sickness resists health. est, non Deus te delectat. Quamdiu adhuc servus facis, te non delectat: delectet te, et liber es. Noli timere poenam, sed ama iustitiam. Nondum potes amare iustitiam? time vel poenam, ut pervenias ad amandam iustitiam. II. Ergo iam iiie ex parte superiore iiberum se esse sentiebat, unde dicebat, Condelector legi Dei secundum interiorem hominem. Delectat me lex, delectat me quod iubet lex, delectat me ipsa iustitia. Video autem alliam legem in membris meis: haec est quae remansit infirmitas: repugnantem legi mentís meae, et captivantem me in lege peccati, quae est in membris meis. Ex hac parte sentit captivitateni, ubi non est impleta iustitia: nam ubi condelectatur legi Dei, non captivus, sed legis amicus est; et ideo liber, quod amicus. Quid ergo ex eo quod restat? Quid, nisi respiciamus ad illum qui dixit, Si vos Filias liberaveñt, tune veré liberi eritis?

Denique et ipse qui loquebatur, ad illum respexit: "Infelix ego homo, quis me líberabit, inquit, de corpote mortis huius? Gratia Dei per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Ergo si vos Filius liberaverit, tune veré liberi eritis." Denique ita conclusit: "Igitur ipse ego mente servio legi Dei, carne autem legi peccati" (Rom 7:19-25). Ipse ego, inquit: non enim duo sumus inter nns coiitratii de diversis principiis venientes; thirst ego ipse mind servio legi Dei, carne autem legi peccati, quamdiu languor obluctatur saluti.
About the Gospel of Saint John

12. But if through the flesh you are subject to the law of sin, do as the Apostle himself says: Do not let sin reign in your mortal body to obey its desires, nor lend your members to sin as weapons of iniquity. It does not say: There is not; but: Do not reign. While sin is in your members by necessity, take away its power so that you do not execute what it commands. Does anger attack you? Don't give him your tongue to curse, don't give him your hand or your foot to hurt. This irrational anger would not arise if sin were not in your members; but take away his power, so that he has no weapons to fight against you; He will learn not to get up when his weapons begin to fail. Do not lend your members to sin as weapons of iniquity, otherwise you will be slaves of sin and will not be able to say that you served the law of God through the spirit. If the spirit holds the weapons, the members will not move to be instruments of raging sin. The inner king preserves the strength, because the weak one lends his assistance under the superior command; Restrain anger, repress concupiscence, because there is always something to restrain, what to repress, what to hold. What else did that righteous man, who in his spirit served the law of God, desire but to feel absolutely nothing to restrain? And this must be strived for by those who strive for perfection, so that concupiscence, the lack of obedient members, becomes weaker every day in the proficient. In my will, he says, it is to will what is good, but not to execute it. Did he say, perhaps, that it is not 12. Sed si carne servís legi peccati, fac quod ait -ipse Apostolus: Non ergo regnet peccatum in vestro mortali corpore ad obediendum desideriis eius, ñeque exhibitatis membra vestra arma iniquitatis peccato (Rom 6,12.13). Non ait, Non sit; sed, Non regnet. Quamdiu peccatum necesse est esse in membris tuis, saltem illi regnum auferatur, non fiat quod iubet. Anger arose? noli daré irae linguam ad maledicendum; noíi daré irae manum aut pedem ad feriendum. Non ariseret ira ista irrationabilis, nisi peccatum esset in membris: sed tolle illi regnum, non habeat arma unde contra te pugnet; discet etiam non surgere, cum arma coeperit non invenire. Non exhibitionatis membra vestra arma iniquitatis peccato; alioquin toti captivi eritis, et non erit dicere, Mente servio legi Dei.

Mens enim si teneat arma, membra non moventur in ministerium furentis peccati. Teneat arcem imperator interior, quia sub maiore imperatore iuvandus assistit; frenet iram, coerceat concupiscentiam. Inest tamen quod frenetur, inest quod coerceatur, inest quod teneatur. Quid autem volebat ille iustus mente serviens legi Dei, nisi ut omnino non esset quod frenetur? Et hoc debent conari omnis qui tendit ad perfectionem, ut et ipsa concupiscentia cui non dantur ad obediendum membra, quotidie in proficiente minuatur. Velle, inquit, adiacet mihi, perficere autem bonum non (Rom 7:18). Numquid dixit, Non mihi adiacet faceré bonum? Si hoc dixisset, spes nulla esset. Non ait, Non mihi adiacet faceré, sed, Non mihi adiacet perficere. Quae est enim perfectio boni, nisi consumptio et finis mali?
About the Gospel of Saint John

Was it in his power to do good? If he had said this, there would be no hope left. He did not say: Do good; but: Execute good. And what is the perfect execution of good but the destruction and death of evil? And what is the destruction of evil, except what the Law says: Thou shalt not covet? To covet absolutely nothing is the perfection of good, because it is the destruction of evil. This is what he said: Perfecting good is not in my power, because I could not stop feeling concupiscence; He worked, however, to restrain her, so as not to give her his consent and not lend her his members as executors. To do good with perfection, he says, is not in my power; I cannot fulfill the command: You shall not covet. What, then, is necessary? May you fulfill that: Do not let yourself be carried away by your passions. Do this while illicit lusts exist in your flesh: do not allow yourself to be carried away by them. Remain in the service of God, in the freedom of Christ; With your spirit submit to the law of your God. Do not give in to your lusts. By following them, you increase their strength, and by giving them more strength, how can you win when you help your enemies with your own strength? 13. This full and perfect freedom in the Lord Jesus, who said: If the Son will set you free, then you will be truly free, when will it be full and perfect freedom? When there is no enmity, when death, which is the last enemy, is destroyed. It is fitting that this corruptible body put on incorruption and that this mortal body put on immortality. Then what is written will be fulfilled: Death has been swallowed up by victory. Where is it, oh death!, your Quae est autem consumptio mali, nisi quod Lex dicit, Non concupisces? (Ex 20,17). Omnino non concupiscere perfectio boni est, quia consumptio mali est. Hoc dicebat ille, Perficere bonum non mihi adiacet; quia non poterat faceré ut non concupisceret: faciebat tantum ut concupiscentiam refrenaret, ut concupiscentiae non consentiret, et concupiscentiae membra ad sateílitium non praeberet. Perficere ergo, inquit, bonum non mihi adiacet: non possum implere quod dictum est, Non concupisces. What is this opus? Ut impleas, Post concupiscentias tuas non eas (Eccli 18,30).

Hoc age interim quamdiu insunt iüicitae concupiscentiae in carne tua, Post concupiscentias tuas non eas. Mane in servitute Dei, in liberate Chtisti; mind servi legi Dei tui. Noli I will give you concupiscentiis tuis: sequendo eas, vires eis addis; giving eis vires quornodo vincis, when against you inimicos you nourish viribus tuis? 13. If we understand power by the hand, one is the power of the Father and the Son, because one is the divinity; But, if by hand we understand what the prophet said: To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?, then the hand of the Father is the Son himself. If, then, all things were made through Him, it is not surprising that through Him one was resurrected, when through Him so many are born daily. It is more to create a man than to resurrect him. Not everything the Lord Jesus did is written, as the evangelist Saint John himself affirms, saying that Christ acted and said many other things that have not been written. We have read in the Gospel that the Lord raised three dead people, which perhaps contains some mystery, because the works of the Lord are not only acts, but also signs; and, for the same reason, apart from the wonderful thing, they have a meaning whose intelligence is sometimes more laborious than hearing or reading it. When the Gospel was read we heard, astonished at the sight of such a great miracle, how Lazarus had come back to life. But, if we pay attention to more wonderful works of Christ, everyone who believes is resurrected; and if we run all kinds of deaths, we will find among the most detestable the death of the one who sins. Everyone fears the death of the body, but few fear the death of the soul. Everyone strives to prevent the death of the flesh from coming, which inevitably must come, and that is why they work. But sometimes one sins in thinking; You liked what was bad, you consented; you sinned; That consent gave you death, but that death is internal, because the bad thought did not pass into the work. But in this way the perverse Judas also served Christ, since he was the one who carried the purse, and although he criminally stole the things that were put in it, nevertheless, through him what was necessary was prepared. Hence, when the Lord said to him: What you do, do it quickly, some thought that he was ordering them to prepare something because it was a holiday, or to give some alms to the poor. Therefore, in no way would the Lord say of such servants: Where I am, there will my servant also be; and: If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him; for we see that Judas, who served such things, is reprobate rather than honest. But why should we look elsewhere for what is meant by serving Christ and not see it in these same words? When he said: If anyone serves me, follow me, he implied that he meant: If anyone does not follow me, he does not serve me. The evangelist then continues saying the words of today's reading: Having performed so many miracles in their sight, they did not believe in Him, to fulfill the words that the prophet Isaiah said: O Lord! Who gave credit to our hearing and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? From which it is clearly deduced that he calls the Son of God himself the arm of the Lord, not because God the Father has a human figure and the Son is united to Him as a member of the body, but because through Him all things were made, which is why he calls it the arm of the Lord. Just as your arm calls the instrument you use for your work, so the Word is called the arm of God, because through Him He made the world. And why does a man use his arm to do something, if not because the work does not immediately respond to his word? But if he had such power that without moving any of his body or doing what he said, his word would be his arm. Our Lord Jesus Christ, only begotten Son of God the Father, as he is not a member of the paternal body, neither is he a ringing and transitory idea or word, because, when all things were made by him, he was already the Word of God. 3. When, therefore, we hear the Son of God called the arm of God, let us not imagine anything carnal, but rather let us think, whatever is given to us with his help, in the power and wisdom didicissent, ambularent, ut totum discerent, ne comprehenderentur a tenebris. Do not open the door to the detestable error of those who say that only the Father exists, and, according to the diversity of operations, he is sometimes called the Son and other times the Holy Spirit, daring to say: You see from these words that, if the Son is the arm of the Father, only the Father exists, because the man and his arm are not two persons, but one. They do not understand or realize that, in the ordinary way of speaking about visible and known things, due to a certain similarity, words of a certain meaning are applied to express other things of a different nature. How much more reason will we use them to express in some way what is ineffable and cannot be expressed according to its own nature! Even men call the man they use to carry out their works their arm, and if they lose it, they say with pain: I lost my arm; and to the one who took it away they say: You have taken my arm from me. Understand, then, how the Son is said to be the arm of the Father, through whom the Father does all things, so that, by not understanding it and remaining in the darkness of their error, they may not become like the Jews themselves, of whom it is said: And the arm of the Lord, to whom has it been revealed? 4. From here arises another question, whose explanation, so that it is complete and reveals all the thorny points that it contains, and is discussed with the dignity that it deserves, I believe that it is not Virtutem Dei et Sapientiam cogitemus, per quam facta sunt omnia. Tale quippe brachium nec porrectum extenditur, nec collectum contrahitur. Non est enim ipse qui Pater, sed unum sunt ipse et Pater; et aequalis Patri ubique totus est sicut Pater: ne aliqua patat occasio detestabili errori eorum, qui dicunt solum esse Patrem, sed pro diversitate causaum ipsum dici Filium, ipsum dici Spiritum sanctum; et in his verbis audeant dicere, Ecce videtis quia solus est Pater, si brachium eius est Filius; non enim duae, sed una persona est homo et brachium eius.

Non intelligentes ñeque advertentes, quomodo verba de rebus alus ad res alias transferantur, propter aliquam similarityinem etiam in locutionibus quotidianis de visibilibus et notissimis rebus; quanto magis ut nobis ineffabilia qualitercumque dicantur, quae dici sicuti sunt, omnino non possunt? Nam et homo alterum hominem per quem solet agere quidquid agit, brachium suum appellat: et si ei auferatur, dolens dicit, Brachium perdidi; et ei qui abstulerit, dicit Brachium meum mihi abstulisti. Intelligant ergo quomodo dictus sit Filius Patris brachium, per quod Pater operatus est omnia; ne hoc non intelligendo, et in sui erroris tenebris permanendo, similes sint Iudaeis ipsis, de quibus dictum est, Et brachium Domini cui revelatum est? 4. Some murmur within themselves, and sometimes, when they have occasion, they say aloud and with turbulent discussions: What did the Jews do or what fault were they, if it were necessary "that the words of the prophet Isaiah should be fulfilled, which says: Lord, who will believe our ear, and the arm of the Lord, to whom it has been revealed?" To this we answer that the Lord, who knows the future, foretold by the prophet the infidelity of the Jews; He predicted it, it was not the cause of it. Just as God does not force anyone to sin because He knows the future sins of men. He foresaw their sins, not his own; nor those of anyone else, but those of themselves. Now, if their sins, which He foresaw, are not theirs, He did not really truly foresaw them; But, since his foreknowledge cannot be deceived, without a doubt those whom God foresaw would sin sin, and no one else sins. Therefore the Jews sinned, to which they were not forced by him who hates sin; but he predicted that those to whom nothing is hidden would sin. If, instead of doing evil, they had wanted to do good, they would not have been prevented from doing so; but that they were to act this way he had precutiantur ut dignum est, nec mearum virium esse arbitior, nec anguishrum temporis, nec vestrae capatis. Tamen quia traniré ad alia vestra expectatione non sinimur, nisi aliquid inde dicamus, accipite quod potuerimus: et ubi vestrae expectationi non sufcerimus, ab illo incrementum poscite qui nos plantare posuit et rigare, quia, sicut dicit Apostolus, Ñeque qui plantat est aliquid, ñeque qui rigai; sed qui incrementntn dat Deus (1 Cor 3,7).

The following words of the Gospel are more terrible and involve a deeper question, since it continues: The reason for not being able to believe is given again by Isaiah, saying: He blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts so that with their eyes they would not see and with their heart they would not understand, and they would convert and I would heal them. If they could not believe, we will be told, what sin does he commit who does not do what he cannot do? But, if they sinned by not believing, they could believe and they did not believe. And if they could believe, how does the Gospel say: They could not believe, because Isaiah had prophesied it for the second time: He blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, as if making them, and this is more serious, guilty of their unbelief for having blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts? And this is not only said of the devil, but also of God, according to the prophetic testimony of Scripture. Because, if we said that the devil blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, it would be very difficult for us to prove the guilt of those who did not believe because they could not believe. And what shall we say of another testimony of the same prophet cited by the apostle Saint Paul: Israel has not found what it sought, but the elect found it, and all the rest were blind, according to what is written: God gave them the spirit of repentance, eyes so that they do not see and ears so that they do not hear to this day? 6.

If you ask me why they couldn't, I quickly answer: Because they didn't want to; for God had planned his perverse will, and through the prophet he announced it from whom the future cannot be hidden. God blinds and hardens by withdrawing and not lending his help, which he does not by wicked judgments, but by hidden judgments; and this must unquestionably and inviolably guard the piety of the faithful, as the Apostle did when dealing with this difficult question: What shall we say then? Is there perversity in God? No way. Therefore, if we are to be far from thinking that there is perversity in God, we must believe that, when he helps, he does so out of his mercy, and that he acts justly when he does not help, because he does not act rashly, but with right judgment. Truly, if the judgments of the saints are just, how much more just must be the judgments of God, who sanctifies and justifies. They are certainly fair, but hidden. Therefore, when questions of this kind arise: why some are treated in one way and others in another; Because he abandons some to remain blind and illuminates others with his light, let us not get involved in judging the judgments of such an excellent judge, before, full of sit cernitis: sed responderus ut possumus. Therefore, I also say that those who are so full of pride that they believe that what they are is due to their own strength alone and that they do not need divine help to live well, cannot believe in Christ. The syllables of the name of Christ and his sacraments are of no use when the faith of Christ is resisted. Because the faith of Christ is to believe that He justifies the wicked, to believe that He is the mediator, without whom we are not reconciled with God; believe that He is the Savior, who came to seek and save what had perished;

believe in Him who said: Without me you can do nothing. And because, despising the justice of God, which makes the wicked righteous, the proud man wants to impose his own to justify himself, he cannot believe in Christ, and for the same reason they could not believe, not because as men they could not become better, but because, as long as they have such ideas, they cannot believe. From here comes their obstinacy and hardening, that, denying divine help, they are not helped. God had foreseen this blindness and hardening of the Jews, and by his Spirit he announced it through the prophet. 11. As for what follows: And they should be converted and healed, it must be understood No, that is, not converted, because of the connection it has with the previous sentence: Lest they see and understand in their hearts, since here it is evidently not to understand. Is it not possible to see here an effect of the medicinal divine mercy, that, because they had a haughty and perverse will and wanted to establish their justice as a norm, they were abandoned, so that they would become blinded; blind, stumble on the stone of stumbling and cover their faces with ignominy and thus, humiliated, take refuge in the name of God and his justice, which makes the wicked righteous, and leave theirs, which inflates the proud? Ecce dico et ego, quod qui tam superbe sapiunt, ut suae voluntatis viribus tantum existencement esse tribuendum, ut negent sibi esse necessarium divinum adiutorium ad bene vivirdum, noA possunt credere in Christum. Non enim aliquid prosunt syllabae nominis Christi, et Sacramenta Christi, ubi resistitur fidei Christi. Fides autem Christi est, credere in eum qui iustificat impium (Rom 4:5); credere in Mediatorem, sine quo interposito non reconciliamur Deo; believe in Salvatorem, qui venit quod perierat quaerere atque salvare (Luke 19:10);

credere in eum quid dixit, Sine me nihil potestis ¡acere (lo 15,5). Quia ergoignons Dei iustitiam qua iusrificatur impius, suam vult constituere qua convincatur superbus, in hunc non potest credere. These things Isaiah said when he saw his glory and spoke of Him. What Isaiah saw and how everything refers to Christ, our Lord, be read and understood in his book. He saw Him not as He is, but in a significant way, as suited the vision of the prophet. Moses also saw him, and yet he said to him who saw: If I have found favor in your presence, show me yourself so that I may see you clearly, because I did not see him as he is. And when we will achieve this, this same evangelist, Saint John, tells us in his epistle: Dearest, we are children of God, and it does not yet appear what we will be; We know that when He appears, we will be like Him, because we will see Him as He is. He could have said because we will see Him, without adding, as He is. Do not be deceived, therefore, brothers, by those who say that the Father is invisible and only the Son is visible. This is what those who believe him to be a pure creature say, without understanding why he said: I and the Father are one. Certainly, the Son is invisible in the form of God, by which he is equal to the Father; But to make himself visible to men, he took the form of a servant, and, being made in the likeness of men, he became visible. It had already been shown Dei habent, sed non secundum scientiam: tune enim et hoc subiunxit, atque ait, Ignorantes enim Dei iustitiam, et suam volentes constítuere, iustitiae Dei non sunt subiecti (Rom 10,2.3). 12. FROM THESE WORDS OF JESUS: "HE WHO BELIEVES IN ME DOES NOT BELIEVE IN ME, BUT IN THE ONE WHO SENT ME", TO THESE OTHERS: "THE THINGS THAT I SPEAK, I SAY THEM AS MY FATHER HAS TOLD ME"

1. When Our Lord Jesus Christ spoke among the Jews and worked so many miracles, some of those predestined to eternal life, also called by Him His sheep, believed; but others did not believe, nor could they believe, because, due to hidden, but not unjust, judgments of God, they were blinded and hardened, experiencing the abandonment of Him who resists the proud and grants his grace to the humble. Some of those who believed confessed him to the point of going out to meet him with palms and with great contentment in the confession of his praises. Others, however, of the principal ones, did not dare to confess to him publicly for fear of being thrown out of the synagogue, and whom the evangelist rebukes, saying that they valued the glory of men more than the glory of God. Among those who did not believe there were some who were to believe later, these he already had in mind when he said: When you have lifted up the Son of man, then you will know that I am he. But others were to remain in their disbelief, whose imitators are this race of Jews who, later destroyed, according to the prophetic testimony of Christ, are today dispersed throughout the world.

1. Loquente Domino nostro Iesu Christo apud Iudaeos, et tanta miraculorum signa faciente, quidam ciediderunt praedestinati in vitam aeternam, quos etiam vocavit oves suas: quidam vero non crediderunt, nec poterant credere, eo quod occulto, nec tamen iniusto iudicio Dei fuerant excaecati et indurad, Deserente illo qui superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam (Iac 4,6). Eorum autem qui crediderunt, alii usque adeo confitebantur, ut palmarum ramis acceptis venienti occutrerent, in eadem laudis confessione laetantes: alii vero ex principibus non audebant confiteri, ut de synagoga non eiicerentur; quos Notavit Evangelist say, quod dilexerunt gloriam hominum magis quam gloriam Dei (lo 12,43). Eorum etiam qui non crediderunt, alii erant postea credituri, quos praevidebat, ubi ait, Cum exaltaveritis Vilium hominis, tune agnoscetis quia ego sum (ibid. 8,28): alii vero in eadem infidelitate mansuri, quorum imitatrix est etiam ista gens Iudaeorum, quae postmodum debellata, ad testimonium prophetiae quae de Christo scripta est, in toto penis orb disperses est.

2. In such circumstances and his passion was already close, Jesus cried out and said the words that head today's reading: He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in the One who sent me, and whoever sees me sees the One who sent me. He had already said on one occasion: My doctrine is not mine, but that of Him who sent me. Then we explain that he called the Word of the Father his doctrine, which is Himself; and that by saying My doctrine is not mine, but of Him who sent me, he wanted to imply that He did not come from Himself and that He had someone from whom to come: God from God, Son of the Father; but the Father is not God of God, but GodFather of the Son. And how are we to understand these words of his: He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in Him who sent me, except in the sense that man appeared in the sight of men, while God was hidden in Him? And so that they would not think that He was only what they saw, and wanting to be considered as great as the Father, He says: He who believes in me does not believe in me, that is, in what he sees; but believe in Him who sent me, that is, in the Father. But whoever believes in the Father must believe in Him as Father, and whoever believes in Him as Father must believe that he has a Son; and thus, whoever believes in the Father, must of necessity believe in the Son. But to prevent anyone from assuming that the only begotten Son is called the Son of God, in the manner of those called children of God by grace, but not by nature, according to what the Evangelist says: He gave them the power to become children of God; and of whom the Lord himself, quoting the testimony of the Law, said: You are all gods and children of the Most High; to avoid this he said: He who believes in me does not 2. His ita se habentibus, et sua iam propinquante passione, Iesus clamavit, et dixit; unde lectio coepit hodierna: Qui credit in me, non credit in me, sed in eum qui misit me: et qui videt me, videt eum qui misit me. Iam dixerat quodam loco: Mea doctrina non est mea, sed eius qui misit me (ibid. 7,16). Ubi intelleximus eum doctrinara suam dixisse Verbum Patris quod est ipse; et hoc means saying, Mea doctrina non est mea, sed eius qui me misit, quod a seipso ipse non esset, sed haberet a quo esset (Supra, tr.29). Deus enim de Deo, Filius Patris: Pater autem non Deus de Deo, sed Deus Pater Filii.

Nunc autem quod ait, Qui credit in me, non credit in me, sed in eum qui misit me, quomodo intellecturi sureras, nisi quia homo apparebat hominibus, cum lateret Deus? Et ne putarent hoc eum esse tantummodo quod videbant, talem ac tantum se volens credi, qualis et quantus est Pater, Qui credit in me, inquit, non credit in me, id est, in hoc quod videt; sed in eum qui misit me, id est, in Patiem. Sed qui credit in Patrem, necesse est eum credat esse Patrem; qui autem credit eum Patrem, necesse est ut credat eum habere Filium: ac per hoc qui credit in Patrem, necesse est ut credat in Eilium. Sed ne quisquam hoc credat de only begotten EiLio, quod de iis qui dicti sunt filii Dei secundum gratiam, non naturam, sicut ait Evangelista, Dedit eis potestatem ¡Utos Dei jieri (lo 1,12); unde et ilLud est quod ipseDominus commemoiavit in Lege dictum, Ego dtxi, Dii estis, et filii excelst

He, therefore, truly believes in me who believes not only what he sees in me, but also Him who sent me, and, believing in the Father, believes that He has a Son equal to Him, and thus believes what I truly am. For, if he thinks that the Father only has adopted children by his grace, who are certainly his creatures, but are not the Word, but made by the Word, and that he does not have a Son equal to Him and co-eternal, eternally born, equally immutable, in nothing different and unequal; Whoever thinks this way does not believe in the Father who sent him, because this is not the Father who sent him. 3. And so, having said: He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in Him who sent me, so that no one would imagine that he meant to imply the Father as the Father of many children regenerated by grace and not as the Father of the only Word equal to Him, he immediately added: And whoever sees me, sees Him who sent me. Does he say, perhaps, that he who sees me does not see me, but sees Him who sent me, just as He had said: He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in Him who sent me)? He said this so that he would not be considered only the son of man, as he appeared; and He said this so that it would be believed that He was equal to the Father. And thus he says: Whoever believes in me, does not believe in what he sees in me with his eyes, but in Him who sent me. But when you believe in the Father, who begot me equal to Him, you must believe in me, not according to what you see in me with your eyes, but as you believe in Him who sent me; because to such an extent there is no difference between me and Him, that whoever sees me sees omnes (ibid. 10,34): propterea dixit, Qui credit in me, non cred-it in me; ne totum quod of Christo creditur, secundum hominem crederetur. Ule ergo, inquit, credit in me, qui non credit in me secundum id quod me videt, sed in eum qui me misit: ut cum credit in Patrem, credat eum habere Filium sibi aequalem, et tune veré credat in me. Nam si putaverit eum non habere nisi filios secundum gratiam, qui sunt eius utique creatura, non Verbum, sed facta per Verbum, nec habere Filium aequalem sibi atque coaeternum, semper natum, pariter incommutabilem, ex nullo dissimilem atque imparem; non credit in Patrem qui eum misit, quia non est hoc Pater qui eum misit. 3.

Et ideo cum dixisset, Qui credit in me, non credit in me, sed in eum qui misit me; ne putaretur sic voluisse Patrem intelligi tanquam Patrem multorum filiorum per gratiam regeneratorum, non unici Verbi aequalis sibi, continuo subiecit, Et qui videt me, videt eum qui misit me. He. Certainly Christ sent his apostles, because just as those called in Greek angels are called ambassadors in Latin, those called in Greek apostles are called envoys in Latin. And no doubt it occurred to none of the apostles to say: He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in Him who sent me. In no way would I say: Whoever believes in me; Well, we believe the apostle, but we believe in the apostle, because it is not the apostle who justifies the wicked. But whoever believes in him who justifies the wicked, his faith is considered righteousness. The apostle could say: He who receives me, receives Him who sent me; or: He who hears me, hears Him who sent me; for this is what the Lord Himself said to them: Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives Him who sent me, since the Lord is honored in the servant, and the father in the son; but as seeing the father in the son and the master in the servant. On the other hand, the only begotten Son could well have said: Believe in God and believe also in me; and as he now says: He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in Him who sent me. He did not take away the believer's faith in Him, but He did not want the believer to stand in the form of a servant; for whoever believes in the Father, who sent him, certainly believes in the Son, without whom he knows that the Father cannot exist, and believes in Him as equal to the Father, according to what follows: And whoever sees me sees Him who sent me. 4. Apostólos suos cene ipse Dominus Christus misit, quod eorum etiam nomen indicat: nam sicut gtaece angelí, latine nuntii vocantur, ita graece apostoli, latine missi appellantur. Nunquam tamen aliquis apostolorum dicere auderet, Qui credit in me, non credit in me, sed in eum qui misit ine: omnino enim non diceret, Qui credit in me. Credimus enim apostólo, sed non credimus in apostolum: non enim apostolus iustificat impium. Credentí autem in eum qui iustificat impium, deputatur fides eius ad iustitiam (Rom 4:5). Posset dicere apostolus, Qui tecipit me, recipit eum qui me misit; ve!, Qui audit me, audit eum qui me misit: hoc enim eis ipse Dominus ait, Qui vos recipit, me recipit, et qui recipit me, recipit eum qui me misit (Mt 10,40). Quia dominus honoratur in servo, et pater in filio: sed pater tanquam in filio, dominus tanquam in servo.

In another place he said to his disciples: You are the light of the world; A city built on the top of a mountain cannot be hidden, nor is a candle lit to put it under the bushel, but rather on the lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house; Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. He did not say to them: You, who are the light, have come into the world so that whoever believes in you may not remain in darkness. And I assure you that you will not read this anywhere. All the saints are candles, kindled in Him by faith, which are extinguished when they depart from Him. But the light that gives them light cannot be separated from itself, because it is immutable. We believe, therefore, in the lighted candles, such as the prophets and the apostles; But we give them faith in such a way that we do not believe in the same illuminated candle, but through it we believe in that light that illuminates them, so that we too may be illuminated, not by them, but with them by that light from which they receive theirs. And by saying that he came so that everyone who believes in me would not remain in darkness, he clearly states that he found everyone wrapped in darkness; But, so that they do not remain in the darkness in which they were found, they must believe in the light that came into the world, because by it the world was made. 5. And if anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him. Remember what you have heard in previous lessons, and if you have forgotten it, remember it; and those of you who were not present and are now present, observe that the Son says: I am lux mundi. Non potest civitas abscondi super montem constituía, ñeque accendunt luzernam, et ponunt eam sub modio, sed super candelabrum, ut luzat ómnibus qui in domo sunt: sic luzat lumen vestrum coram hominibus, ut videant opera vestra bona, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in caeüs est (Mt 5,14-16): non tamen eis dixit, Vos lux venistis in mundum, ut omnis qui credit in vos, in tenebris non maneat. Nusquam hoc legi posse confirmed. Lumina ergo sunt omnes sancti; sed credendo ab eo illuminantur, a quo si quis recesserit tenebrabitur. Lumen autem illud quo illuminatur, a se recedere non potest; quia in commutabile omnino est.

Credimus ergo lumini illuminato, sicut prophetae, sicut apostólo: sed ideo illi credimus, ut non in ipsum credamus quod illuminatur, sed cum illo credamus in illud lumen a quo illuminatur; ut et nos illuminemur, non ab illo, sed cum illo a quo ille. Cum autem dicit, Ut omnis qui credit in me, in tenebris non maneat; satis manifestat omnes se in tenebris invenisse: sed ne in eis tenebris maneant in quibus inventi sunt, debent credere in luzem quae venit in mundum, quia per illam factus est mundus. 5. Et si quis audierit, inquit, verba mea, et non custodierit, ego non iudico eum. Mementote quae vos audisse in superioribus lectionibus novi; et qui obliti forte estis, recolite; et qui non adfuistis, sed adestis, audite quomodo dicit Filius, Ego non iudico eum; cum dicat alio loco.

I do not judge him, having said in another place: The Father judges no one, but gave all judgment to the Son. But it must be understood that I do not judge him NOW. Why don't you judge now? I have not come, he says, to judge the world, but to save it, that is, to make it saved. Now is the time of mercy, later will be the time of judgment; for I will praise your mercy and your judgment, O Lord! 6. Now see what it says about the last judgment that is to come: He who despises me and does not receive my words will find someone to judge him; The word that I have preached will be your judge on the last day. It does not say: Whoever despises me and does not listen to my words, I do not judge on the last day; Because, if I had said this, I don't see how I would fail to be contrary to that sentence: The Father judges no one, but he gave all judgment to the Son. But having said: Whoever despises me and does not receive my words, has someone to judge him; and for those who were waiting to know who that judge was, he added: The doctrine that I have preached, that will judge him on the last day, with which he clearly stated that he himself will judge on the last day. Because He has preached Himself, He has announced Himself, He has made Himself a door through which the shepherd must enter his sheep. Those who did not hear him will be judged in one way and those who heard him and despised him in a different way. Those who sinned outside the law, says the Apostle, will be judged outside the law; but those who have sinned in the law will be judged by the law. 7. I have not spoken, he says, on my own behalf. And Pater non iudicat quemquam, sed omne iudicium dedil Filio says (lo 5,22): nisi quia intelligendum est, Modo non iudico eum. Quare non iudicat moda? Attende quid sequitur: Non enim veni, inquit, ut iudicem mundum, sed ut salvificem mundum: id est ut salvum faciam mundum. Nunc ergo est tempus miseticordiae, post etit iudicii: quia, Misericordiam, inquit, et iudicium cantabo tibí, Domine (Ps 100,1). 6. Sed de ipso etiam future novissimo iudicio videte quid dicat: Qui sper-nit me et non accipit verba mea, hahet qui iudicet eum: sermo quera locutus sum, Ule iudicabit eum in novissimo die. Non ait, Qui spetnit me, et non accipit verba mea, ego non iudico eum in novissimo die. Hoc enim si dixisset, non video quomodo posset non esse contiarium illi sententiae ubi ait, Pater non iudicat quemquam, sed omne iudicium dedit Filio.

Cum vero dixit, Qui spernit me, et non accipit verba mea, habet qui iudicet eum; exspectantibus autem quisnam Ule esset, secutus adiunxit, Sermo quem locutus sum, Me iudicabit eum in novissimo die: satis manifestavit semetipsum iudkatutum in novissimo die. Seipsum quippe locutus est, seipsum annuntiavit, seipsum ianuam posuit, qua ipse ad oves pastor intraret. Alitet itaque iudicábuntur qui non audietunt, alitet qui audietunt et contempseiunt. Who enim without? Lege peccaverunt, ait Apostolus, sine Lege et peribnnt: et qui in Lege peccaterunt, per Legem iudicábuntur (Rom 2,12). 7. Quia ego, inquit, ex meipso non snra locfítus. Who is not filled with amazement when they see their feet washed by the Son of God? And although it was a sign of reckless audacity for the servant to resist the Lord, the man to resist God, Peter nevertheless preferred to do so rather than consent to his Lord and God washing his feet. Nor should we think that, the other disciples having previously tolerated it with pleasure, or at least with equal spirit, only Peter among them all trembled and rejected it, since this seems the most obvious meaning of the evangelist's words, because when he said: He began to wash the feet of the disciples and wipe them with the towel that he tied, adding later: He came to Simon Peter, it seems that he had already washed some and that after them he came to the first. For who ternum periret, nisi illum Deus humilis inveniret. Venit enim Filius hominis quaerere et salvum faceré quod perierat (Luke 19:10). Perierat autem superbiam deceptoris secutus, ergo humilitatem Redemptoris sequatur inventus.

Jesus says to him: He who is clean has no need to wash other than his feet, and everything is clean. Someone may say: If everything is clean, what need does he have to even wash his feet? But the Lord knew well what he was saying, although our weakness cannot penetrate his secrets. However, according to what He deigns to teach us with His words and with those of His Law, and according to my limited scope, I too, with His help, am going to say something about this profound question; and first of all I am going to demonstrate very easily that there is no contradiction in this phrase. Who cannot say with all correctness: Everything is clean except his feet? It would be more elegant to say: Everything is clean except the feet; which is the same. And this is what the Lord says: He only needs to wash his feet, and everything is clean. Everything except the feet, or perhaps the feet, which needs to be washed. 4. What does this mean? Our feet are washed daily by the one who interposes his help on our behalf, and it is necessary for us to wash our feet daily, that is, to straighten the paths of our spiritual steps, as we confess in the Sunday prayer: Forgive us our debts, just as we forgive our debtors. Thus, then, the Church, washed by Christ with water and his word, appears without stains or wrinkles, not only in those who, after receiving baptism, are immediately caught up in the contagion of this life, nor do they set foot on the earth so as not to have the need to wash their feet, but also in those whom the mercy of the Lord brought out of this world with clean feet. But in all those who live here, even if it is clean, because they live in righteousness, they nevertheless need to wash their feet, because they are not exempt from sin. This is why the Song of Songs says: I have washed my feet, how can I defile them again? And he says this because, having to go to Christ, he is forced to step on the earth to go. From here arises another difficulty. Isn't Christ up there? Has he not ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father? Is she afraid of getting her feet dirty when the one who washed the feet of her disciples comes to her? And so he could have said: He who receives the one I send receives me, as a man; and whoever receives me, as God, receives Him who sent me. But with these words he did not intend to imply the unity of nature, but rather to declare the authority of the messenger, so that, upon receiving him, he is considered the person of the one who sent him. If you look at Christ in Peter, you will find the disciple's Master; and if you look to the Father in the Son, you will find the Begetter of the Only Begotten; and in this way, without fear of making a mistake, you receive in the messenger the person of the sender. The following words of the Gospel cannot be submitted to the brevity of time. Therefore, dear brothers, if this sermon, or delicacy of the holy sheep, is sufficient, take it with health; and if it is scarce, ruminate on it with appetite.

The question that St. John's Gospel proposes to us is no small matter, brothers, when it says: Having said verborum regula, qua dictum est, Qui accipit si quem misero, me accipit, ut unius naturae sit Filius et apostolus. Posset quidem non ínconvenienter et hoc intelligi, quoniam geminae est ille gigas substantiae, qui exsultavit ad currendam viam (Ps 17,6): Verbum enim caro factum est (lo 1,14), hoc est, Deus homo factus est. Proinde ita dixisse posset videri, Qui accipit si quem misero, me accipit secundum hominem: Qui autem me secundum Deum accipit, accipit eum qui me misit. Sed cum ista dicebat, non ab illo naturae unitas; sed in eo qui mittitur, mittentis commendabatur auctoritas. Sic itaque eum qui missus est unusquisque accipiat, ut in illo eum qui misit attendat. If ergo you attend Christum in Petro, invenies discipuli praeceptorem; si autem atiendas Patrem in Filio, invenies Unigeniti Genitorem: ac sic in eo qui missus est, sine uUo accipis errore mittentem. 2. He who has the power to give his life and to take it back was troubled. Is it that such a great power is disturbed, the firmness of the stone is disturbed, or rather is it our weakness that is disturbed? That's how it is. Do not let your servants have unworthy thoughts about their Lord, but rather recognize yourselves as members in your head. He who died for us is also troubled for us. He who died by his power was also troubled by his power. He who transfigured the body of our weakness, making it take on the form of his glory, also transfigured in himself the affection of our weakness, having compassion on us because of the affection of his heart. And so, when we see the great, the strong, the undefeated, the true troubled, let us not fear for Him, as if He were weakening: He does not perish, He seeks us. He seeks us, and only us, in this way; We must see ourselves in their confusion, so as not to despair when we see ourselves disturbed. When someone is disturbed who is not disturbed except when he wants to, it is the consolation of those who are disturbed even without wanting it. 3. Let the arguments of the philosophers who deny the disturbances in the souls of the wise fall to the ground, for God turned the wisdom of this world into foolishness, and God knew that the thoughts of men are full of vanity. Certainly the soul of the Christian is disturbed, not by misery, but by mercy; He fears that men will be lost to Christ; He is saddened when someone dies for Christ; He wants everyone to turn to Christ; it rejoices when they return to Christ; He fears losing Christ; He is saddened by living far from Christ; longs

reign with Christ and rejoices in the hope of reigning with Christ. These are the four so-called disturbances of the soul: fear, sadness, love and joy. Let Christian souls have them for reasonable reasons, without paying attention to the gossip of the Stoics or other similar philosophers, who, just as they call vanity truth, call dullness health, ignoring that illness is more hopeless, both of the soul and of any member of the body, when it becomes insensitive to pain. 4. Perhaps someone will ask if the Christian's spirit should also be disturbed by the imminence of death. How, then, do we explain the Apostle's desire to dissolve himself to be with Christ, if what he desires can cause him confusion when it presents itself? Easy is the answer for those who call joy a disturbance. What is there to say about someone who is disturbed by the imminence of death because he rejoices in its proximity? But this, they say, should be called joy, not joy. This is nothing more than experiencing the same sensations and giving them different names. Meanwhile, let us listen to the Sacred Letters and, according to them, resolve this question with the help of God. But when reading these words: When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit, let us not say that he was troubled with joy, so as not to see ourselves confused by Him with these words: My soul is sad to the point of death. Well, a similar thing must be understood on this occasion, when Jesus was troubled in spirit when he saw his betrayer leaving alone to return later with his group.

5. Christians are very brave, if there are some who are not disturbed at the sight of death; but are they braver than Christ? Who, no matter how crazy, would dare to say such a thing? Why, then, was He troubled except to console the weak members of His body, which is the Church, with the voluntary likeness of His weakness, so that, if any of His people are troubled in spirit at the imminence of death, they might fix their eyes on Him so as not to be surprised by the most unhappy death of despair, considering themselves condemned by feeling such disturbance? How much good from the participation of his divinity must we not desire and hope, who are calmed by his confusion and strengthened by his weakness? Whether, then, on this occasion he was disturbed by compassion for Judas, who was lost; Because of the proximity of his death, it is beyond any doubt that He was troubled not by his weakness, but by his power, so that desperation to save ourselves does not arise in us when, not because of strength, but because of weakness, we are troubled. He carried upon himself the weakness of the flesh, which was to disappear with the resurrection. But he who was not only man, but also God, in strength of spirit surpasses the entire human race by an ineffable distance. And thus, his confusion was not forced by anyone, but He troubled Himself, as it was expressly said of Him when He raised Lazarus, since that is where it is said that He troubled Himself, so that in this sense it is understood when it is read that He was troubled, although it is not expressed so clearly. What does it mean, then, that one of you will betray me, but that one must come out from among you who will betray me? One of his disciples was lying on the bosom of Jesus, the one whom Jesus loved. What the breast was, he declares shortly afterwards, when he says: On the breast of Jesus. It is John himself, author of this gospel, as he later states. It was the custom of those who transmitted the Sacred Letters to us that, when one of them narrated the acts of the Lord and himself intervened, they spoke of him as a third party, introducing himself into the order of the narration as a writer of the facts and not as a preacher of himself. This is what Saint Matthew did, who, having to name himself in the text of the narrative, says: He saw a publican sitting at the counter, by the name of Matthew, and he said to him: Follow me. It does not say: He saw me and told me. Moses also did so, telling everything about him as if it were someone else's, saying: The Lord said to Moses. A less common twist is used by Saint Paul, not in the historical part, in which he explains the events he narrates, but in his epistle, where he says: I know that a man in Christ fourteen years ago (whether in the body or out of the body, I do not know, God knows), this one was caught up to the third heaven. Thus, then, in the fact that the holy evangelist did not say: I was reclining in the bosom of Jesus; but dihuman alterum de alter stimularet infirmitas. Note quidem sibi erat cuiusque conscientia; verumtamen quia proximi erat ignota, ita sibi unusquisque erat certus, ut incerti essent et in caeteris singuli, et in singulis caeteri. 4. But, since I am completely like Him, now you know Him by knowing me; and you have seen Him if with the eyes of your soul you have seen me.

Nonne ipse dixerat, Et quo ego vado scitis, et viam satis; et se nescire dicentes, eos haec scire convicerat, addendo atque dicendo, Ego sum via, veritas et vita? Quomodo nunc dicit, Tanto tempore vobiscum sum, et non cognovistis me? cum profecto, et quo iret, et viam scirent, non ob aliud nisi quod ipsum utique scirent? Sed facile ista solvitur quaestio, si dicamus quod eum aliqui eorum sciebant, aliqui nesciebant, atque in his qui nesciebant et Philippus erat: ut quod ait, Et quo ego vado scitis, et viam scitis, illis dixisse intelligatur qui sciebant; non Philippo cui dictum est, Tanto tempore vobiscum sum, et non cognovistis me, Philippe? Hic ergo qui Filium iam noverant, etiam illud de Patre dictum est, Et amodo cognoscetis eum, et vidistis eum: dictum est enim propter omnimodam similarityinem quae illi cum Patre est, ut ideo amodo dicerentur nosse Patrem, quia noverant similem Filium. Ergo iam sciebant Filium, etsi non omnes, certe quidam eorum quibus dicitur, Et quo vado scitis, et viam scitis: ipse est enim via. Sed Patrem nesciebat, ideo audiunt, Si cognovistis me, et Patrem meum cognovistis: per me utique et illum. Alius enim ego sum, alius ille. Sed ne putarent dissimilem, Et amodo, inquit, cognoscetis eum, et vidistis eum. Viderunt enim eius simillimum Filium, sed admonendi fuerant talem esse etiam Patrem quem nondum videbant, qualis est Filius quem videbant. et

ad hoc valet quod postea Philippo dicitur, Qui videt me, videt et Patrem. Non quod ipse esset Pater et Filius, quod in Sabellianis, qui vocantur etiam Patripassiani, catholica fides damnat: sed quod tam similes sint Pater et Filius, ut qui unum noverit, both noverit. Solemus enim de simillimis duobus ita loqui eis qni unum illonim vident, et qualis est alius volunt nosse, ut dicamus: Vidistis istum, illum vidistis. Sic ergo dictum est, Qui me videt et Patrem: non utique ut ipse sit Pater qui Filius, sed quod a Patris similarityine in millo prorsus discrepet Filius. Nam nisi duo essent Pater et Filius, non dictum esset, Si cognovistis me, et Patrem meum cognovistis: Utique enim, quia -tender, inquit, venit ad Patrem, nisi per me; si cognovistis me, et Patrem meum cognovistis: quoniam ego per quem venitur ad Patrem, perducam vos ad eum, ut ipsum etiam cognoscatis. Sed quoniam illi sum omnino simillimus, amodo cognoscetis eum, cum cogtioscitis me: et vidistis eum si oculis cordis vidistis me. 3. Quid ergo est quod dicis, Filippe, Ostende nobis Patrem, et suificit nobis? Tanto, inquit, tempore vobismm sum, ei non cognovistis me, Philippe? Qui videt me, videt et Patrem. Quod si ad te multum est hoc videre, saltem quod non vides hoc crede. Quomodo enim dicis inquit, Ostend nobis Patrem? Si me vidisti qui omnimodo similis sum vidisti illum cui similis sum. Quod videre non potes, non saltem credis qtda ego in Patre, et Pater in me est? Poterat hic dicere Philippus-

3. Why then do you say, Philip: Teach us the Father, and it is enough for us? I have been among you for so long, and you have not known me, Felipe? Whoever sees me, also sees the Father. And if it seems like a lot to you to see, at least believe what you don't see. Well, how do you say: Show us the Father? If you have seen me, who am entirely like, you have seen Him, to whom I am like. And if you cannot see this, at least, do you not believe that I am in the Father and that the Father is in me? to this
About the Gospel of Saint John

Philip could reply: I see you and I believe you are very similar to the Father; But does he deserve to be rebuked who, seeing a similar person, also wants to see the one he resembles? I certainly saw the one that resembles it, but I still don't know one without the other; It is not enough for me until I know the other whom this one resembles. Show us the Father, and it is enough for us. But the Master reproached the disciple, because he saw his heart. Philip wanted to know the Father, as if the Father were better than the Son; and, consequently, he did not know the Son either, believing that there was something better than Him. To correct this belief, he said: Whoever sees me, also sees the Father. Why do you say: Show us the Father? I understand your thinking: you do not intend to see another similar person; You think that one is better. Don't you believe that I am in the Father and that the Father is in me? Why do you look for differences in similar people? Why do you want to know separately those who are inseparable? Next he speaks, not only to Felipe, but in plural, to all of them; things that should not be submitted to the brevity of time, in order to expose them with the appropriate breadth when God is served. Video quidem te, et credo simillimum esse Patti; sed numquid arguendus et obiurgandus est qui cum similem videt, etiam illum cui similis est vult videre? Similem quidem novi, sed adhuc alterum sine altero novi; non mihi sufficit, nisi et illum cuius est iste similis noverim. Ostend ¡taque nobis Patrem, et sufficit nobis. Sed ideo magister discipulum arguebat, quoniam cor postulantis videbat. Tanquam enim melior esset Pater quam Filius, ita Philippus Patrem nosse cupiebat: et ideo nec Filium sciebat, quo melius esse aliquid credebat. Ad hunc sensum corrigendum dictum est, Qui videt me, videt et Patrem. How do you say, Ostend nobis Patrem? Video quomodo tu dicas: non alterum quaeris videre similem, sed illum putas esse meliorem. Non credis quia ego in Patre, et Pater in me est? Cur in similibus distantiam cupis cerneré? cur inseparabiles separatim desideras nosse? Deinde non ad solum Philippum, sed ad eos pluraliter loquitur, quae non sunt in anguishes coarctanda, ut adiuvante ipso diligentius exponantur.

1. Listen, dear ones, with your ears and receive in your souls, through the words we address to you, the teachings of Him who does not depart from us. According to the reading you have just heard, the Lord says: The words that I speak to you, I do not speak of myself. The Father, who is in me, He does the works. So, are words works? That's really it. Because he who edifies his neighbor with his words does a good work. But what does it mean: I do not speak of myself, but I, who speak, do not come from myself? The works that He does, He attributes to Him from whom the one who does them comes. For God the Father does not come from another, and the Son is true God equal to the Father, but he is God who comes from the Father. For this reason the Father is God, not of God; and light, not of light; but the Son is God from God, light from light. 2. Because of these two sentences, one that says: I do not speak of myself, and another that is: The Father, who remains in me, He does the works, and by considering them independently, various heretics have arisen, contrary to us, who, without having a common starting point and addressing contrary points, go outside the orbit of the truth. Because they say

1. Audite auribus, accipite mentibus, dilectissimi, Ioquentibus quidem nobis, sed ipso docenta qui non recedit a nobis. Dominus dicit, quod moda cum legeretur audistis, Yerba quae ego loquor vobis, a •meipso non loquor: Pater autem in me ma-nens ipse facil opera. Ergo et verba opera sunt? Plan ita est. Nam profecto qui proximum loquendo aedificat, bonuro opus operatur. Sed quid est, a meipso non loquor, nisi, a meipso non sum qui loquor? Ei quippe tribuit quod facit, de quo est ipse qui facit. Pater enim Deus non est de aliquo, Filius autem Deus est quidem Patri aequalis, thirst for Patre Deo. Ideo ille Deus, sed non de Deo; et lumen, sed non de Lumine: iste vero Deus de Deo, lumen de lumine. 2. Nam in his duabus sententiis, una qua dictum est, Nom a meipso loquor: alia qua dictum est, Pater autem in me manens, ipse facit opera: singulas tenentes, diversi nobis adversantur tiaeretici, qui non ex una parte, sed in contiaiia cenantes, a via veiitatis exorbitant. Aiiarri quippe dicunt: Ecce inaequalis est Patri EiLius, a seipso non loquitur. Dicunt
