Arians: The Son is not equal to the Father, since he does not speak about himself. The Sabellians or Patripasians, on the contrary, say: Here we have that the Father and the Son are the same person, because what does it mean: The Father, who abides in me, He does the works, but that I, who do the works, abide in me? You say contrary things, but not in the way that a false thing is contrary to the truth, but as two falsehoods contrary to each other. Wrong, you go in opposite directions, leaving in your midst the path that you have abandoned. There is a greater distance between you than there is between you and the path from which you are deserters. One from there and the other from there, both come here. Do not pass by one another, but from there and from there come both to us. You Sabellians, admit him whom you reject, and you, Arians, equal him whom you put below, and with us you will walk on the path of truth. There is one thing in both of you that you must mutually warn each other. Listen, Sabellian: To such an extent one is the Father and another is the Son, that the Arian affirms that he is not equal to the Father. Listen, Arian: To such a point is the Son equal to the Father, that the Sabellian claims that he is the same Father. You add to the one you take away, and the other equals the one you decrease, and both of you will be with us; because neither you take away nor the other diminishes Him Who is different from the Father, to convince the Sabellian, and Who is equal to the Father, to convince the Arian. To both he says: I and the Father are one. Listen to the Arians: only one thing; and listen to the Sabellians: we are. And not Sabelliani contra, id est Patripassiani: Ecce qui Pater est ipse et Filius; quid enim est, Pater in me manens, ipse facit opera, nisi, in me maneo ego qui fació? Contraria dicitis: sed non eo moda sicut est falsum contrarium vero, sed sicut sunt inter se duo false contraria. Errando in diverse istis, in medio est via quam reliquistis. inter vos ipsos longiore intervallo separati estis, quam ab ipsa via cuius desertores estis. Vos hinc, vos autem illinc, huc venite: alteri ad alteros traniré nolite, sed hinc atque illinc ad nos coming, invicem vos invenite.

Sabelliani, agnoscite quem praetermittitis; Ariani, aequate quem subditis, et in via vera nobiscum ambulabitis. Est enim quod invicem ex vobis alteri ex alteris admoneri utrique debenatis. Audi, saberliane: usque adeo non ipse Pater, sed alter est Filius, ut eum atianus inaequalem asserat Patri. Audi, ariane: usque adeo Filius aequalis est Patri, ut sepallianus eumdem esse dicat et Patrem. Tu adde quem tollis, tu adimple quem minuis, et nobiscum ambo consistitis: quia nec tu tollis, nec tu minuis eum qui et alter est a Patre, ut convincas sepallianum, et aequalis Patri, ut convincas arianum. Utrisque enim clamat, Ego et Pater unum sumus (lo 10,30). Quod ait, unum, audiant Ariani; quod ait, sumus, audiant Sabelliani: et nec illi aequalem, nec illi alterum negando sint vani. Si ergo quoniam dixit, Verba quae ego loquor vobis, a meipso non loquor,
About the Gospel of Saint John

Let them be fools, denying the former equality, and the latter the difference. But if because he said: The words that I speak, I do not speak of myself, it might seem that in his power he is so unequal that he cannot do what he wants, listen to these others: Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom He wills. Likewise, if because He said: The Father, who abides in me, Himself does the works, it is judged that there is not one Father and another the Son, note this other passage: Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. And so, not one thing is understood twice, but two things are understood. But since one is equal to the other, that one proceeds from the other, therefore he does not speak of himself, because he is not of himself; and for this reason the Father, who abides in Him, does works, because He for whom and with whom He does them comes only from Himself. Then he adds: Do you not believe that I am in the Father and that the Father is in me? Believe it at least for the works. Previously only Felipe was rebuked, but now he states that it was not him alone. By the same works believe that I am in the Father and that the Father is in me, because, if we were separated, it would be impossible for us to act inseparably. 3- But what do the following words mean: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will do the works that I do, and he will do them greater than these, because I am going to the Father. And whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do it; so that the Father may be glorified in the Son; if you ask anything in my name, I will do it?" So, then, he promised that he himself would do those greater works. Let not the servant rise above his Sepropterea putatur usque adeo imparis potestatis, ut non quod ipse vult faciat; audiatur quod dixit, Sicut Pater suscitat mortuos et vivificat, sic et Filius quos vult vivificat. item si quoniam dixit, Pater in me manens, ipse facit opera, propterea putatur non alius esse Pater, alius ipse; audiatur quod dixit, Quaecumque Pater facit, haec et Filius similiter facit (Ibid., 5,21.19); et intelligatur non bis unus, sed duo unum.

Verum quia sic aequalis alter alteri, ut tamen altet ex altero, ideo non loquitur a semetipso, quia non est a seipso: et ideo Pater in illo manens facit opera ipse, quia per quem et eum quo facit, noh ¿st nisi ab ipso. Denique adiungit, et dicit: Non creiiüs quia ego in Patre, et Pater in me est? Alioquin propter operates ipsa credite. Antea solus Philippus arguebatur, nunc autem non ibi eum solum Fuisse qui esset arguendus ostenditur. Propter opera, inquit, ipsa credite quia ego in Patre, et Pater in me est: ñeque enim si separati essemus, insepatabiliter operani ulla ratione possemus. 3. Sed quid est quod sequitur, "Amen, amen dico vobis, qui credit in me, opera quae ego fació, et ipse faciet, et maiora horum faciet; quia ego ad Patrem vado: et quaecumque petieritis in nomine meo, haec faciam. Ut glorificetur Pater in Filio, si quid petieritis in nomine meo, hoc faciam". Ergo et illa maiora opera seipsum facturus esse promisit. Non se extollat servus supta Dominnm, et discipulus su-
About the Gospel of Saint John

lord, nor the disciple over his Master. He says that they will do greater works than His, but He will do them in them and through them, and not them for themselves. Praise is directed to Him: I will love You, Lord, who are my strength, And what are those greatest works? Did his shadow, as it passed, heal the sick? Well, it is a greater miracle to heal with the shadow than with the contact of the fiber of the dress. This He did Himself; that, for them; But He did both. However, when He said this, He was referring to the works of His words; for he had said: The words that I speak to you, I do not speak of myself; but the Father, who abides in me, He does the works. What works was he referring to if not the words he spoke? They heard and believed, and faith was the fruit of those words; But with the preaching of the disciples, not a few, as they were, but entire peoples believed. And these are, without a doubt, major works. And it is noteworthy that he does not say: You will do greater things than these, as if implying that only the apostles would do them, but he said: He who believes in me will do the works that I do, and will do them greater than these. So whoever believes in Christ does the things that He did or greater than the things that Christ did? This should not be treated lightly nor done hastily in haste; That is why today's talk, which we are going to close, requires its postponement. pra magistrum (Ibid., 13,16): maiora quam ipse facit, dicit eos esse facturos; sed in eis vel per eos se faciente, non ipsis tanquam ex seipsis. Ei quippe cantatur, Diligam te, Domine, virtus mea (Ps 17,2). Sed quae sunt tandem ista maiora? An forte quod aegros ipsis transeuntibus, etiam eorum umbra sanabat? (Acts 5,15). Maius est enim ut sanet umbra quam fimbria (Mt 14:36). Illud per se, hoc per ipsos; sed tamen utrumque ipse. Verumtamen quando ista dicebat, verborum suorum opera commendabat: sic enim dixerat, Verba quae ego loquor vobis, a meipso non loquor; Pater autem in me manens, ipse facit opera. Quae opera tune dicebat, nisi verba quae loquebatur? Audiebant et credebant illi, et eorumdem verborum fructus erat fides illorum: verumtamen evangelizanribus discipulis, non tam pauci quam illi erat, sed gentes etiam crediderunt; haec sunt sine dubitatione maiora.

Nec tamen ait, Maiora horum facietis, ut solos Apostólos ea putaremus esse facturos; sed, Qui credit in me, inquit, opera quae ego jacio, et ipse faciet, et maiora horum faciet. Itane quicumque credit in Christum, facit quae Christus, vel maiora quam Christus? Non praetereunter ista tractanda sunt, nec debent festinatione praecipitari; sed ea cogit concludingus iam sermo iste differri.
On the Gospel of Saint John TREATISE
ON THE SAME PASSAGE

1. What these words of the Lord mean and how these words of the Lord should be understood: He who believes in me will do the works that I do, it is not easy to understand; and although this was very difficult to understand, he added something more difficult: And it will make them even greater. What is this? We could not find anyone who could do the things that Christ did, and will we find anyone who can do them greater than Him? We already said in yesterday's explanation that it was a greater miracle to heal the sick with the shadow, as they passed by, done by the disciples, than to heal them with touch, as the Lord did; And since there were many more who believed in the preaching of the apostles than in that of the Lord Himself, done through His own mouth, these works seem much greater, not because the disciple was greater than the Master, or the servant greater than the Lord, or the adopted son greater than the Only Begotten, or the man greater than God, but because for them He who in another place told them: Without me you can do nothing deigned to do those greater works. For He, overlooking others, which are innumerable, created them without them, without them He made this world, and without them He made Himself when He also deigned to become a man. What can they do without Him more than sin? And immediately he started
IN EAMDEM LECTrONEM

1. Quid sibi velit, et quomodo accipiendum sit quod Dominus ait, Qui credit in me, opera quae ego fació, et ipse faciet, non est fací le comprehendere: et cum hoc ad intelligendum difficillimum sit, adiecit aliud difficilius, Et maiora horum faciet. Quid est hoc? Qui faceret opera quae Christus fecit, non inveniebamus; qui etiam maiora faciet, inventuri sumus? Sed dixeramus sermone prístino quia maius Fuit umbrae suae transitu, quod discipuli fecerunt (Act 5,15), quam fimbriae suae contacto, quod ipse Dominus fecit (Mt 14,36), sanare languentes; et quia plures Apostolis, quam ipso per os proprium praedicante Domino crediderunt: ut haec viderentur opera intelligenda esse maiora: non quo maior esset Magistro discipulus, veL Domino servus, vel adoptus Only begotten, vel homo Deo; sed quod per iJlos ipse dignretur eadem maiora faceré, qui dicit illis alio loco, Sine me nihü potestis faceré (lo 15,5). Ipse quippe, ut alia omitram, quae sunt innumerabilia, sine ipsis fecit eos, sine ipsis fecit hunc muadum; et quia homo etiam ipse fieri dignitus est; sine ipsis fecit et seipsum. Quid autem illi sine ipso, nisi peccatum? Denique et hic id quod de hac te poterat nos moveré, mox abstulit: cum enim dixisset, Qui credit in me, opera quae ego fa-
About the Gospel of Saint John

us every shadow of trouble, because, having said: He who believes in me will do the works that I do, and will do them greater than these, immediately he added: Because I am going to the Father, and whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do it. He who said: He will do, said afterwards: I will do; as if he said: Do not think this is impossible, for he who believes in me cannot be greater than I; but I must then do greater works than those now; greater through him who believes in me than what I do without him. I do them without him and I do them for him; but, when I do them without him, he does not do them; and when I do them through him, although he does not do them by himself, he also does them. Furthermore, doing greater things for him than without him is not a defect, but condescension. What retribution will the servants give to the Lord for all the benefits he has granted them? Especially when, among other goods, he has deigned to grant them the ability to do greater works for them than those he did without them. Didn't that rich man leave sad when he went in search of advice on eternal life? He heard it and rejected it. However, later, what one did not do when he heard it from his mouth, many did when the good Master spoke through the mouth of the disciples. Despicable in the eyes of that rich man, advised by Himself, and lovable to those whom He made poor from rich. See how he did greater works by preaching to believers than by speaking to hearers. 2. But there is still something else. He did these greater works for the apostles, but he does not say, referring only to them: You will do the works that I do, and you will do greater works; but, wanting to include those who would belong to his facio, et ipse faciet, et maiora horum faciet; continuous secutus adiunxit, Quia ego ad Patrem vado, et quaecumque petieritis in nomine meo, haec faciam. Qui dixerat faciet, post ait faciam; tanquam diceret, Non vobis impossibile hoc video: non enim poterit esse maior me qui credit in me, sed ego facturus sum et tune maiora quam nunc; maiora per eum qui credit in me, quam praeter eum per me: ego tamen ipse praeter eum, ego ipse per eum: sed quando praeter eum, non faciet ipse; quando autem per eum, quamvis non per semetipsum, faciet et ipse.

Porro autem maiora faceré per eum quam praeter eum, non est defectio, sed dignitatio. Quid enim retribuant serví Domino, pro omnibus quae retribuit eis? (Ps 115,12). Quandoquidem inter caetera bona etiam hoc eis donare dignitus est, ut maiora faceret per illos quam praeter illos. Nonne ab ore illius dives ille tristis abscessit, quando vitae aeternae consilium quaesivit? (Mt 19,16-22). Audivit, abiecit: et tamen postea quod ab illo auditum non fecit unus, fecerunt multi, eum loqueretur per disciples magister bonus; contemptibilis ei quem divitem per seipsum monuit, amabilis eis quos ex divitibus pauperes per pauperes fecit. Ecce maiora fecit praedicatus a credentibus, quam locutus audientibus. 2. Verum hoc adhuc movet, quod haec maiora per Apostólos fecit: non autem ipsos tantum significans ait, Opera quae ego fació et vos facietis, et maiora horum facietis: sed omnes ad suam familiam perti-
About the Gospel of Saint John

milia, says: He who believes in me will do the works that I do, and he will do them greater than these. Therefore, if he who believes does them, he who does not do them does not believe, as can be deduced from those words: He who loves me keeps my precepts, from which it follows that he who does not keep his precepts does not love him. He also says in another place: Whoever hears these my words and puts them into practice, I will compare him to a wise man, who builds his house on rock; and he who is not like the prudent man, either hears the words and does not observe them or does not even hear them. He who believes in me, he says, will live even if he is dead. The same in this case: He who believes in me will do; Therefore he who does not do, does not believe. What do we say to this, brothers? Should not he who does not do greater works than Christ be considered a believer in Christ? This is hard, absurd, unsustainable, intolerable, if it is not well understood. Let us listen, then, to the Apostle, who says: The faith of one who believes in him who makes the wicked righteous serves for his justification. Having faith, let us do the works of Christ, since believing itself is a work of Christ. He works this in us, but not without us. Listen, then, now how you are to understand it. Whoever believes in me will do the works that I do: first I do them and then he will do them too, because I make him do them. And what works are these except that from a sinner he becomes righteous? 3. And he will make them greater than these. Older than which? Tell me. Will he do works greater than all the works of Christ who works his own salvation with fear and trembling? This la nentes intelligi volens, Qui credit in me, inquit, opera quae ego fació, et ipse faciet, et maiora horum faciet. Si ergo qui credit faciet, non credit utique qui non faciet: sicuti est, Qui diligit me, mandata mea custodit (lo 14,21); unde profecto qui non custodit, non diligit. item alio loco, Qui audit, inquit, verba mea haec et jacit ea, úmilabo eum viro prudenti qui aedificat domum suam supra petram (Mt 7,24): qui ergo non est similis huic viro prudenti, procul dubio aut verba haec audit et non facit, aut omnino nec audit. Qui credit, inquit, in me, licet moriatur, vivet (lo 11,25): qui ergo non vivet, non utique credit. Tale etiam hoc est, Qui credit in me, faciet: non utique credit qui non faciet. Quid est hoc, brothers?

Numquid inter ctedentes in Christum non est computandus, qui non fecetit opera maiora quam Christus? Durum est, absurdum est, ferri non potest: non toleratur nisi intelligatur. Apostoluffl igitur audiamus: Credenti, inquit, in eum qui iustificat impium, deputatur fides eius ad iustitiam (Rom 4,5). In hoc opere faciamus opera Christi, quia et ipsum credere in Christum, opus est Christi. Hoc operatur in nobis, non utique sine nobis. Audi ergo iam, et intellige, Qui credit in me, opera quae ego fació, et ipse faciet: ptius ego fació, deinde et ipse faciet; quia fació ut faciat. Quae opera, nisi ut ex impío iustus fiat? 3. 1. The Savior, highly recommending to his disciples the grace that makes us saved, says: My Father is glorified if you bear much fruit and are my disciples. Whether said glorified or clarified, both verbs have been translated from the Greek doxasein, Doxa, in the Greek language, is equivalent to glory in Latin. I have thought it opportune to tell you this, because the Apostle says that, If Abraham was justified by his works, he has glory, but not meritorious, before God. And therefore the glory that has merit before God is the glory that glorifies not man, but God, if man acquires his justification not by his works, but by faith, so that from God comes the power to do good; because, as I said before, the branch itself cannot produce fruit. If, then, God the Father has his glory in our bearing many fruits and being disciples of Christ, let us not attribute it to our glory, as if we did this for ourselves. The grace is His, and to Him, and not to us, belongs the glory; And so, having said in another place: Let your light shine before men so that they may see your good works, so that they may not attribute those good works to themselves, he added: So that they may give glory to your Father who is in heaven. Because it is the glory of the Father TRACTATUS DE

1. Magis magisque Salvator gratiam, qua salvamur discipulis loquendo commendans: In hoc, inquit, clarifyus est Pater meus, ut fructum plurimum afferatis, et efficiamini mei discipuli. Sive glorificatus sive clarifytus dicatur, ex uno graeco verb utrumque translatum est, quod est Soíjáíjeiv. Aófja enim quae graece dicitur, latine gloria est. Quod ideo commemorandum existimavi, quia dicit Apostolus, If Abraham ex operibus iustificatus est, habet gloriam, sed non ad Deum (Rom 4:2). Haec est ad Deum gloria qua glorificatur non homo, sed Deus, si non ex operibus, sed ex fide iustificatur, ut ex Deo illi sit quod etiam bene operatur: quoniam palmes, sicut iam superius dixi, non potest ferré fructum a semetipso (Tr.81 n.2). Si enim in hoc clarificatus est Deus Pater ut fructum plurimum afferamus, et eficiamur Christi discipuli; non hoc gloriae nostrae tribuamus, tanquam hoc ex nobis ipsis habeamus. Eius est enim haec gratia, et ideo in hoc non nostra, sed eius est gloria. Unde et alibi cum dixisset, Sic luzat lumen vestrum coram hominibus, ut videant opera vestra bona; ne a semetypsis putarent esse bona opera sua, mox addidit, & glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in caelis est

May we bear much fruit and be disciples of Christ. And who makes us disciples of Christ but He who through His mercy came to us? And where should that goodness come from in our works if not from the faith that works through love? How could we love if we were not loved first? This same evangelist says it openly in his epistle: Let us love God, because He loved us first. But when he said: I have loved you as my Father loved me, he did not mean the equality of his nature with ours, as his is with the Father's, but rather the grace of having the man Christ Jesus as mediator between God and men. For as a mediator he manifests himself when he says: To me the Father, and I to you. Because the Father also loves us, but he loves us in Him, since he puts his glory in our bearing much fruit by being united to the vine, that is, to the Son, and becoming his disciples. 3. Abide in my love. In what way? Listen to what follows: If you observe my precepts, you will remain in my love. Is it love that makes its precepts observed or is it the observance of its precepts that makes love? But who doubts that it precedes love? He who does not love has no reason to observe the precepts. Then when saying: If you keep my precepts, (Mt 5,16). In hoc enim glorificatur Pater ut fructum plurimum afferamus, et efficiamur Christi discipuli. A quo efficimur, nisi ab illo cuius mercy praevenit nos? Ipsius enim figmentum sumus, creati in Christo Iesu in operibus bonis (Eph 2,10). 2. you will remain in my love, wants to indicate not the cause of love, but how love manifests itself. As if he were saying: Do not imagine that you remain in my love if you do not keep my precepts; but, if you observe them, you will remain in it; That is to say, it will be known that you remain in my love if you keep my commands, so that no one is deceived by saying that he loves him if he does not keep his precepts, because we love him as long as we keep his commandments, and the less we love him the less diligence we put into the observance of his commands. And although in these words: Abide in my love, it does not appear which love it refers to, whether it is the love with which we love Him or the love with which we love ourselves, it can be clearly deduced from the previous phrase. For, having said: I have loved you, He immediately added: Abide in my love, that is, in the love with which He has loved us. And what does "Abide in my love" mean, if not remain in my grace? What: If you observe my commandments, you will abide in my love, but by this you will know your abiding in the love that I have for you, if you observe my commandments? We do not first keep His precepts so that He may love us, because, if He loves us, we cannot keep His commands. And this is the grace granted to the humble and hidden from the proud. 4. Quamvis quod ait, Manete in dilectione mea, non apparet quam dixerit dilectionem, utrum qua eum diligimus, an qua ipse diligit nos: sed ex verbo superiore dignified. Dixerat quippe, Et ego dilexi vos; cui continuous verb subiunxit, Manete in dilectione mea: illa ergo qua dilexit nos. Quid est ergo, Manete in dilectione mea, nisi, manete in gratia mea?

Et quid est, Si praecepta mea servaveritis, manebitis in dilectione mea, nisi, ex hoc scietis quod in dilectione mea qua vos diligo, manebitis, si praecepta mea servabitis? I have loved you, and having added: Abide in my love, that is, in the love with which I have loved you, in the same way, when saying here of the Father: I remain in his love, the love with which the Father has loved him must be understood. But shall we say that this love is a grace with which the Father loves the Son, as the love with which the Son loves us is grace, since we are children by grace, not by nature, and the Only Begotten is such by nature and not by grace? Should the same be said of the Son with respect to us? That's really it. For, in saying: As the Father loved me, so I have loved you, he manifested the grace of his mediation, since the mediator between God and men is Christ Jesus, not as God, but as man. And as a man it is said of Him: Jesus increased in wisdom, age and grace before God and before men. Accordingly, we can safely say that, although human nature does not belong to the divine nature, it belongs by grace to the person of the only begotten Son of God, and by such grace that there can be no greater nor equal. No merit could precede that union, but from that union all are derived. Therefore, the Son remains in the love with which the Father loves him, and through him he keeps his precepts. Because what is that humanity if not God has taken it for himself? The Word was God; the Only Begotten, coeternal to the Begetter; but, in order to be able to give us a mediator, the Word, by an ineffable grace, became flesh and dwelt among us. 1. You have heard, dear ones, the Lord say to his disciples: These things I have told you so that my joy may be with you, and yours may be filled. What joy can Christ have in us if He does not deign to rejoice with us? What is that our joy that is to be filled, but to have participation with Him? Therefore he had said to the blessed Peter: If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me. His joy in us is the grace he has given us; and that grace is our joy. He already enjoyed this grace from eternity, when he chose us before the formation of the world, without us being able to say that his joy was not complete, since God does not have imperfect things. But that joy was not in us then, because we did not yet exist to have it, nor were we born with it when our existence began. He, on the other hand, always had it, because through his infallible foreknowledge he already enjoyed our future existence. His joy, therefore, of us was already perfect when in his foreknowledge we were destined for existence and predestination. His joy grew when he began the execution of what he had determined to do, because, in this case, he would be happier after having created us. No, brothers; God's happiness was not less without us nor does it receive an increase from us. But that joy of our salvation, which He always had since He foresaw and predestined us, began to be in us when He called us; and we rightly call this joy ours, which will make us happy, and this joy of ours grows and is perfected until it reaches its perfection with perseverance. It begins with the faith of those who are reborn and is fulfilled with the reward of those who are resurrected. Here I believe I find the explanation of these words: I have told you these things so that my joy may be in you, and yours may be filled; May mine be in you, may yours be filled. Because mine was always full, even before you were called, in foreknowledge of your calling; but it is born in you when you realize in you what I had planned for you. May yours be filled, for you will be blessed, which you are not yet, just as you were created, which you were not before. 2. This is my precept: that you love one another as I have loved you. Whether you say precept or command, both words are translations of the same Greek word entole. I had already uttered this phrase before, about which you must remember that I spoke to the best of my ability. Then he said: A new command I give you: that you love one another; As I have loved you, so love one another. The repetition of this mandate is nothing more than a recommendation. Only there it says: A new mandate esse praescivit, gaudium eius, quo beatus est, crevit; alioquin beatior factus est, quia nos fecit. Absit hoc, fratres: Dei beatitudo quia nec minor fuet sine nobis, non fit maior ex nobis. Gaudium igitur eius de salute nostra, quod in illo semper Fuit cum praescivit et praedestinavit nos, coepit esse in nobis quando vocavit nos; et hoc gaudium merit nostrum dicimus, quo et nos beati futuri sumus: sed hoc gaudium nostrum crescit et proficit, et ad suam perfectionem persevering pettendit. Ergo inchoatur in fide renascentium, implebitur in praemio resurgentium. Ecce unde dictum existimo, Haec locutus sum vobis, ut gaudium meum in vobis sit, et gaudium vestrum impleatur: in vobis sit meum; impleatur vestrum.

Semper enim erat meum plenum, et antequam vocaremini, cum vocandi a me praesciremini; sed fit et in vobis, cum hoc efficimini quod praescivi de vobis. Impleatur autem vestrum: quia beati eritis, quod nondum estis; Sicut creati estis qui non fuestis. 2. Hoc est, inquit, praeceptum meum, ut diligatis invicem, sicut dilexis vos. I give you; and here: This is my mandate. There, as if no such mandate had existed before; and here, as if there were no other command from him. There he said new, to get us out of the antiquated, and here he says mine, so that we may hold it in veneration. 3. As for the fact that he said here: This is my command, as if there were no other, will we think, brothers, that this command of the love with which we must love one another is his alone? Isn't there another greater one, which is that we love God? Or did God only give us the precept of love so that we would not worry about others? The Apostle recommends three things to us when he says: These three virtues now remain: faith, hope and charity; but the greatest of them is charity. And, although those two precepts are contained in charity, he has said that it is the greatest, not the only one. Who can enumerate the number of recommendations about faith and hope? But let us notice what the Apostle himself says: The fullness of the Law is charity. What is missing where there is charity? And where there is no charity, what can be of benefit? If you have heard: No one has greater love than he who gives his life for his friends, the conclusion is drawn that the evangelist Saint John himself drew in his epistle, saying that, just as Christ gave his life for us, so we must give ours for our brothers, loving one another as He loved us, who came to give his life for us. How are we to understand that the good servant is a servant and a friend, if he says: I no longer call you servants, because the servant does not know what his master is doing? In such a way he gives them the name of friends, that he withdraws from them the name of servants, not so that both remain in the same person, but that one name replaces the other that is withdrawn. What does this mean? Will we stop being servants when we fulfill the commands of the Lord? Will we stop being servants when we become good servants? But who will dare to go against the Truth, which says: I no longer call you servants? And he points out the reason for his words, saying: Because the servant does not know what his master is doing. Does not the lord entrust his secrets to the good and faithful servant? Why then does he say that the servant is ignorant of what his master does? Suppose it is true, that you ignore what you do, will you stop knowing what burns? For if you ignore this, how can you serve it? Or how can he who serves not be a servant? However, the Lord says: You are my friends, if you do what I command you. I no longer call you servants. Oh prodigy! Since we cannot be servants without fulfilling the precepts of the Lord, how can we stop being servants by fulfilling his commands? If I will not be a servant executing the orders, and if I do not execute the orders, I will not be able to serve; then by serving I will cease to be a servant.

3. Let us understand, brothers, and let us understand. May the Lord grant us to understand it and make us execute what we have understood. If we know this, we know, without a doubt, what the Lord

does; because no one makes us know except the Lord, and that is why we belong to his friends. Just as there are two fears, which form two types of fearful people, so there are two types of bondage, which form two types of servants. There is fear that is cast out by charity, and there is another chaste fear, which remains forever and ever. The Apostle alluded to that fear that is outside of charity when he said: You have not received the spirit of slavery to act again under fear. And he was referring to chaste fear when he said: Do not be conceited, rather fear. In that fear that is cast out by charity, there is also bondage, which with fear will be excluded by charity; for the Apostle put both things together, saying: You did not receive the spirit of bondage again in fear. And the Lord was also referring to the servant who belongs to this servitude when he said: I no longer call you servants, because the servant does not know what his master is doing. This servant is certainly not the one who has chaste love, to whom he says: Very well, good servant, enter into the joy of your Lord, but the servant who has that fear that must be banished by charity, of which he says in another place: The servant does not remain in the house forever, but the son always remains. And since he gave us the power to become children of God, let us be children and not servants, so that by a way that is ineffable, no less than true, we servants can be non-servants, that is, servants with the chaste fear, of which is the servant who enters into the joy of his master, and not servants with the fear that is to be excluded by the house.

And the Apostle himself says that we have been saved by the bath of regeneration; saying in another place that we have been saved in hope and that the hope of things that are seen is not hope, because who hopes to see what they already see? And if we wait for what we do not see, we wait patiently. This is why the apostle Saint Peter says: Now you believe in Him without seeing Him; When you see him, you will have ineffable and glorious joy, receiving the salvation of your souls as a reward for your faith. If, then, now is the time of faith, and the reward of faith is the salvation of our souls, who doubts that we must spend our lives in the faith that works through charity, to receive at the end of time, as a reward, not only the ransom of our bodies, of which Saint Paul speaks, but also the salvation of our souls, which Saint Peter mentions? The happiness of each during this mortal life, more than in reality, lies in hope. But there is a difference between them, and that is that, as the body begins to dissolve, the inner man, that is, the soul, is renewed every day. Just as we expect the future immortality of the flesh and the salvation of souls, although we say that we have already been saved by the pledge received, in the same way we must expect the future knowledge of what the Only Begotten heard from the Father, although Christ has said that he has already communicated it to us. cam sicut et cognitus sum; et nunc per speculum in aenigmate, tune autem jacte ad faciem (1 Cor 13,10.12). 2. You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you. This is that ineffable grace. What were we when we had not yet chosen Criso and that is why we did not love him? Because how can someone who has not chosen him love him? Did we already practice what is said in the Psalm: I preferred to live despised in the house of God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners? Nothing of the sort. What were we, then, but wicked and sinners? We had not yet believed in Him to choose us; because, if he had chosen those who already believed in him, he would have chosen those already chosen. And why would I say: You have not chosen me, if He had not gone ahead of us with His mercy? The vain argument of those who defend the foreknowledge of God against grace is unnecessary, therefore, saying that we were chosen before the formation of the world, because God in his foreknowledge knew that we would be good, not that He had to make us good. He does not say this who says: You have not chosen me. Because, if He had chosen us because He had foreseen that we would be good, He would have also foreseen that we had to first choose Him. Otherwise we could not be good, unless he who does not choose good is called good. Shall we say that he chose those who were not good? For those who would not be good if they had not been chosen were not chosen for being good. Otherwise, grace is no longer grace if we say that merits preceded it. Certainly this election is the effect of grace, of which the Apostle says: Thus are some, reserved by the election of grace. Non vos me elegistis, inquit, sed ego vos chose. Charity, then, is our fruit, which, according to the Apostle, comes from a pure heart, from a right conscience and from a faith without pretense. With this love we love each other and love God, because our love for each other would not be true without the love of God. You love your neighbor as yourself if you love God, because he who does not love God does not love himself either. The entire Law and the Prophets are dependent on these two precepts of charity: this is our fruit. About this fruit he tells us: This is what I command you: that you love one another. Consequently, the Apostle wanting to recommend the fruits of the spirit against the works of the flesh, places charity as a basis: The fruits of the spirit are charity, and then, as emanating from this source and in intimate connection with it, he lists the others, which are: joy, peace, firmness of soul, kindness, goodness, faith, meekness and chastity. And, truly, who can have joy if he does not love the good in which he rejoices? Who can have true peace if they do not have it with someone who truly loves them? Who can have the strength of mind to remain in goodness if it is not for love? Who is benign if he does not love the one he helps? Who becomes good if not for love? Of what benefit can faith be that does not work through charity? What use can there be in meekness if it is not governed by love? Who flees from what can stain him if he does not love what makes him chaste? Remember the words I told you: A servant is not over his master; If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you too, and if they keep my words, they will also keep yours. By saying that the servant is no more than his master, does he not clearly indicate the sense in which we should take what he had previously said: I will no longer call you servants? Well now he calls them servants, because what else does he mean by these words: The servant is not over his master; If they have persecuted me, will they also persecute you? It is, therefore, very clear that when he says: I will no longer call you servants, he refers to the servant who does not remain forever in the house, to the servant who has the fear that casts out charity; and that, when he says here: The servant is not above his master: if they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you, he refers to the servant who belongs to chaste love, which endures forever and ever. This is the servant who will hear: Very well, good servant, enter into the joy of your Lord. 2. But they will do all these things to you for my name's sake, because they have not known Him who sent me. What are all these things except those that he had said before: they will hate you, they will persecute you and they will despise your words? For if they do not keep his words, but do not hate them or persecute them, they would not do all things. But when he says that they will do all these things to you for my name's sake, what does he mean except that in you they will hate me, persecute me, and despise your doctrine because it is mine? And all these things they will do to you for my name's sake,

not for yours, but for mine. Those who do all this for that name are all the more miserable as those who suffer for this name are more blessed, as He Himself said in another place: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice. This is what it means by me or by my name. For, as the Apostle teaches, God made Him wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and our redemption, so that, according to the Scripture, whoever boasts may boast in the Lord. The wicked also do these things to the wicked, but not for the love of justice, and thus both those who do them and those who suffer them are miserable. 1. The Lord had said: He who hates me hates my Father. Because he who hates the Truth must necessarily hate Him from whom the Truth was born; and we have already discussed this according to my possibilities. Then he added these words, which we are now going to discuss: If he had not done works in them that no one else has done, they would not have sin. It is the same great sin that he had mentioned before, when he said: If I had not come and spoken to you, you would have had no sin. It is the sin of not having believed in Him, who spoke and acted; although they were not exempt from all sin before He spoke and acted among them; but he mentions the sin of unbelief, because it contains all the others. If they were exempt from this sin, believing in Him, all others would be forgiven. 2. But why, after saying: If he had not done works among them, did he add that no one else has done it? Deinde addidit unde nobis nunc loquendum est: Si opera non fecissem in eis, quae nemo alius fecit, peccatum non haberent. Peccatum illud scilicet magnum, de quo et superius ait, Si non venissem, et locutus eis Fuissem, peccatum non haberent. Hoc est peccatum quo in eum loquentem et operantem non crediderunt. Ñeque enim nullum habebant peccatum, antequam loqueretur eis et operanetur in eis; sed hoc peccatum quo in eum non crediderunt, ideo sic commemoratur, quia ipso peccato tenentur et caetera. Hoc enim si non haberent, et in eum crederent, dimitterentur et caetera. 2. Sed quid est hoc quod cum dixisset, Si opera non fecissem in eis, mox addidit, quae nemo alius fecit? We may be told that others did things that neither He nor anyone else did. The three young men Ananias, Azariah and Mishael walked unharmed through the flames, which burned and did not burn. 3. Seeing that they are sufficient, I overlook many other miracles performed by some saints, and which no one else has performed. But none of the ancients is read to have cured so many deformities, so many diseases and so many human tortures with a power never equaled. Omitting the innumerable ones that he cured with his word as they appeared, the evangelist Saint Mark says in one place: In the evening, when the sun had already set, they brought to him all the sick and demon-possessed, and the whole city gathered at the door, and he healed many of various diseases and cast out many demons from them. Recounting these events, Saint Matthew wrote down this prophetic testimony: So that what was said by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: He bore our illnesses and took our weaknesses upon Him. And in another place Saint Mark says: And in all the villages, towns and cities where he entered, they placed the sick in the squares and asked to touch even the hem of his dress, and all who touched him saw themselves cured. No one did these things in them. This in them does not mean between them or before them, but in them, because he healed them all. And by these things he wanted to imply that they were not only wonderful things, but that they were manifest healings, to which they should respond with love and not with hatred. But more than all miracles is being born of a virgin, and only He could preserve the integrity of the mother both at being conceived and at birth; but that was not done either in them or in their sight. For the apostles came to the knowledge of the iubendo, sicut occurrebant, salvos singulos fecit; Marcus evangelista quodam loco ait: Vespere autem jacto cuín occidisset sol, ajjerebant ad eum omnes male habentes, et daemonia habentes; eiiciebat (Mark 1,32-34).

Id autem cum commemorasset Matthaeus, etiam testimonium propheticum addidit dice: Ut adimpletetur quod dictum est per Isaiam prophetam dicentem, Ipse injirmitates nostras accepit, et aegrititudines portavit (Mt 8,17). item alio loco dicit Marcus: Et quocumque introibat in vicos, vel in villas, aut in civitates, in piafes ponebant infirmos, et deprecabantur eum ut vel jimbriam vestimenti eius tangerent; et quotquot tangebant eum, salvi jiebant (Mark 6,56). Haec nemo alius fecit in eis. Sic enim intelligendum est quod ait, in eis, non inter eos vel coram eis; sed prorsus in eis, quia sanavit eos. Haec quippe intelligi voluit quae non solum facerent admirationem, verum etiam manifesta conferrent salutem; pro quibus beneficiis utique amorem, non odium retribuere debuerunt. Omnia quidem caeterorum miracula superat, quod est natus ex virgine, matrisque integritatem solus potuit nec conceptus violare nec natus: sed hoc nec coram eis factum est, nec

truth of this miracle not by common appearances, but by discreet learning. All these miracles are surpassed by the fact that three days after the sacrifice of his body he emerged from the tomb alive and with his flesh went to heaven never to die again. And neither was this miracle done among the Jews nor in their presence, nor had it been done even when he said: If he had not done for them things that no one else has done. 4. These, then, are those miracles that he manifested in his numerous healings such as no one had done before in them, and that were wrought in his sight; and this is what he reproaches them, saying: But now they have seen them, and they have hated me and my Father; But what is written in their Law must be fulfilled: That they have hated me gratuitously. He calls the Law his Law, not because they forged it, but because it was given to them; just as we say: Our daily bread, which, nevertheless, we ask of God, saying: Give us this day. He hates gratuitously who does not expect any advantage from his hatred or to avoid any harm. This is how the wicked hate God and this is how the righteous love God, that is, freely, without expecting other goods outside of Him, because He will be all in all. But whoever considers more carefully these words of Christ: If he had not done in them works that no one else has done (and although these works have been done by the Father and the Holy Spirit, no one else has done them, because the substance of the whole Trinity is one), he will realize that Christ himself did what any man of God could have done on some occasion. He can do everything by himself, in eis. Ad cognoscendam quippe huius miraculi veritatem, non communi cum eis aspectu, sed discreet ab eis discipulatu Apostoli pervenerunt. Iamvero illud quod die tertia in carne in qua occisus fuet, de sepulcro se reddidit vivum, et nunquam deinde moriturus cum illa ascendit in caelum, superat etiam cuneta quae fecit: sed ñeque hoc factum est in Iudaeis, ñeque coram eis; et nondum hoc fecerat, quando dicebat, Si opera non jecissem in eis, quae nemo alius fecit. 4. Nimirum ergo sunt illa quae in eorum valetudinibus tanta miracula salutis ostendit, quanta in illis antea nemo donavit: haec enim viderunt, et hoc eis exprobrans adiungit, et dicit, Nunc autem et viderunt, et oderunt et me et Patrem meum: sed ut adimpleatur sermo qui in hege eorum scriptus est, Quia hate habuerunt me gratis.

And having said that they did not know the One who sent him and that, nevertheless, they hated the Son and the Father, that is, the one who was sent and the One who sent him, all of which we have already discussed in previous talks, he comes to say these words: So that what is written in their Law may be fulfilled: that they have freely hated me. And, as a consequence, I add the words that have served as my theme: "When the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, and who proceeds from the Father, He will testify about me, and you will also testify, because you have been with me from the beginning." What do these words have to do with those: "But now they have seen me and have hated me and my Father; but in order that what is written in their Law may be fulfilled: that they have freely hated me"? Is it that, when the Paraclete, who is the Spirit of truth, came, he convinced those who had seen and hated with a more manifest testimony? To better understand it, let's remember the event. On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon one hundred and twenty assembled men, among whom were all the apostles, who, being filled with Him, began to speak in all languages, and many of those who hated, stupefied at such a wonder (because they came to see by the great and divine testimony that Peter gave of Christ, proving that He who, crucified for them, was numbered among the dead, had risen and lived), repentant of heart, they were converted, and obtained forgiveness of that divine blood so impiously and cruelly shed, redeemed by the same blood they had shed. For quo missus est, de quibus omnibus in allus sermonibus iam dissetuimus: ad hoc pervenit ubi ait, Ut adimpleatur sermo qui in Lege eorum scriptus est, Quia odio habuerunt me gratis. Deinde tanquam consequenter adiunxit, unde modo disputare suscepimus: "Cum autem venerit Paracletus quem ego mittam vobis a Patre, Spiritum veritatis qui a Patre proceedit, ille testimonium perhibebit de me; et vos testimonium perhibebitis, quia ab initio mecum estis."

Quid hoc pertinet ad illud quod dixerat, "Nunc autem et viderunt, et oderunt et me et Patrem meum: sed ut impleatur sermo qui in Lege eorum scriptus est, Quia odio habuerunt me gratis?" Because you have been with me from the beginning, you can preach what you know, which you cannot do now, because you do not yet have the fullness of that Spirit. He will therefore bear witness to me, and you will also bear witness, because the charity of God poured into your hearts by the Holy Spirit, who will be given to you, will give you strength to bear that witness. This charity was lacking in Peter when, frightened by the interpellation of that servant woman, he was not able to give true testimony; Before, he was dragged, by the great fear he felt, to deny him three times against what he had promised. Quid sibi ergo vult quod hic ait, Haec autem vobis ab initio non dixi, qttia vobiscum eram: nisi quia ea quae hic dicit de Spiritu sancto, quod sit venturus ad eos et testimonium perhibiturus, quando mala illa passuri sunt, haec ab initio eis non dixit, quia cum ipsis erat? 2.

Consolator ergo ille vel advocatus (utrumque enim interpretatur quod est graece paracletus), Christo abscendent fuet necessarius; et ideo de illo non dixerat ab initio quando cum illis erat, quia eius praesentia consolabantur: abscessurus autem oportebat ut diceret illum esse venturum, per quem futurum erat ut charitate diffusa in cordibus suis verbum Dei cum fiducia praedicarent; et illo intrinsecus apud eos testimonium perhiberent of Christ, ipsi quoque testimonium perhiberent; ñeque scandalizarentur cum inimici Iudaei absque synagogis facerent eos, et interficerent arbitrantes obsequium se praestare Deo: quoniam charitas omnia tolerat (1 Cor 13,7), quae diffundenda erat in cordibus eorum per Spiritus sancti donum (Rom 5,5). Hinc ergo iste totus ducitur sensus, quia facturus eos erat martyres suos, id est testes suos per Spiritum sanctum; util illo in eis operante, persecutionum quaecumque áspera tolerarent, nec frigescerent a charitate praedicandi, illo divino igne succensi. Haec ergo, inquit, locutus sum vobis, ut cum venerit hora eorum, reminiscamini quia ego dixi vobis (lo 16,4). Haec scilicet

I have said not only because you have to suffer all this, but because, when the Paraclete comes, he will bear testimony of me, so that you do not remain silent for fear of these calamities and to make you fearless in giving the same testimony. I have not told you these things from the beginning because I was with you and consoled you with my bodily presence, manifested to your senses so that in your littleness you could understand it. 3. Now I go to Him who sent me, and none of you asks me: Where are you going? He implies that he must leave in such a way that no one has the need to ask, because he will see it clearly with his bodily eyes. They had previously asked him where he was going to go, and he had answered that they couldn't go where they couldn't go then. And now he promises them that he must leave so that no one will have to ask him where he is going. A cloud greeted him when he ascended to heaven, and the disciples, silent, followed him with their eyes. 4. But because I have told you these things, your heart has been filled with sadness. He saw the storm that those words of his were going to raise in their hearts, because, still lacking the spiritual comfort of the Holy Spirit, they were afraid of losing the bodily presence of Christ. And since they knew that Christ spoke the truth, they could not doubt that they would lose him, and that is why their human affections were saddened at being deprived of his carnal presence. He knew well what was most convenient for them, because the interior vision with which He had consolocutus sum vobis, non tantum quia passuri estis ista was much better; sed quia cum venerit paracletus ille, testimonium perhibebit de me, ne ista timenda taceatis, unde fiet ut etiam vos testimonium perhibeatis. Haec autem vobis ab initio non dixi, quia vobiscum eram, et ego vos consolabar mea corporali praesentia, exhibita humanis sensibus vestris, quam parvuli capere poteratis. 3. Nunc autem vado ad eum qui me misit: et nemo, inquit, ex vobis interrogat me, Quo vadis? Significat sic se iturum ut nullus interrogaren quod palam fieri visu corporis cernerunt: nam superius interrogaverant eum quo esset iturus, et responderat eis se iturum quo ipsi tune vinore non possent (lo 13,36). Nunc vero ita se promittit iturum, ut nullus eorum quo vadit interroget. Clouds enim suscepit eum quando ascendit ab eis; et euntem in caelum non verbis quaesierunt, sed oculis deduxerunt (Acts 1:9-11). 4.

Sed quia haec locutus sum vobis, inquit, tristitia implevit cor vestrum. Videbat utique quid illa sua verba in eorum cordibus agerent: spiritualem quippe nondum interius habentes consolationem, quam per Spiritum sanctum fuerant habituri, id quod exterius in Christo videbant amittere metuebant; et quia se amissuros esse illum vera denuntiantem dubitare non poterant, contristabatur humanus affectus, quia carnalis desolabatur aspectus. lar the Holy Spirit, not by bringing a body visible to human eyes, but by infusing Himself into the breasts of believers. Finally, he adds: But I tell you the truth: it is better for you that I go, because if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send it to you. As if to say: It is good for you that this form of servant be separated from you: as the Word, made flesh, I live among you, but I do not want you to continue loving Me with carnal love, and, being content with this milk, you always want to be like children. It is better for you that I go, because if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you. If I do not take away from you the tender delicacies with which I have fed you, you will not desire solid delicacies; If you are carnally attached to the flesh, you will never be capable of the spirit. But what does it mean: If I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; But if I go away, will I send it to you? Couldn't I send it even though I lived here? Who would dare to say such a thing? Because He had not departed from the place where He is, and had come from the Father without leaving the paternal bosom. How, in short, could he not send Him even though He lived here, when we know that at His baptism He came and rested on Him; even more so, when we know that it has always been inseparable? What does it mean then, if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you, but that you cannot have the Spirit of Christ as long as you persist in knowing Christ according to the flesh? For this reason he, who had already received the Spirit, says: Although we had known Christ according to the flesh, but now we no longer know Him in that way. Because he knew the very flesh of Christ, not according to the flesh, when he knew the Word made flesh.

And this the good Master wanted to convey with these words: If I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you. 5. After Christ's bodily departure, not only the Holy Spirit, but also the Father and the Son were with them spiritually. Because, if Christ left so that the Holy Spirit remained with them, not together with Him, but in His place, where is that promise of His: Behold, I am with you until the end of the ages; and that other, when he promises to send them the Holy Spirit to be with them eternally: Shall we come to him and establish our home within him? For this reason, when they have become spiritual from animals and carnal, they will have become more capable of having the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. For it is not to be believed that in anyone there is the Father without the Son and the Holy Spirit, or the Father and the Son without the Holy Spirit, or the Son without the Father and the Holy Spirit, or the Holy Spirit without the Father and the Son, but that where any one of them is, there will be the Trinity, which is one God. It was convenient to make the manifestation of the Trinity in this way, in order to separately inculcate the distinction of persons, even though there is diversity in substance; and thus, those who rightly understand it, can never see separation in natures.

Christo autem discedente corporaliter, non solum Spiritus sanctus, sed et Pater et Filius illis adfuit spiritualiter. Nam si ab eis sic abscessit Christus, ut pro illo, non eum illo in eis esset Spiritus sanctus; ubi est eius promissio dicetis, Ecce ego vobiscum sum usque in consummationem saeculi (Mt 28,20); et, Veniemus ad eum ego et Pater, et mansionem apud eum faciemus (lo 14,23): eum et Spiritum sanctum ita se promiserit esse missurum, ut eum eis esset in aeternum? Ac per hoc eum ex carnalibus vel animalibus essent spirituales futuri, profecto et Patrem et Filium et Spiritum sanctum capacius fuent habituri. In nullo autem credendus est esse Pater sine Filio et Spiritu sancto, aut Pater et Filius sine Spiritu Sancto, aut Filius sine Patre et Spiritu Sancto, aut sine Patre et Filio Spiritus sanctus, aut Pater et Spiritus sanctus sine Filio: sed ubi eorum quilibet unus, ibi Trinitas Deus unus. Oportebat autem ita insinuari Trinitatem, ut quamvis nulla esset diversitas substantiarum, singillatim tamen commendaretur distinctio personarum; ubi eis qui recte intelligunt, nunquam videri potest separatio naturarum. 6. I do in order to sin, in order to justice and in order to judgment: in order to sin, because they do not believe in me; in order to justice, because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me; in order to the judgment, because the prince of this world has already been judged; as if there were no other sin than not believing in Christ; as if the same justice were not seeing Christ; as if the judgment were that the prince of this world, that is, the devil, had already been judged. ABOUT THESE WORDS FROM THE PREVIOUS READING: "WHEN HE COMES, HE WILL ARGUMENT THE WORLD REGARDING SIN, JUSTICE AND JUDGMENT", ETC.

1. When the Lord promised that He would send the Holy Spirit, He says: When He comes, He will accuse the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment. What does this mean? Did not Christ our Lord accuse the world of sin when he said: If I had not come and spoken to you, you would have had no sin; but now his sin has no excuse? And lest there be anyone who says that this refers properly to the Jews and not to the world, does it not say elsewhere: If you were of the world, the world would love what peccato, et de iustitia, et de iudicio: de peccato, quidem, quia non credunt in me; de iustitia vero, quia ad PaPrem vado, et iam non videbitis me; de indicia autem, quia princeps huius mundi iudicatus est (ibid. 16,8-11): tanquam solum sit peccatum non credere in Christum, et tanquam ipsa sit iustitia non videre Christum, et tanquam ipsum sit iudicium quod princeps huius mundi, hoc est diabolus iudicatus est: valde latebrosum esr, nec isto sermone coarctandum, ne fiat obscurius brevitate; sed alio potius quantum Dominus adiuverit explicandum.
LECTIONIS, CUM VENERIT ILLE, PECCATO, ET DE IUSTTIA, ETC.

1. Promittens Dominus missurum se Spiritum sanctum, Cum venerit, inquit, ille arguet mundum de peccato, et de iustitia, et de iudicio. Quid est hoc? Numquidnam Dominus Christus non arguit mundum de peccato, cum ait: Si non venissem, et locutus eis Fuissem, peccatum non haberent; never autem excusationem non habent de sin suo? Sed ne quis forte dicat hoc ad Iudaeos proprie pertinere, non ad mundum; nonne ait alio loco: Si de mundo essetis, mundus quod suum esset di•ligeret? (ibid. 15,22.19). Numquid non arguit de iustitia, ubi ait: Pa-
About the Gospel of Saint John

Does it belong to him? Did he not argue with him about justice when he said: O just Father, the world has not known you? And did I not argue with him about the judgment when he said that he should say to those placed on his left: Go into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels? Many other passages are found in the Gospel in which Christ argues to the world. Why, then, do you attribute this property to the Holy Spirit? Perhaps because Christ spoke only to the Jews, will it seem that he did not argue with the world, as if only he who listens to the arguer is an arguer? On the other hand, it is understood that the Holy Spirit, infused into the hearts of his disciples scattered throughout the world, argues not only with one nation, but with the entire world. When he was about to ascend to heaven, he told them: It is not yours to know the times and moments that the Father reserved for his power; But you will receive power from the Holy Spirit, who will come upon you, and you will serve as my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea, in Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. This is arguing with the world. But who will dare to say that the Holy Spirit speaks to the world through the disciples of Christ and is not Christ himself, the Apostle saying: Do you want to prove the power of Christ, who speaks through my mouth? Christ, then, argues with those whom the Holy Spirit argues. But it seems to me that, since by the Holy Spirit the charity that casts out the fear, which could prevent them from arguing against the world, unleashed in persecutions, was to be poured into their hearts; for this reason he said that He will argue the world; as if he said: El spiller iuste, mundus te non cognovit? (17.25). Numquid non arguit de iudicio, ubi se ait sinistris esse dictutum: he in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo et angelis eius? (Mt 25,41). Et Fine allia reperiuntur in sancto Evangelio, ubi de his Christus arguit mundum. Quid est ergo quod tanquam proprie tribuit hoc Spiritui sancto? An forte, quia Christus in Iudaeorum tantum gente locutus est, mundum non videtur arguisse, ut ille intelligatur argui qui audit arguentem? Spiritus autem sanctus in discipulis eius toto orbe diffusis, non unam gentem intelligitur arguisse, sed mundum.

Nam hoc illis ait ascensurus in caelum: Non est vestrum scire tempora vel momenta, quae Pater posuit in sua potestate; sed accipietis virtutem Spiritus sancti supervenientis in vos, et eritis mihi testes in lerusalem, et in tota ludaea, et in Samaria, et usque in fines terrae (Acts 1,7 et 8). Hoc est arguere mundum. Sed quis audeat dicere quod per disciples Christi arguit mundum Spiritus sanctus, et non arguat ipse Christus; cum clamet Apostolus, An vultis experimentum accipere eius qui in me loquitur Christus? (2 Cor 13:3). Quos ¡taque arguit Spiritus sanctus, arguit utique et Christus. Be quantum mihi videtur, quia per Spiritum sanctum diffundenda erat charitas in cordibus eorum (Rom 5,5), quae foras mittit timorem (1 lo 4,18), quo impedimenti possent ne arguere mundum qui persecutionibus fremebat, auderent; propterea dixit, Ule arguet mundum: tanquam diceret, Ule diffundet in cordibus vestris charitatem; sic enim timote depulso, arguendi
About the Gospel of Saint John

Charity will grow in your hearts, and with it, all fear expelled, you will have greater freedom to argue with the world. I have frequently told you that the works of the Trinity are inseparable, but that one by one the Persons are recommended, so that not only the Unity without separation, but the Trinity without confusion may be understood. 2. Next he explains what is to be understood by justice, sin and judgment. He says: Of sin, because they did not believe in me. He put this sin in preference to the others, as if this one alone existed, because, with this one existing, the others are retained, and, once this one is removed, the others are forgiven. He says: Of justice, because I am going to the Father, and you will see me no more. The first thing to decipher here is that, if one is rightly accused of sin, how can one reasonably also be accused of justice? Perhaps because the sinner must be argued for being a sinner, the righteous must be argued for being righteous? No. For if the righteous person is ever reproached, it is not without reason that he is reproached, according to what is written: There is no righteous person on earth who does good and is free from all sin. And so, when the righteous is argued, it is because of sin, not because of justice. And also in that sentence of divine inspiration: Do not want to be too fair; It is not the justice of the wise that is reproached, but the pride of the presumptuous. He who becomes too just, becomes unjust because of that excess. And he who claims not to have sin or who believes that his will is sufficient and does not need the grace of God to be just becomes too righteous; nor is it just because of his righteous life, but rather habebitis libertatem. Saepe autem diximus inseparabilia opera esse Trinitatis (Supra, tr.20); sed singiUatim commendandas fuesse personas, ut non solum sine separatione, verum etiam sine confusione et unitas intelligatur et Trinitas. 2. Exponit deinde quid dixerit de peccato, et de iustitia et de indice. De peccato quidem, inquit, quia non crediderunt in me. Hoc enim peccatum quasi solum sit, prae caeteris posit; quia hoc manente caetera detinentur, et hoc discedente caetera remittuntur. Ve iustitia vero, inquit, quia ad Patrem vado, et iam non videbitis me. Hic primo videndum est, si recte quisque arguitur de peccato, quomodo recte arguatur et de iustitia.

Numquid enim si arguendus est peccator propterea quia peccator est, arguendum putabit quisquam et iustum propterea quia iustus est? absit. Nam et si aliquando iustus arguitur, ideo recte arguitur, quia, sicut scriptum est, Non est iustus in terra qui faciet bonum, et nos peccabit. Quocirca etiam cum iustus arguitur, de peccato arguitur, non de iustitia. Quoniam et in illo quod legimus divinítus dictum, Noli effici iustus multum (Eccle 7,21.17); non est notata iustitia sapientis, sed superbia praesumentis. Qui ergo fit multum iustus, ipso nimio fit iniustus. Multum enim se facit iustum, qui dicit se non habere peccatum; aut qui se putat non gratia Dei, sed sua volúntate sufficiente effici iustum: nec recte vivir iustus est, sed potius inflatus, putting se esse quod non est. a proud man believing himself to be what he is not. And in what sense is the world to be argued from justice, if not from the justice of believers? He is accused of sin because he does not believe in Christ, and he is accused of the justice of those who believe. The very recruitment of the faithful is a reproach for the infidels. Which emerges quite clearly from the same exhibition. Well, wanting to declare the meaning of his words, he says: Of justice, because I am going to the Father and you will see me no more. He does not say: Those of whom he said: Because they did not believe in me will see them. Because when exposing what sin he was referring to, he mentions those who did not believe in me; but, in explaining what justice he spoke of and of which the world is accused, he addresses those same people to whom he spoke, saying: For I am going to the Father and you will see me no more. Therefore, in speaking of sin, the world is argued by its own; but, when speaking of justice, it is argued by another, how darkness is rejected by light, as the Apostle says: Everything that is reprehensible is revealed by light. How great the evil of those who do not believe is, can be inferred not only from the evil itself, but from the good of those who believe. And since infidels often say: How are we to believe what we do not see?, it was convenient to define the justice of believers in this way: Because I am going to the Father and you will no longer see me, since blessed are those who do not see and believe. For among those who saw Christ, their faith is not praised for believing what they saw, that is, the Son of Man, but because they believed what they did not see, that is, the Son of God. But, when it is taken from their sight, arguendus est de iustitia, nisi de iustitia credentium? Arguitur itaque de peccato, quia in Christum non credit; et arguitur de iustitia eorum qui credunt. Ipsa quippe fidelium compared, infidelium is reviled. Hoc et ipsa expositio satis indicat. Volens enim aperire quid dixerit, De iustitia vero, inquit, quia ad Patrem vado, et iam non videbitis me. Non ait, Et iam non videbunt me; de quibus dixerat, quia non crediderunt in me. Sed peccatum quid vocaret exponens, de illis locutus est dices, quia non crediderunt in me: exponens autem quam diceret iustitiam, de qua mundus arguitur, ad ipsos quibus loquebatur se convertit, atque ait, Quia ad Patrem vado, et iam non videbitis me.

Quapropter mundus de peccato quidem suo, de iustitia vero arguitur aliena, sicut arguuntur de lumine tenebrae: Omnia enim quae arguuntur, ait Apostolus, a lumine manifestantur (Eph 5,13). Quantum enim malum sit eorum qui non credunt, non solum per seipsum, verum etiam ex bono potest eorum apparere qui credunt. Et quoniam ista vox infidelium esse consuevit, Quomodo credimus quod non videmus? ideo credentium iustitiam sic oportuit definiti, Quia ad Patrem vado et iam non videbitis me. Beati enim qui non vident, et credunt (lo 20,29). Nam et qui viderunt Christum, non in eo laudata est fides eotum, quia credebant quod videbant, id est Eilium hominis; sed qui a credebant, quod non videbant, id est Filium Dei. Cum veto et ipsa forma servi subtracta eorum esset aspectibus, tum vero ex omni parte im-
About the Gospel of Saint John

the form of a servant, then he fully fulfilled that the righteous lives by faith. It is, then, faith, as defined in the Epistle to the Hebrews, the foundation of those who hope and the conviction of things that do not appear. 3. What do these words mean: You will no longer see me? It does not say: I am going to the Father and you will no longer see me, as if wanting to indicate the space of time, short or long, but which must have an end, in which it must not be seen; but the Truth said: You will see me no more, in the sense that you would never see Christ anymore. Could this be justice, to no longer see Christ and yet believe in Him, when faith is praised, which gives life to the just, because it believes in Christ, whom it does not see now, but who will see it one day? Shall we say that, according to this justice, the apostle Saint Paul was not just, who declares that he saw Christ after his ascension to heaven, precisely at that time of which he had said: You will see me no more? Was not the most glorious Stephen just according to this justice, who said when he was being stoned: I see heaven open and the Son of man sitting at the right hand of God? What does it mean then, I am going to the Father and you will no longer see me, but that you will no longer see me as I am now among you? It was then mortal in the likeness of sinful flesh, which could hunger and thirst, be weary and sleep; and this Christ with such a nature, after passing from this world to the Father, they would no longer see him. And in this consists the righteousness of faith, of which the Apostle says: Although we knew Christ according to the flesh, but now we no longer know him according to the pletum est, Iustus ex fide vivit (Hab 2,4 et Hebr 11,1). Est enim fides, skut in Epistle quae ad Hebraeos est definitur, sperantium substantia, convictio rerum quae non videntur. 3. Sed quid est, lam non videbitis me? Non enim ait Ad Patrem vado, et non videbitis me; ut temporis intervallum quo non videbitur, significasse intelligeretur, sive breve, sive longum, tamen utique terminatum: sed dicendo, lam non videbitis me, velut nunquam eos de caetero visuros Christum, veritas praenuntiavit. Haeccine iustitia est nunquam Christum videre, et in eum tamen credere; cum proptetea laudetur fides ex qua iustus vivit, quoniam credit, quem moda non videt Christum, se aliquando esse visurum?

Postremo secundum hanc iustitiam, numquid dicturi sumus Paulum apostolum non Fuisse iustum, confitentem se Christum vidisse post ascensionem eius in caelum (1 Cor 15:8), de quo utique iam tempore dixerat, lam non videbitis me? Numquid secundum hanc iustitiam iustus non erat gloriosissimus Stephanus, qui cum lapidaretur, ait: Ecce video caelum apertum, et Filium hominis stantem ad dexteram Dei? (Act 7,55). Quid ergo est, Ad Patrem vado, et iam non videbitis me; nisi, quomodo sum, cum vobiscum sum? Tune enim adhuc erat mortalis in similarityine carnis peccati (Rom 8,3), who esurire poterat ac sitire, fatiguen atque I will sleep: hunc ergo Christum, id est talem Christum, cum transisset de hoc mundo ad Patrem, non erat iam visuri; et ipsa est iustitia fidei, de qua dicit Apos-
About the Gospel of Saint John

meat. It will be your justification, of which the world will be rebuked: I am going to the Father and you will no longer see Me, because you believe in Me without seeing Me; and when you see me as I will be then, you will not see me as I am now among you, you will not see me humiliated, but exalted; You will not see me mortal, but everlasting; You will not see me as a criminal, but as a judge; and of this your righteousness the Holy Spirit will rebuke the unbelieving world. 4. He will also argue with him about judgment, because the prince of this world has already been judged. Who is this prince but the one of whom it says in another place: The prince of this world comes and will find nothing in me, that is, nothing of his property, nothing that belongs to him in me, absolutely no sin? Through sin the devil is the prince of this world, not of heaven and earth, and of all that is in them, according to the meaning of the word world in that passage: And by Him the world was made; but prince of that world of which he next says: And the world did not know him, that is, the unfaithful men who populate the world, and among whom the faithful world groans, chosen out of the world by Him who made the world, and of whom he says: The Son of man has not come to judge the world, but that through Him the world may be saved. Your Charity will remember that I already spoke to you about this when I explained to you those words of the holy Gospel: I still have many things to tell you, but now, you cannot bear them. By this I do not mean that I have discovered secrets hidden in them, that, even if the Master revealed them, the disciple could not understand them; but those same things that we read and write, hear and say for the knowledge of men about the doctrine of religion, if Christ wanted to say them in the same way that he says them to the angels in himself, the only begotten Word of the Father and coeternal with the Father, what men could bear that burden, even if they were as spiritual as the apostles were not yet then, when the Lord spoke these words, and as they were after the coming of the Holy Spirit? Because everything that can be known about creatures is less than the Creator himself, who is the supreme, true and unchangeable God. And who doesn't talk about Him? Where is it not named by those who read, discuss, ask, respond, praise, sing, in any way speak, and, finally, by the same ones who blaspheme? And speaking of all of Him, who is it that understands Him as it should be understood, even though He always has Him on his tongue and in his ears? What intelligence can approach it? Who would have thought that He was a god if He had not manifested it? And who doesn't talk about the Trinity? And who understands that Trinity like the angels? The same things that are said at every step about the eternity, truth and holiness of God, are well understood by some, and misunderstood by others; or by sancti Evangelii verba tractaremus, ubi Dominus ait, Adhuc plana drooling vobis dicere, sed non potestis portare moda. Non ut in his Domini verbis nescio quae secreta nimis abdita suspicemur, quae cum dici a teacher possint, portari a disente non possint: sed ea ipsa quae in doctrina religionis in quorumlibet hominum notitia legimus et scribimus, audimus et dicimus, si vellet eo moda nobis Christus dicere, sicut ea dicit Angelis sanctis in seipso only begotten Patris Verbo, Patrique coaeterno; quinam portare nomines possent, etiam si iam essent spirituales, quales adhuc Apostoli non fuerunt, quando ista eis Dominus loquebatur, qualesque postea veniente sancto Spiritu facti sunt?
