I already warned you in the previous talk that you be careful, especially those of you who are still children and need dairy foods, not to be curious in listening to those who, on the occasion of these words of the Lord: I still have many things to tell you, but now you cannot bear their burden, they are deceived and try to deceive you, wanting to know unknown things who are not yet able to discern what is true from what is false; especially in view of the very obscene clumsiness that Satan taught to volatile and carnal souls, God allowing it so that his judgments are feared at all times, and by the comparison of impure evil the purity of discipline is sweeter, and so that whoever did not fall into those evils, or who with his help came out of them, gives honor to God and proceeds with fear and modesty.

With fear and prayer, free yourself from falling into that enigma of Solomon, in which a foolish and reckless woman, feeling the lack of bread, calls out to passers-by, saying: Take gladly the hidden bread and the sweetness of the furtive water. This woman represents the vanity of the wicked, who, being the most foolish, believe they know something; Lacking bread, like this woman, they promise bread, while they need it; that is, not knowing the truth, they promise knowledge of the truth. He promises the hidden breads, which he says are tasted with pleasure, and the sweetness of furtive water, so that with more pleasure and sweetness the things that are forbidden to be openly said and believed in the Church can be heard and done. The same concealment is the seasoning with which the nefarious doctors give their poisons to the curious who imagine they learn something great precisely because they have deserved the secret, and thus more gently absorb the foolishness, which they take for science, whose knowledge, in a certain way forbidden, they have stolen. 3. Hence the teaching of the magical arts recommends its nefarious rites to men who have already been or will be deceived by their sacrilegious curiosity. Hence those illicit divinations by inspection of the sounds or the viscera of sacrificed animals, or by the flight of birds, or by multiform signs of demons, whispered in the ears of those who are going to perish because of their conversations with the lost. For these illicit and punishable secrets, that woman is branded not only

foolish, but also reckless. But not only the execution of these things, but even his name is banished from our religion. And what are we to say, seeing that this foolish and audacious woman, under the name of Christian, has founded so many perverse heresies and forged so many nefarious fables? May we regret his foolishness as much as we admire his audacity in inventing fables such as those sung, danced or laughed at in theaters with buffoonery mimics, and not the fables he has invented against God. Because all the most ignorant heretics who want to appear as Christians, strive to give color to their audacious fictions, deeply abhorred by common sense, relying on the evangelical sentence in which the Lord says: I still have many things to tell you, but you cannot understand them now; as if these were things that the disciples could not endure then, and which the Holy Spirit taught, while the human spirit is ashamed of his teaching and preaching despite its audacity. 4. Foreseeing these by inspiration of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says: The time will come when they will not be able to endure sound doctrine, and they will surround themselves with teachers suited to their desires, who have the itch to make themselves heard, and they will turn their ears away from the truth and run after fables. The memory of that secret and that theft, indicated in these words: Take with pleasure the hidden bread and the sweetness of the stolen water, causes an itch in the ears of the spiritually loved ones, similar to the libidinous itch, which corrupts even the illicit caste atque punienda secreta, mulier illa non solum insipiens, verum audax etiam nuncupatur. Sed haec non solum a re ipsa, verum et a nomine nostrae religionis aliena sunt. Quid quod mulier haec insipiens et audax, sub christiano vocabulo all scelestas haereses condidit, all nefandas fables finxit? Utinam such quales in theatris sive cantantur, sive saltantur, sive mime scurrilitate ridentur; et non quasdam tales, quales adversus Deum fingere potuísse sic illam doleamus insipientiam, ut miremur audaciam.

Omnes autem insipientissimi haeretici, qui se christianos vocari volunt, audacias figmentorum suorum, quas máxime exhorret sensus humanus, occasione evangelicae sententiae colorare conantur, ubi Dominus ait, Adhuc plana drooling vobis dicere, sed non potestis portare moda: quasi haec ipsa sint quae tune discipuli portare non poterant, et ea docuerit Spiritus sanctus, quae palam docere atque praedicare, quantalibet feratur audacia, spiritus erubescit immundus. 4. Illa enim secreti furtique commemoratio qua dicitur, Panes oceultos libenter attingite, et aquae jurtivae dulcedinem, pruritum facit audientibus in auribus spiritualiter fornicantibus, sicut pruritu quodam libidinis etiam in

integrity of the meat. Listen to the Apostle, who has foreseen such things and gives healthy advice to avoid them. Avoid, he says, profane novelty in words, because they contribute a lot to impiety, and their conversation spreads like gangrene. He was not content with saying new words, but added profane ones. Because there are new words that are in complete consonance with the doctrine of religion, as when the name Christians began to be used. It was in Antioch that the disciples first began to call themselves Christians after the Ascension, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles. New names were also given to the inns and monasteries, without changing their purpose, and they are based on the truth of religion, with which they are defended even against the evil ones. Against the impiety of the Arians the word Homousion was introduced, applied to the Father, but without any other novelty under that name; for Homousion is the same as: I and the Father are one and the same thing, that is, of one and the same substance. Furthermore, if every new thing were profane, the Lord would not have said: A new command I give you; nor would the Testament be called New, nor would a new song be sung in all the earth. But new are the words that the foolish and bold woman says: Take with pleasure the hidden bread and the sweetness of stolen water. The Apostole distances us from this offer of false science when he says: "O Timothy!, defend the deposit by avoiding the profane novelty in the words and the contradictions of the science that falsely bears the name of such, with whose promise flesh corruptitur integritas castitatis. Audite taque Apostolum talia praevidentem, et ea vitanda salubriter admonentem: Profanas, inquit, verborum novitates avoid: multum enim proficiunt ad impietatem, et sermo eorum sicut cancer serpit (ibid. 2,16.17).

In Antiochia enim primum post ascensionem Domini appellati sunt discipuli Christiani, sicut legitur in Actibus Apostolorum (Act 11,26): et xenodochia et monasteria postea sunt appellata novis nominibus, res tamen ipsae et ante nomina sua erant, et religionis veritate firmantur, qua etiam contra improbos defenduntur. Adversus impietatem quoque Arianorum haereticorum novum nomen Patris Homousion condiderunt: sed non rem novam tali nomine signaverunt; hoc enim vocatur Homousion, quod est, Ego et Pater unum sumus (lo 10,30), unius videlicet eiusdemque substantiae. Nam si omnis novitas profana esset nec a Domino diceretur, Mandatum novum do vobis (ibid. 13,34); nec Testamentum appellaretur Novum, nec cantoretur in universa terra Canticum novum. Sed profanae sunt verborum novitates, ubi dicit mulier insipiens et audax: Panes oceultos libenter attingite, et aquae dulcedinem. Ab hac pollicitatione falsee scientiae prohibet etiam illo loco Apostolus ubi dicit: "O Timothee, depositum custodi, devitans profanas vocum novitates, et contradictiones falsi nominis scientiae, quam quidam promittentes,

Will anyone say: Will the spiritual people cease to have in their doctrine things that they hide from the carnal and reveal to the spiritual? If I answer no, they will bring me to the point what the apostle Paul says in the Epistle to those of Corinth: "I could not speak to you as to spiritual, but as to carnal; "I have given you milk to drink as infants in Christ instead of solid foods, because then you were not capable, nor are you still, because you are still carnal"; and that other passage: "Among the perfect we speak wisdom"; and this other: "Providing spiritual things to the spiritual, because the animal man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God: for him it is nonsense." We will discuss the meaning of these texts in another talk with the help of God, so that, because of these words of the Apostle, do not seek secrets with profane novelties of words, and let it be said that the carnal cannot endure those things that both the soul and the body of the chaste must avoid. And let us end this sermon circa fidem exciderunt" (1 Tim 6,20). ON THE SAME ISSUE

1. I remember that I have postponed the difficult question arising from these words of our Lord: I still have many things to tell you, - but now you cannot understand them, to deal with it more calmly, because the prudent length of the previous talk advised ending it. Now the time has come to fulfill what was promised. Let us treat it according to the lights that the Lord deigns to grant us, since He infused it into our hearts to propose it. The question is this: If the spiritual have something in their doctrine that they hide from the carnal and reveal it to the spiritual. If I answer no, it will be answered: Why then in his letter to the Corinthians did the Apostle say: "I have not been able to speak to you as to spiritual people; therefore I have given you milk as to Christ's infants, instead of the delicacies of which you were not capable, nor are you yet, because you are still carnal?" On the contrary, if I say yes, it is to be feared that, with this pretext, nefarious things will be hiddenly taught that, under the name of spiritual and incapable of being understood by the carnal, appear not only whitewashed with this pretext, but still worthy of praise. 2. that he feeds his infants; and that his own flesh, which suffered death and the royal wounds of the crucified and shed blood through his wounds, is not considered in the same way by the carnal and by the spiritual: for the former it is milk, for the latter it is delicacy, because, although they do not listen to it more than the others, they understand it better than they. Some and others do not equally understand what they equally receive by faith. From this arises that Christ crucified, preached by the Apostle, was a scandal for the Jews, a foolishness for the Gentiles, and for the elect, both Greeks and Jews, the virtue and wisdom of God; but carnal children do not see this except by faith; but the spiritual ones, as more capable, see it with their intelligence. For them it is like milk; for these, as a solid delicacy; Not because those in the squares heard it in a different way and those in the chambers, but because, both hearing the same public preaching, each one understood it according to his ability. For, since Christ was crucified to shed his blood for the remission of sins and through the passion of the only begotten Son divine grace was manifested to us, so that no one would place his glory on men, how did those who still said: I am of Paul understand Christ? Did they understand it, perhaps, like Paul himself, who said: Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of Our Lord Jesus Christ? From the crucified Christ himself he took food according to his ability, and he fed them with milk because of their weakness. But, knowing that what he had written to the Corinthians could be understood in one way by the infants and in another by the more capable, he says: If

There is some project or spiritual among you, understand that what I write to you is a command from the Lord; and if anyone ignores it, he will be ignored. He wanted the science of spirituals to have solidity, having certain knowledge, not being content with faith alone; and for this reason they believed what the spiritualists also understood. He will be, he says, ignored who ignores it, because it has not been revealed to him to know what he believes. And when this happens in the mind of man, it is said that he is known by God, because God makes him knower, as he says in another place: I see now, having known God, or rather, being known by God. It was not then that God knew them, having planned and chosen them before the formation of the world, but then he made them know him. 3. Taking this as a starting point, that is, that the things that the carnal and the spiritual hear simultaneously, each one understands according to his capacity: they as children, these as adults; the former as dairy foods, the latter as solid delicacies, the need to hide some doctrinal secrets is ruled out, hiding them from the faithful children to declare them apart from the elders, that is, the most intelligent; and at the same time the foundation imagined in these words of the Apostle falls: I have not been able to speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal people. Because the only thing that he thought he knew among them, which was nothing other than Christ, and Christ crucified, he could not say it to them as to spiritual people, but as to carnal people, because they could not understand it like the spiritual ones. Among them were spiritual, hearing it, as the carnal heard it, they grasped it with spiritual intelligence; and in this sense it must be understood: I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal ones; as if to say: Not as spiritual, but as carnal, you have been able to grasp my words. Latin interpreters made use of both translations, because the same Greek word doxa, from which the verb doxasei is derived, means clarity and glory. Through glory one becomes enlightened, and through enlightenment one is glorious. And that is why both verbs indicate the same thing. Ancient and enlightened Latin authors defined glory this way: It is a constant laudatory fame of someone. For the praise of the good is not beneficial to the one being praised, but to those who praise. 2. These words of the Lord A little more and you will no longer see me, and a little more and you will see me again, because I am going to the Father, were so obscure to the disciples before they saw them fulfilled, that with the questions they asked each other about their meaning they made it clear that they did not understand them. The Gospel continues saying: So the disciples said to each other, what does this mean to us: In a little while you will no longer see me, and in a little while you will see me again, because I am going to the Father? They said, well, what is this that He calls little? We don't know what he wants to tell us. They were agitated because he had told them: In a little while you will not see me, and after a little while you will see me again. In the preceding words, where he had not said: In a little while, but only: I am going to the Father and you will no longer see me, it seemed to them that he spoke clearly, and they questioned nothing about them. For them this was obscure then, and destractabitur, ubi dicit Unigenitus Patri, Et mea omnia tua sunt, et tua mea sunt (lo 17,10): ut hic iste sermo claudatur; quoniam quae sequuntur, aliud poscunt, quo disserantur, exordium.

He had already risen, he had already shown himself to them in his body, he was already seated at the right hand of the Father, when the same apostle Saint John, whose Gospel is this, said in his Epistle: Dearly beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we will be; We know that when He is revealed, we will be like Him, because we will see Him as He is. This vision is not of this life, but of the future; It is not temporary, but eternal. This is eternal life, says Life itself: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you sent. Of this vision and knowledge the Apostle says: We see now through a glass and in riddles, but then we will see face to face; now I know in part, but then I will know as I am known. This fruit of all its labors is now produced by the Church with desire, then it will be produced with vision; with tears now then

with joy; now with prayers, then with praises. That is why this fruit is of the masculine gender, because all the efforts of action are directed towards this fruit of contemplation. On the Gospel of Saint John TREATISE
ABOUT THESE WORDS OF THE LORD: "TRULY, TRULY, I TELL YOU: IF YOU ASK THE FATHER FOR ANYTHING IN MY NAME, HE WILL GIVE IT TO YOU", UNTIL THESE: "AGAIN, I LEAVE THE WORLD AND GO TO THE FATHER"

1. The words of the Lord that we are now going to explain are these: Truly, truly, I say to you, if you ask anything of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. In view of the fact that many ask the Father for things in the name of Christ and do not get them, we have already said in previous explanations about this sermon of the Lord that what is requested against salvation is not requested in the name of the Savior. Because, when it is said in my name, one must not take the material meaning of the syllables and letters, but rather the meaning of that sound and what is really and truly meant by that sound. And so, whoever does not think of Christ what should be thought of the only Son of God, does not ask in his name even if he pronounces the syllables of Christ's name with his tongue, because he asks in the name of the one of whom he thinks when he asks. He, however, who thinks of Him what should be thought, asks in His name and obtains what he asks for, if he does not ask for things contrary to salvation; but he receives them when he should receive them. Many things are not denied, but rather their concession is postponed for the opportune time. And so, these words: He will give it to you, must be understood from the benefits that they properly refer to whoever asks: All the righteous are attended to when they ask in

Non enim sonum litterarum ac syllabarum, sed quod sonus ipse significa, et quod eo sonó recte ac veraciter intelligitur, hoc accipiendus est dicere cum dicit, in nomine meo. Quaedam enim non negantur, sed ut congruo dentur tempore differuntur. And he continues saying: Until now you have asked nothing in my name; -ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete. This complete joy of which he speaks is certainly not a carnal joy, but a spiritual one, and it will only be complete when there is no more to add to it. Therefore, everything that is asked to achieve this joy must be asked in the name of Christ, if we understand divine grace, if we ask for the truly blessed life. To ask for something else is to ask for nothing; not because those things are nothing, but because, in comparison with such an excellent thing, nothing is what one desires. It is not that the man, of whom the Apostle says that he is considered something while being nothing, has no value; But, compared to the spiritual man, who knows that what is is is by the grace of God, he who boasts about vain things is nothing. The words can rightly be understood in this sense: Truly, truly, I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you, so that by something is not meant just anything, but something that, compared to the blessed life, comes to nothing. Also what follows: Until now you have not asked for anything in my name, can be understood in two ways: you have not asked for anything in my name, which you have not known as it should be known; or this other: you have not asked for anything, because what you have asked for is nothing compared to the blessed life, which

you should have asked. Exhorting them, then, to ask in his name, not for what is nothing, but for his complete joy (for if they ask for something else, that something is nothing), he tells them: Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete; That is to say: ask in my name that your joy may be complete, and you will obtain it. Because divine mercy will not disappoint his chosen ones who persevere in the request for this good. 3. Since animal man, then, is not capable of perceiving the things of the Spirit of God, he conceives everything that refers to the nature of God as something corporeal, although very broad and immense, most beautiful and most lucid, because he can only perceive corporeal things; and for this reason all things that wisdom has said about the incorporeal and immutable substance are like parables to him; and not because he considers them to be parables, but because he thinks like those who usually hear parables without understanding them. But, when he begins to see them as spiritual and no longer allow himself to be influenced by other people's judgments, although in this life he still sees them in part and as in a mirror, without the help of the senses or images that in some way reflect the bodily similarities, he understands with the firm intelligence of the spirit that God is not a body, but a spirit, in such a way that, when the Son speaks openly about the Father, he understands that the speaker is of the same substance as the Father. For they had said: We know that you know all things; It is more obvious that he who knows everything is questioned by the ignorant, to hear what they want to know from him who knows everything, and not to ask who knows everything, as if wanting to learn something. So what does it mean that, seeming that they should have said to the one who knows everything: "You have no need to ask anyone," they chose to say: "There is no need for anyone to ask you"? So what if we read both things as having happened: that the Lord asked and that he was questioned? But this is quickly resolved, saying that this was necessary, rather than to Him, to those whom He questioned or by whom He was questioned. Because He did not question them to learn something from them, but rather to teach them something. And those who questioned Him to learn something from Him evidently needed to ask to learn something from Him who knew everything. That's why it wasn't necessary for anyone to ask him. When we are questioned by those who want to know something about us, through their very questions we know what they want to know. And so we need to be questioned by those to whom we want to teach something, to know their inquisitions, to which we must respond. But this was not necepraebet, quia nondum eum capiunt, solidum cibum, saltem lacteum non denegat alimentum. Ex hoc aliment est, quod sciebant eum nosse omnia, nec opus ei esse ut eum quis interroget: quod quidem cur dixerint, quaeri potest. Videtur enim potius Fuisse digandum, Non opus est tibí ut quemquam interrogates; non, ut quis te interrogate.

Dixerunt quippe, Scimus quia nosti omnia: et utique qui novit omnia, magis a nescientibus interrogan solet, ut interrogantes audiant quod volunt, ab eo qui novit omnia; non ipse interrogare, tanquam volens aliquid scire, qui novit omnia. Quid sibi ergo vult, quod ei quem sciebant nosse omnia, cum dicere debuisse videantur, Non opus est tibi ut quemquam intetroges, dicedum potius putaverunt, Non opus est tibi ut quis te interroget? Quid quod utrumque legimus factum, et interrogasse scilicet Dominum, et interrogatum Fuisse? Sed hoc cita solvitur: quia hoc non ei, sed illis potius opus erat quos interrogabat, vel a quibus intetrogabatur. Ñeque enim aliquos ille interrogabat, ut ab eis aliquid disceret, sed eos potius ut doceret. Et qui interrogabant eum, volentes ab eo aliquid discere, illis prefecto id opus erat, ut scirent aliqua ab illo qui noverat omnia. Nimirum ergo propterea non opus erat ut eum quis interrogaren Quoniam nos quando interrogamur ab eis qui volunt aliquid a nobis scire, ex ipsis intetrogationibus eorum cognoscimus quid velint discere; opus est etgo nobis ab eis interrogari, quos docere aliquid volumus, ut

He was the one who knew everything, nor did He need their questions to know what they wanted to know, because, before being questioned, He already knew the desires of those who wanted to question Him. But he tolerated being questioned to show, both to those who were then present, and to those who were to hear these things orally or read them in writing, what those who asked him were like, and in this way we would come to know the frauds that prevent us from reaching Him and the paths that lead us to Him. Knowing in advance the thoughts of men, and, consequently, not needing anyone to question him, was nothing extraordinary for God, but it was something extraordinary for the little ones, who said to him: This is why we believe that you have come from God. This inquisitiones eorum quibus responderdum est noverimus: illi autem ne id quidem opus erat, qui omnia noverat; nec opus habebat quod ab eo quisque scire vellet, per eius interrogationem cognoscere, quia prius quam interrogaretur, interrogaturi noverat voluntatem. If we examine the Greek codices from which the Epistles of the Apostle have been translated into Latin, the word glory that is read in the Latins is doxa, from which the verb doxason is derived, which the Latin translator renders as clarifies, meaning that it can also be said to glorify, which is the same thing. And so in the Epistle of the Apostle clarity could be placed where glory is placed; and if this is done, it doesn't matter. And, by preserving the sound of the words, clarification is derived from clarity, as from glory glorification. For in order for Christ Jesus, as a man, to be clarified or glorified with the resurrection, he must first have gone through the humiliation of the passion, because, if he had not died, he would not have been resurrected from the dead. The humiliation of clarity is merit; the glorification of humility is the reward. But this as to the form of a servant; because as for the form of God, it always had and always will have clarity, or rather, it did not have it, as if it no longer has it, nor will it have it, as if it still does not have it, but it is a permanent clarity, without beginning and without end. FROM THESE WORDS OF THE LORD: "SO THAT YOUR SON MAY GLORIFY YOU", TO THESE: "WITH THE CLARITY THAT I HAD IN YOU BEFORE THE WORLD WAS"

1. No Christian doubts, and everything indicates that the Son was glorified by the Father according to the nature of a servant, whom the Father raised from the dead and placed at his right hand. But since he did not only say: Father, glorify your Son, but added: So that your Son may glorify you, it may be asked how the Son glorified the Father, since his clarity was not diminished in the human form nor could he have an increase in his divine perfection. Not even in itself is the glory of the Father susceptible of increase or decrease. But there is no doubt that it was less among men, when it was only known in Judea, because infants had not yet praised the Lord from sunrise to sunset. And since through the Gospel of Christ it was achieved that the knowledge of the Father reached the people through the Son, there is no doubt that the Son also glorified the Father. Declaring more openly the glorification of the Son by the Father, he says: For you have given him power over all flesh, so that he may give eternal life to those whom you have handed over to him. But, if by saying: I manifested your name to the men whom you have given me from the world, he understood all those who were to believe in Him, as members of that great Church that was to be formed from all nations, and of which it is sung in the Psalm: I will sing to you in a great assembly, then, yes, he accomplishes this glorification with which the Son glorifies the Father, making his name known to all nations and to such numerous human generations. And thus, the meaning of these words: I manifested your name to the men that you have given me in the world, is like that of those said before: I have glorified you on earth, placing, both here and there, the past for the future, as one who knows that its realization is predestined, and thereby saying that he has done what he must do without a doubt. 2. And that He said these words: I have manifested your name to the men that you have given me from the world, referring only to those who were already His disciples then and not to those who would later believe in Him, the following makes it more credible. For, having said this, he added: They were yours, and you have handed them over to me, and they have kept your doctrine; Now they have known that everything you have given me comes from you; for I gave them the words that you gave me, and they have received them, and they have known that truly I came from you, and they have believed that you sent me. And although all these things could have been said of all the future faithful, as realized in hope those that were still future, what follows prompts us to understand them as said of only the disciples he had then.

It says: When I was with them, I kept them, in your name: I preserved those whom you gave me, and none of them perished except the one who was the son of perdition, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, alluding to Judas, who betrayed him, since he alone was lost among the twelve apostles. And then he adds: But now I am going to you. From which we conclude that He spoke of His bodily presence when He said: When I was with them, I kept them, as if I were not among them now with that presence. With which he wanted to imply his upcoming Ascension, of which he said: But now I go to you; He was to go to the right hand of the Father, from where he must come to judge the living and the dead in his own bodily presence, according to the norms of faith and sound doctrine; because with his spiritual presence he was to be with them after his Ascension, and with all his Church in this world until the end of the ages. They are not correctly understood to be included in these words: When I was with them, I kept them, but those believers whom I had already begun to keep with my bodily presence, of which I was going to deprive them, in order to keep them, together with the Father, with the spiritual presence. Then he includes all his people, saying: I do not pray to you only for them, but for all those who will believe in me through their word. Wherein he manifestly declares that he did not refer to all his people when he previously said: I have manifested your name to the men you have given me; but only to those who were listening to him when he spoke.

But it is to be noted that the Lord did not say: so that we may all be one thing, but: So that all may be one thing, like you, O Father, in me and I in you, it is understood that we are one thing, which is later said more clearly, because before, referring to the disciples who were with Him, He had said: So that they may be one thing, like us. Therefore, in such a way is the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, that they are one thing, because they are of one substance; We, on the other hand, can be in them, but we cannot be one with them, because they and we are not of one.

I will die in three days. And in this way, although He does not say it, it must be understood that He gave Himself that clarity that He says was given to Him by the Father. He frequently says that the Father only does what He Himself does with the Father, by attributing all that He is to Him from whom it comes. But sometimes, silencing the Father, he says that He does what He does together with the Father, so that we understand that the Son should not be separated from the works of the Father when he says that He does something without naming Himself, and that likewise the Father should not be separated from the works of the Son when it is said that the Son does them without mentioning the Father, because they both do them together. And so, when the Son is silent in his cooperation in the works of the Father, he recommends his humility to us, so that it may be more profitable for us; When, however, the Father's cooperation in his works is silent, he also recommends his parity to us, so that he is not believed to be inferior. In this way, on this occasion he does not declare himself alien to the Father's operation even though he said: The clarity that you have given me, because He also gave it to Himself. Neither does he distance the Father from his works even if he says: I gave it to them, because the Father also gave it to them. Inseparable are the operations not only of the Father and the Son, but also those of the Holy Spirit. And just as with his prayer to the Father for all of his people he wanted to achieve that they would all be one thing, so also with this benefit of his that he says: this clarity that you have given me, I have given it to them, he wanted to do what he then said: May they be one thing, as we are. 4. He briefly hints himself here as a Mediator between God and men; but this does not mean that the Father is not in us or that we are not in the Father, having said in another place: We will come to him and make our home within him. But he did not say before: I in them and you in me, as he said now: They in me and I in you, but he said: You in me and I in you, and they in us. As for what he now says: I in them and you in me, he says it as a mediator, according to the words of the Apostle: You are from Christ, and Christ is from God. But in what he added: In order that they may be consummated in unity, he declares to us that the reconciliation made by the Mediator leads us to perfect blessedness, to which nothing can be added. Therefore, I believe that these words: So that the world may know that you sent me, should not be taken as if he were again saying: So that the world may believe, because sometimes the verb know is replaced by the verb believe, as when he said above: And they have known that I came from you and they believed that you sent me, where the same means they believed that they knew. But, when it refers to the consummation, then we must take that knowledge by knowledge by vision, and not by knowledge by faith. And this order seems to keep in what was said previously: So that the world may believe, and in what was said now: So that the world may know. For although he has there said: That they may all be one and be one in us, yet he does not say that they may be consummated in unity, but ends the phrase thus: That the world may believe that you sent me;

But let us not believe ourselves to be equal to the only begotten Son, who created us and preserves us, because He said: You have loved them as you loved me; because he who says that this is like that does not always indicate equality, but sometimes he only means: Because this is so, also that, or: Because this is, let it be tamUt sint, inquit, consummati in unum; ac deinde non addidit, Ut credat mundus, sed, Ut cognoscat mundus quia tu me misisti. well that. For who will dare to say that Christ sent the apostles into the world in the same way that He was sent by the Father? He loves the Son according to divinity, for having begotten him equal to Himself, and He also loves Him as man, because the only begotten Word Himself became flesh, and through the Word the flesh of the Word is very dear to Him; but he loves us because we are members of his Beloved, and so that we might be so he loved us before we existed. 6. But, in saying that we have been reconciled to God through the death of his Son, we should not hear it or take it as if the Son had reconciled us to Him to begin to love those whom he previously hated, in the way that an enedixeriteo prorsus moda in mundum a Christo Apostólos missos, quomodo est ipse missus a Patre? My friend reconciles with another enemy to become friends, later loving each other who previously hated each other; but we were reconciled to him who already loved us and whose enemies we were because of sin. The Apostle testifies to the truth of both things, saying: God commends his love toward us because Christ died for us while we were still sinners. He loved us even when we did evil by enmity against Him, and yet it was truly said of Him: You hated, Lord, all those who do evil. And so, in an admirable and divine way He loved us when He hated us, because He hated in us what He had not done; but, because our iniquity had not completely destroyed his work, each of us hated our work and loved his. And in this sense we must understand what has been truly said about Him: You have not hated anything you have done. In no way would He have wanted the things that He hated to exist, nor would those that the Omnipotent would have wanted to exist, if in the same things that He hates there was not something that He could love. With good reason he hates vice and condemns it as alien to the canon of his art; But he loves the most vicious things in me, either his benefit in straightening them, or his judgment in condemning them. And thus God has no hatred for any of his works, because, being the Creator of natures, not of vices, He hates evils, which He has not done; and good are the very things that He does, whether correcting evil by His mercy, or allowing it by His secret judgments. Having no hatred, then, for any thing that He has made, who can measure with

Exactly the love that he has for the members of his Only Begotten, and much less that which he has for the Only Begotten Himself, by which both visible and invisible things were created, whom he loves most rightly according to the ordering of their natures? And with the abundance of his grace he leads the members of his Only Begotten to equality with the holy angels; but the Only Begotten, because He is the Lord of all things, is certainly the Lord of the angels, and by His divine nature He is equal, not to the angels, but to the Father Himself; And because of the grace that he has as a man, how can the excellence of the highest angel not exceed, since man and the Word are one person? 7. There is no shortage of those who make us superior to the angels, saying that for us, and not for the angels, Christ died. But what does this mean if not wanting to glory in evil? Because, as the Apostle says, Christ at the appointed time died for the wicked. In which the mercy of God and not our merits shines. How can one glory in having contracted through his vices a disease that can only be cured with the death of the doctor? The death of Christ is not the reward for our merits, but rather the medicine for our illnesses. Will we consider ourselves superior to the angels because nothing was done for them to erase their sin? As if we had been given more than them. And even granting that this is so, it may be asked whether it was because we were more excellent or because we were in more desperate depths. But seeing that the Creator of all good things did not grant the evil angels any grace to repair their misfortune,

We already know, if we have drawn any benefit from this Gospel, that everything that claims to be done by the Father is also done by Himself with the Father. Those that He received from the Father are the same ones that He chose from the world and chose them so that they would no longer be of the world, as He is not of the world; but in such a way that they also form part of the world that believes and knows that Christ was sent by the Father so that the world could be freed from the world, so that the world that is to be reconciled with God may not perish with the world, its irreconcilable enemy. It says in the exordium of this prayer: you have given power over all flesh, that is, over all men, so that to all those whom you have given it may give eternal life. In these words he declares that he received power over all men so that he could save and condemn those he wanted, as judge of the living and the dead; but these have been given to Him so that He may give them eternal life. This is how he says it: So that to all those whom you have given him he may give eternal life. Nam illud quod dixisse legitur propinquante passione, Verum non quod ego voló, sed quod tu vis, Pater (Mt 6:39), quasi alia Patris, alia Filii sit voluntas aut fuerit, sonus est nostrae infirmitatis, quamvis fidelis, quam in se caput nostrum transfiguravit, quando etiam peccata nostra portavit. understand that he would soon ascend to heaven, saying that he was already where he would be later. He was also able to say it in the sense that he had previously said when speaking with Nicodemus: No one ascends to heaven except he who came down from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven. He said it will not be there either, in attention to the unity of person by which he is God - Man and Man - God. He promised, then, that we must be in heaven, where the form of a servant, which he took from the Virgin, was elevated and placed at the right hand of the Father. For the hope of so much good the Apostle says: God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love he had for us, when we were terrified by sin, gave us life in Christ, with whose grace he saved us, and with him he raised us up and with him he made us sit in the heavenly mansions in Christ Jesus. This can be understood as saying the Lord: Where I am, they may also be with me. Of himself he affirmed that he was already there; He said about us that He wanted us to be there with Him, not that we were already there. The Apostle spoke as if what the Lord wanted to be done had already been done. For it does not say that he must rise again and make sit in the heavens, but rather that he rose and made sit in the heavenly mansions, considering as already faithfully executed what he has no doubt must be accomplished. But, if we wanted to understand these words: I want that where I am they also be with me, referring to the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, all thoughts of corporeal images must be far from our soul, excluding everything that is long, wide, corporeal, colored by any corporeal light, diffused by any esiam ibi esse that is saidret ubi fuet mox futurus. This is not a usual locution: The love that you have loved me; commonly it would be said: The love with which you have loved me. It is translated from Greek, but there are also similar phrases in Latin; Thus we say: He served faithful service, he fought with brave militia, when it seems that it should be said: He served with faithful service, he fought with brave militia. The Apostle used a similar phrase when he said: I have fought a good fight. He does not say: I have fought a good fight, which would be more common and more elegant. But how is the Father's affection for the Son in us, except because we are his members and in him we are loved when he is loved totally, that is, as head and body? That is why he added: And I am in them, as if to say: because I am in them. In one way he is in us as in his temple, and in another because we are his members, since, being our head because he became man, we are his body. The Savior's prayer has ended and his passion begins. Simon Peter, who had a sword, drew it and struck a servant of the prince of the priests and cut off his right ear. This servant was called Maleo. This only evangelist recorded the name of this servant, just as Luke alone said that the Lord touched his ear and healed him. Maleo means that it must

dum reum, servato ordine legitimae potestatis, ut nullum tenentibus auderet obsistere: quanquam et manus tanta fuet congregata, et sic armata veniebat, ut vel terreret vel etiam repugnaret, si quisquam Christum I will defend auderet. Quid iudicaturus faciet, qui iudicandus hoc fecit? Qui regnaturus poterit, qui moriturus hoc potuit? Et nunc ubique per Evangelium, Ego sum, dicit Christus; et a ludaeis exspectatur Antichristus, ut retro redeant, et in terram cadant, quoniam deserentes caelestia, terrena

reign. What does the ear amputated in defense of the Lord and restored by Him mean, if not that the ear, detached from the old, has been renewed so that it is in the renewal of the spirit, already amputated from the oldness of the letter? And who will doubt that he to whom Christ granted this benefit will reign with Christ? The quality of servant belongs to that old age that engenders slaves, which is Hagar. But when he receives health, he is a figure of freedom. However, the Lord rebuked Peter for what he had done, forbidding him to go any further, saying: Put the sword in the sheath. 1. After the persecutors had arrested, for the betrayal of Judas, and had bound the Lord, who loved us and gave himself up for us, and whom the Father did not forgive, handing him over for all of us, and so that we would understand that Judas is not worthy of praise for the usefulness of his betrayal, but execrable for his criminal will, they took him, according to the evangelist Saint John, first to Anas. And he specifies the reason, saying that he was the father-in-law of Caiphas, who was the pontiff in that year. It was Caiphas who had given the advice to the Jews, saying that it was appropriate for a man to die for the people. St. Matthew wanting to abbreviate his narrative, says that he was taken to Caiphas, since he was previously taken to Anas because he was Caiphas's father-in-law, which can be understood as being done by Caiphas' will. autem quando eum illo moda comprehenderunt, tune ab illo longius recesserunt: et ligaverunt eum a quo solví potius velle debuerunt. Et erant fortassis in eis qui tune imposuetunt Christo liga sua, atque ab eo postea liberati dixerunt, Disrupisti liga mea (Ps 115,16). Haec hodie satis sint; tractabuntur, Deo volente, sermone alio quae sequuntur.
ERGO NEGAVIT PETRUS,

1. Posteaquam persecutors tradente luda comprehensum Dominum ligaverunt, qui dilexit nos et tradidit semetipsum pro nobis (Eph 5,2), et cui Pater non pepercit, sed pro nobis ómnibus tradidit eum (Rom 8, 32); ut intelligatur ludas, non laudabilis utilitate traditionis huius, sed sceleris volúntate damnabilis: Adduxerunt eum, sicut Ioannes evangelista narrat, ad Annam primum. Nec tacet causam cur ita factum sit: Erat enim, inquit, socer Caiphae, qui erat pontifex anni illius. Erat autem, inquit, Caiphas qui consilium dedit ludaeis, Quia expedit unum hominem mori pro populo. Merit et Matthaeus cum id brevius narrare voluisset, eum ad Caipham ductum Fuisse commemorat (Mt 26:57); quia et ad Annam prius ideo ductus est, quod socer eius fuerit: ubi intelligendum est hoc eumdem Caipham fieri voluisse.

2. Simon Peter and another disciple followed Jesus. The identification of this disciple is not easy, since his name is not said. But Saint John used to name himself in this way, adding: the one whom Jesus loved. Maybe this disciple is himself. But whatever, let's move on. "That disciple was known to the high priest and entered with Jesus into the atrium of the high priest; but Peter remained at the door on the outside. The disciple who was known to the high priest came out and spoke to the concierge, and brought Peter in. The maid who was the concierge then said to Peter: Are you not one of that man's disciples? He answers: I am not." There you have the very firm column shaking from top to bottom at the impulse of a light wind. Where are his bold promises and such self-confidence? Where are those words of his: Why can't I follow you now? Is it following the Master to deny being his disciple? Is this how one gives one's life for the Lord, being afraid of the voice of a servant so as not to give it? But how can it cause admiration, if God had predicted the truth and man had presumed falsehood? Evidently, in this already begun denial of the apostle Peter we must note that not only does he deny Christ who says he does not know Christ, but also he who denies being a Christian. The Lord did not say to Peter: You will deny that you are my disciple, but: You will deny me. And so he denied Him when he denied being His disciple. What else did he do with this but deny that he was a Christian? For although the disciples of Christ were not yet called by this name, since for the first time the

name of Christians to the disciples of Christ in Antioch after the Ascension, already then there was the reality that this name would later have, already then there were disciples who would later be called Christians, and this common name, as the faith was common, they transmitted to those to come. He who denied being a disciple of Christ, denied the very reality for which he is called Christian. How many later, I'm not saying old men and women, who, due to the weariness of life, could more easily despise death in the confession of Christ; nor young people of either sex, of whose age strength can precisely be demanded; but boys and girls and an innumerable army of holy martyrs, who entered with courage and violence into the kingdom of heaven, were able to do what this one who received the keys to his kingdom could not do! See the reason for having said: Let these go, when He who redeemed us with His blood gave Himself for us, to fulfill what He had said: Of those you have given me I have not lost any. For if Peter had gone away after denying Christ, what would happen to him but perish? 3. The servants and ministers were by the fire, because it was cold, and they were warming themselves. It was not winter, and yet it was cold, as sometimes happens at the spring equinox. "Peter was also standing with them and warming himself. Meanwhile, the high priest questioned Jesus about his disciples and his doctrine. Jesus answered him: I have spoken openly to the world, I have always taught in the synagogue and in

2. Sequebatur autem, inquit, lesum Simón Petras, et alias discipulus. Quisnam iste sit discipulus, non teréré affirmandum est, quia tacetur. Solet autem se idem Ioannes ita significare, et addere, quem diligebat lesas (lo 13,23 et 19,26). Fortassis ergo et hic ipse est: quisquís tamen sit, sequentia videamus. "Discipulus autem ille", inquit, "erat notus pontifici, et íntroivít cum Iesu in atrium pontifícis: Petrus autem stabat ad ostium foris. Exiit ergo alius discipulus qui erat notus pontifici, et dixit ostiariae et introduxit Petrum. Dicit ergo Petro ancilla ostiaria: Numquid et tu ex discipulis is hominis istius? Dicit ille: Non sum". Ecce column firmissima ad unius aurae impulsum tota contremuit. Ubi est illa promittentis audacia, et de se plurimum praefidentis? Ubi sunt verba illa, quando ait, Quare non possum te sequi moda? animam meam pro te ponam? (13.37). Hoccine est sequi magistrum, will discipulum deny? siccine pro Domino anima ponitur, ut hoc ne fiat, vox ancillae formidetur? Sed quid mimm si Deus vera praedixit, homo autem false praesumpsit? Sane in ista quae iam coepta est negatione apostoli Petri, debenmus advertere non solum ab eo negari Christum, qui dicit eum non esse Christum; sed ab illo etiam qui cum sit, negat se esse christianum. Dominus enim non ait Petro, Discipulum meum te negabis; thirst, you deny me (Mt 26,34). Negavit ergo ipsum, cum se negavit eius esse discipulum. Quid autem aliud isto moda quam se negavit esse Christianum? Quamvis enim discipuli Christi nondum appellarentur hoc nomi-

ne: post ascensionem quippe eius in Antiochia primum coeperunt appellari discipuli Christiani (Act 11,26): iam tamen erat res ipsa illo postea vocabulo nuncupanda, iam erant discipuli qui postea appellati sunt Christiani; et hoc commune lomen, sicut communem fidem, etiam ad posteros transmiserunt. Qui ergo se Christi negavit esse discipulum, ipsam rem negavit, cuius nomen est vocari christianum. Quam multi postea, non dico senes et anus, ¡n quibus huius vitae satietas facilius potuit mortem pro Christi confessione contemnere; nec solum iuventus utriusque sexus, de qua aetate convenientr videtur exigi fortitudo; sed etiam pueri puellaeque potuerunt, et innumerabilis societas sanctorum martyrum in regnum caelorum fortiter et violenter intravit, quod tune iste non potuit, qui keys regni eius accepit? (Mt 16,19). Ecce unde dictum est, Sinite hos abire, quando se pro nobis tradidit, qui suo sanguine nos redemit; ut impleietur sermo quem dixit, Quia quos dedisti mihi, no perdidi ex eis quemquam. LTtique enim Petrus si negato Christo hinc iret, quid aliud quam periret? 3. Stabant autem serví et núnistri ai prunas, quia frígus erat, et calefaciebant se. Non hiems erat, sed tamen frigus erat: quod solet etiam aequinoctio verno aliquando contingere. "Erat autem cum eis et Petrus stans, et calefaciens se. Pcntifex ergo interrogavit lesum de discipulis eius, et de doctrina eius. Respondit ei Iesus: ego palam locutus sum mundo, ego semper doeni in synagoga et in temple, quo omnes
About the Gospel of Saint John

the temple, where all the Jews go, and I have not said anything in private, why ask me? Ask those who heard what I have spoken to them. They know what I have said." From here arises a question that should not be overlooked: in what sense did the Lord say: I have spoken openly to the world, and, above all, in private I have said nothing. Did he not say to the disciples in this recent sermon that he addressed to them after dinner: These things I have told you in parables; the time has come for me to no longer speak to you in parables, but I will clearly announce to you the Father? If, then, he did not speak to his closest disciples openly, but promised them the time to do so, how did he speak openly to the world? And if those same disciples of his, according to the authorized testimony of the other evangelists, when he was alone with them, far from the crowds, he spoke to them more clearly than to the others who were not his disciples, since then he declared to them the parables that he secretly proposed to the others, why does he say: I have not said anything in private? But we must understand that He said: I have spoken openly? to the world, as if he said: Many heard me openly, in one sense it was openly, in another it was not. It was openly in that many heard him, and it was not, in that they did not understand him. And, speaking apart to the disciples, he did not speak secretly. Who can say that he speaks secretly when he speaks before so many men, since it is written that by the word of two or three witnesses the whole truth is declared, especially when what is said is told to a few. He wants many to know it through them, as the Lord says to the few he still had: What I say to you in the Iudaei conveniunt, et in occulto locutus sum nihil: quid interrogates me? eos qui audierunt quid locutus sum ipsis: ecce hi sciunt quae dixerim ego. Non praetereunda nascitur quaestio, quoroodo dixerit Dominus lesus, Ego palam locutus sum mundo; et máxime illud quod ait, In occulto locutus sum nihil. Nonne in hoc ipso recentiore sermone, quem post coenam discipulis est locutus, ait illis: Haec in proverbiis locutus sum vobis: venit hora cum iam non in proverbis loquar vobis, sed palam de Patre meo annuntiabo vobis? (16.25).

Si ergo ipsis coniunctioribus discipulis suis non loquebatur palam, sed horam promittebat quando palam erat locuturus, quomodo palam locutus est mundo? Deinde illis ipsis suis, sicut aliorum quoque evangelistarum testatur auctoritas, in eorum comparatione qui discipuli eius non habert, multo utique manifestius loquebatur, quando cum solis erat, remotus a turbis: tune enim eis et parabolas aperiebat, quas clausas proferebat ad alios. Quid est ergo, In occulto locutus sum nibil? Sed intelligendum est ita eum dixisse, Palam locutus sum mundo; ac si dixisset, Multi me audierunt. Ipsum autem palam moda quodam erat palam, moda autem quodam non erat palam. Palam quippe erat, quia multi audiebant; et rursum non erat palam, quia non intelligebant. Et quod seorsum discipulis loquebatur, non in occulto utique loquebatur. Quis namque in occulto loquitur, qui coram tot hominibus loquitur; cum scriptum sit, In ore
About the Gospel of Saint John

darkness, announce it in the light of day, and what you hear in the ear, say it on the roof? Therefore, the same thing that he seemed to say hiddenly, in a certain way he did not say it hiddenly, since he did not say it so that those who had heard it would silence it, but rather so that it would be preached everywhere. In this way a thing can be said openly and not openly, hidden and not hidden, just as it was said: So that seeing they may see and not see. How are they to see except because it is open and not hidden, and how are they not to see except because it is hidden and not open? But the things they had heard and had not understood were such that they could not justly and truly rebuke themselves. And as many times as they questioned him maliciously to find out what to accuse him of, he answered them in this way, to blunt all their deceptions and frustrate their slander. That's why I said: Why are you asking me? Ask those who heard what I have spoken to them; They know what I have said. 4. When He had said this, one of the attending ministers slapped Jesus, saying: Is this how you answer the high priest? Jesus replied: If I have spoken evil, bear witness to what was evilly said; But if I have spoken well, why do you hurt me? Can anything be truer, mansoy just, than this answer? It was given by Him of whom it was prophesied: Walk and advance in prosperity and reign by truth, meekness and 'righteousness. If we look at the one who received the slap, wouldn't we want that duorum vel trium testium stabit omne verbum (Deut 19,15): praesertim si hoc loquitur paucis, quod per eos velit innotescere multis; sicut ipse Dominus ait illis, quos adhuc paucos habebat, Quod dico vobis in tenebris, dicite in lumine; et quod in aure auditis, praedicate super tecta? (Mt 10:27). Ergo et hoc ipsum quod ab ipso dici videbatur oceulte, quodammodo non dicebatur in occulto: quia non ita dicebatur, ut ab eis quibus dictum fuetat, taceretur; sed ita potius, ut usquequaque praedicaretur. Sic ergo dici potest aliquid et palam simul et non palam, vel in occulto simul et non in occulto, quomodo dictum est, Ut videntes videant, et non videant (Mark 4,12). Quomodo enim videant, nisi quia palam, non in occulto; et quomodo Idem ipsi rursus non videant, nisi quia non palam, sed in occulto?

Ea tamen ipsa quae audierant et non intellexerant, talia erant, ut non possent iuste ac veraciter criminari: et quotiescumque interrogando tentarunt, ut invenirent unde aecusarent eum, sic eis responderit, ut omnes eotum retunderentur doli, et calumniae frustrarentur. Ideo saysbat, Why are you questioning me? Interroga eos qui audierunt quid locutus sum ipsis: ecce hi sciunt quae dixerim ego. 4. Haec autem cum dixisset, unus assistens ministerum dedit alapam lesu, they say: Sic respons pontifici? Respondit ei lesus: Si male locutus sum, testimonium perhibe de malo; If autem bene, why do you fall for me? Quid is this responsione verius, mansuetius, iustius? Eius est enim de quo prophetica vox praecesserat, Intend, et prospere proceed, et regna; propter veritatem, et mansuetudinem, et iustitiam (Ps 44,5). Si cogitemus quis acceperit alapam, nonne vellernus eum qui percussit, aut caelesti igne
About the Gospel of Saint John

who wounded him would be burned by fire coming down from heaven, or that the earth would open and swallow him, or that he would be rolled by demons like a condemned man, or that he would be punished with another similar or even more cruel punishment? What of these could not He by whom the world was created have ordered with His power, if He had not preferred to teach us patience, with which the world is conquered? But perhaps someone will say: And why did He not do what He Himself commanded? Instead of responding like that, he should have turned the other cheek. But what is there to say about his true, meek and just response, and that he not only prepared the other cheek to be wounded again, but his entire body to be nailed? With this he demonstrated rather what he had to demonstrate, that is, that his great precepts of patience had to be executed with the preparation of the heart rather than with bodily manifestations. For it may well happen that one visibly turns the other cheek, but that he does so full of anger. How much better would it be to respond calmly to the truth and with a calm spirit to be prepared for greater offenses? Blessed is he who, in all that he suffers for justice, can truly say: He is ready, O God, my heart, he is ready; with which you obtain what it means: I will sing and salmear; as Paul and Barnabas did in their prisons. 5. But let us follow the Gospel narrative. And Anas sent him bound to the pontiff Caiphas. According to Saint Matthew, from the beginning he was taken to Caiphas, because he was the prince of the priests that year. Since it should be known that every year I alternately consumed, aut terra dehiscente sorberi, aut correptum daemonio volutari, aut aliqua huiusmodi qualibet poena, vel etiam graviore puniri? Quid enim horum per potentiam iubere non potuisset per quem factus est mundus, nisi patientiam nos dore maluisset qua vincitur mundus? Hic dicet aliquis: Cur non fecit quod ipse praecepit? (Mt 5:39) percutienti enim non sic I will respond, sed maxillam debuit alteram praebere. Quid quod et veraciter, mansuete, iusteque responder, et non solum alteram maxillam iterum percussuro, sed totum corpus figendum praeparavit in ügno?

Et hinc potius demonstravit, quod demonstrandum Fuit, sua scilicet magna illa praecepta patientiae non ostentatione corporis, sed cordis praeparatione facienda. Fieri enim potest ut alteram maxillam visibiliter praebeat homo et iratus. Quanto ergo melius et respondert vera plaquetus, et ad perferenda graviora tranquillo animo fit paratus? Beatus est enim qui in omnibus quae iniuste pro iustitia patitur, potest veraciter dicere, Paratum cor meum, Deas, paratum cor meum: hinc fit quippe quod sequitur, Cantaba et psallam (Ps 56,8); quod Paulus et Barnabas etiam in vinculis durissimis faceré potuerunt. 5. Sed ad narrationis evangelicae sequentia redeamus. Et missile eum Annas ligatum ad Caipham pontificem. Ad illum, sicut Matthaeus dicit, ab initio ducebatur, quoniam ipse erat illius anni princeps sacerdotum. Alternos quippe intelligendi sunt agere soleré annos both pontiffs,
About the Gospel of Saint John

The princes of the priests exercised their ministry, who at that time were Anasy Caiphas, mentioned by Saint Luke when he records the time in which the precursor of the Lord, John the Baptist, began to preach the kingdom of heaven. It goes like this: Under the princes of the priests Annas and Caiaphas the word of the Lord was spoken to John, son of Zechariah, in the desert, etc. And so these two pontiffs took their places for alternate years, and Caiphas corresponded to that year in which Christ suffered. That is why Saint Matthew says that, when Jesus was arrested, he was led to him; but, according to Saint John, he was taken first to Annas, not because he was his colleague, but because he was his son-in-law. And it is to be believed that this was done according to the will of Caiaphas or also because their houses were placed in such a way that they could not fail to pass by the house of Anas. 6. After the evangelist has said that Anas sent him bound to Caiaphas, he returns to the point in his narrative where he left Peter, to explain what happened in Anas's house regarding his three denials. And it says: Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. He recapitulates what he had already said before and adds what happened next: So they said to him, Are you not one of his disciples? He denied it, saying: I am not. I had already denied him once; this is the second. Then, to complete the three, one of the pontiff's servants, a relative of the one whose ear Peter cut off, says: Did I not see you with Him in the garden? Peter denied again, and immediately the rooster crowed. The pre id est principes sacerdotum is already fulfilled, qui weret illo tempore Annas et Caiphas, quos Lucas evangelista commemorat, natrans quo tempore coeperit Domini praecursor Ioannes praedicare regnum caelorum, et congregare disciples. Sic enim dicit: Sub principibus sacerdotum Anna et Caipha, factum est verbum Domini super loannem Zachariae jilium in deserto (Le 3,2), et caetera. Proinde isti both pontiffs vicissim suos annos agebant: et erat annus Caiphae quando passus est Christus. Respondit Iesus: You say quia rex sum ego. Talem quippe ille sentiebat qui dixerat, Ergo rex es tu? cui responsum est, Tu dicis quia rex sum ego. Dictum est enim, Tu dicis, ac si dictum esset, carnalis carnaliter dicis. 4.

Deinde subiungit: Ego in hoc natus sum, et ad hoc veni in mundum, ut testimonium perhibeam veritati, Non est producedda huius pronominis syllaba, quod ait, In hoc natus sum, tanquam dixerit, In hac te natus sum: sed corripienda, tanquam dixerit, Ad hanc rem natus sum, vel ad hoc natus sum; sicut ait, Ad hoc come in mundum. In graeco namque Gospel nihil est huius locutionis ambiguum. Unde manifestum est eum temporalem nativitatem suam hic commemorasse, qua incarnatus venit in mundum; non illam sine initio qua Deus erat, per quem Pater condidit mundum. In hoc ergo se dixit natum, id est propter hoc natum, et ad hoc venisse in mundum, utique nascendo
About the Gospel of Saint John

to the world, being born of a virgin, to bear witness to the truth. But, since not everyone has faith, he added: Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice. He certainly hears it with his inner ears, that is, he obeys my voice, which is as valid as if he said: he believes me. When, therefore, Christ bears witness to the truth, he bears witness to himself, because his voice is: I am the truth; and in another place he said: I testify of myself. But insofar as he says: Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice, manifests the grace, with which he calls according to predestination. Of which the Apostle says: We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to God's purpose; namely, according to the purpose of him who calls them, not of those called; which in another place is more clearly stated: Cooperate with me in the Gospel according to the virtue of God, who saves us and calls us to his holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace. Because, if we look at the nature in which we were created, since we were all created by the truth, who does not come from the truth? But not everyone receives from the truth the power to hear the truth, that is, to obey the truth and believe in the truth, of course without prior merits, so that grace does not cease to be grace. If he had said: Everyone who hears my voice belongs to the truth, it might be that he would believe that he belongs to the truth because he obeys the truth; But he did not say this, but: Everyone who belongs to the truth hears my voice. Therefore, Virgine does not lose, ut testimonium perhibeat veritati. Sed quia non omnium est fides (2 Thess 3,2), adiunxit, atque ait: Omnis qui est ex verilate, audit meam vocem. Audit utique interioribus auribus, id est, obaudit meae voci: quod tantumdem valeret si dicetet, Credit mihi. Cum itaque Christus testimonium perhibet veritati, profecto testimonium perhibet sibi: eius quippe vox est, Ego sum verilas (lo 14,6): et dixit alio quoque loco, Ego testimonium perhibeo de me (ibid. 8,18). Quod vero ait, Omnis qui est ex veritate, audit vocem meam, gtatiam commendavit qua secundum propositum vocat.

De quo proposito dicit Apostolus, Scimus quia diligenlibus Deum omnia cooperantur in bonum, his qui secundum propositum Dei vocati sunt (Rom 8:28); propositum scilicet vocantis, non vocatorum: quod alibi apettius ita positum est, Collabora Gospel secundum virtutem Dei, safe nos facientis et vocantis vocatione sua sancta; non secundum opera nostra, sed secundum suum propositum et gratiam (2 Tira 1,8.9). Nam si naturam cogitemus in qua creati sumus, cum omn.es veritas cieaverit, quis non est ex veritate? Sed non omnes sunt quibus ut audiant veritatem, hoc est ut obaudiant veritati, et credant in veritatem, ex ipsa veritate praestatur; nullis ptocul dubio praecedentibus meritis, ne gratia non sit gratia. Si enim dixisset, Omnis qui audit meam vocem, ex veritate est: ideo dictus ex veritate putaretur, quia obtemperat veritati; non autem hoc ait; thirst ait, Omnis
About the Gospel of Saint John

He dies to the truth because he hears its voice, but he hears its voice because it belongs to the truth, that is, because he has received this gift from the truth. And what does this mean except that he believes in Christ because Christ has given him that gift? 5. Pilate said to him: What is truth? But he didn't wait for the answer; But having said this, he went out again to the Jews and said to them: I find no crime in this man. It is customary among you that I release one to you at the Passover, do you want me to release the king of the Jews to you? I believe that, when Pilate said: What is the truth?, the custom of the Jews that one was set free at Passover came to his mind, and that is why he did not wait for Jesus to respond, so as not to let the memory of the custom pass by, making his freedom possible, since there is no doubt that he wanted it that way. But he could not tear from his heart that Jesus was the king of the Jews, as if this had been engraved in him, like a title, the truth, of which he asked what it was. But when they heard this, they all cried out again, saying, Not this man, but Barabbas. Barabbas was a thief. We do not rebuke you, O Jews, for wanting to free an evildoer for the Passover, but for having put to death the innocent, even though, if you did not do so, there would be no true Passover. But the Jews, ignorant, preserved the shadow of the truth, while, by an admirable disposition of divine wisdom, through deceitful men the truth of the shadow was fulfilled; because, in order for the true Passover to be made, Christ was sacrificed like a sheep. From here come the insults that later qui est ex veritate, audit meam vocem. Ac per hoc non ideo est ex vinote, quia eius audit vocem; sed ideo audit, quia ex veritate est, id est, quia hoc illi donum ex veritate collatum est. Quod quid est aliud, quam donor Christo credit in Christum? 5. Dixit ei Pilatus: Quid est veritas? Nec exspectavit audire responsum; sed cum hoc dixisset, iterum exivit ad ludaeos, et dixit eis: Ego nullam invenio in eo causam. Est autem consuetudo vobis ut unum dimittam vobis in Pascha; vultis ergo dimittam vobis regem ludaeorum?

Credo cum dixisset Pilatus, Quid est veritas? inmentem illi venisse continuo consuetudinem ludaeorum, qua solebat eis dimitti unus in Pascha: et ideo non exspectavit ut responderet ei Iesus quid est veritas, ne mora ieront, cum recoluisset morem quo posset eis per Pascha dimitti; quod eum valde voluisse manifestum est. Avelli tamen ex eius corde non potuit lesum regem esse ludaeorum, tanquam hoc ibi, sicut in titulo, ipsa veritas fixerit, de qua quid esset interrogavit. Sed hoc audito, Clamaverunt rursum omnes dicentes; Non hunc, sed Barabbam. Erat autem Barabbas latro. Non reprehendimus, o Iudaei, quod per Pascha liberatis nocentem, sed quod occiditis innocentem: quod tamen nisi firet, verum Pascha non ieront. Sed umbra veritatis a Iudaeis errantibus tenebatur, et mirabili dispensatione divinae sapientiae per nomines fallaces eiusdem umbrae veritas implebatur; quia ut verum Pascha ieront, Christus velut ovis irnmolabatur. Hinc ea sequuntur quae
