they made Christ Pilate and his cohort, of which we will deal in another sermon.
ABOUT THIS THAT FOLLOWS: "THEN PILATE TOOK JESUS AND SCOURGED HIM", UNTIL THIS: "THEY TOOK JESUS AND TOOK HIM OUT"

1. The Jews having asked Pilate not to release Jesus but Barabbas to them on the occasion of the Passover; not to the Savior, but to the criminal; not to the giver, but to the taker of life: Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him. It is not to be believed that Pilate did this except with the intention that the Jews, satisfied with his insults, would be satisfied and desist from persecuting him until he had him killed. For this reason, the president allowed his cohort to do the following things, or perhaps ordered them, although the evangelist has kept quiet about it. He then says what the soldiers did, but he does not say that Pilate ordered it. It says: And the soldiers, weaving a crown of thorns, put it on his head and wrapped him in a purple cloak. And they came to Him and said: Hail, king of the Jews, and they slapped Him. In this way what Christ had predicted about himself was fulfilled; This is how the martyrs informed themselves to suffer whatever pleased their persecutors; Thus, hidden for a short time his tremendous power, he recommended the imitation of his patience; Thus the kingdom that was not of this world defeated the proud world, not with the atrocity of the struggle, but with the iniurious humility Christo Pilatus et cohors eius ingessit; sed allia disputatione tractanda sunt.
SEQUITUR, TUNC ERGO APPREHENDIT PILATUS USQUE AD I D, SUSCEPERUNT AUTEM IESUM, ET
IESUM, ET EDUXERUNT

1. Cum Iudaei clamassent non lesum sibi a Pilate dimitti velle per Pascha, sed Barabbam latronem; non salvatorem, sed interfectorem; non datorem vitae, sed ademptorem: Tune apprehendit Pilatus lesum et flagellavit. Hoc Pilatus non ob aliud fecisse credendus est, nisi ut eius iniuriis Iudaei satiati sufficere sibi existimarent, et usque ad eius mortem saevire desisterent. Ad hoc pertinet quod Idem praeses cohortm suam etiam permisit faceré quae sequuntur; aut fortassis et iussit, quamvis hoc Evangelista tacuerit. Dixit enim quid deinde fecerint milites; Pilatum tamen id iussisse non dixit. Et milites, inquit, plectentes coronam de spinis im-posuerant capiti eius, et veste purpurea circumdederunt eum. Et veniebant ad eum et dicebant: Ave, res ludaeorum. Et ibant ei alapas. Sic implebantur quae de se praedixerat Christus: sic martyres informabantur ad omnia quae persecutors libuisset faceré, perferenda; sic paulisper oceultata tremendous potentia, commendabatur prius imitanda patientia; sic regnum quod de hoc mundo non
About the Gospel of Saint John

of suffering; Thus that grain that was to be multiplied was sown among so much contumelia so that it would flourish with admirable glory. 2. Pilate came out again and said to them: Behold, I am bringing him out to you so that you may know that I find no crime in him. So Jesus came out wearing the crown of thorns and dressed in purple. And he says to them: See here the Man. From which it is seen that Pilate was not unaware of what the soldiers did, either with his command or with his authorization, for that reason that I mentioned before, so that his enemies would drink all those mockery with pleasure and no longer feel the thirst for his blood. Jesus appears before them, raising the crown of thorns and the purple garment, not in the glory of his empire, but full of shame, and they are told: See there the Man; If you have animosity against the king, forgive him now seeing him so dejected: he was scourged, he was crowned with thorns, he was covered with a dress of scorn, he was mocked with bitter insults, he was slapped; Before the boiling of ignominy, envy remains cold. But it does not cool down, but rather becomes hot and inflamed. 3. "When the priests and ministers saw him, they cried out, saying: Crucify him, crucify him. Pilate said to them: Take him and crucify him, for I find no crime in him. The Jews answered: We have the law and, according to the law, he must die, because he became the Son of God." Here is another reason for greater envy. That of the royal power, claimed with illicit audacity, seemed small to them, and yet neither of these things was erat, superbum mundum non atrocitate pugnandi, sed patiendi humilitate vincebat; sic illud granum multiplicandum seminabatur horribili contumelia, ut mirabili pullularet in gloria. 2. Exiit iterum Pilatus joras, et dicit eis: Ecce adduco eum joras, ut cognoscatis quia in eo nullam causam invento. Exiit ergo Iesus portans spineam coronam et purpureum vestimentum. Et dicit eis: Ecce homo. Hinc apparet non ignorante Pilate haec a militibus facta, sive iusserit ea, sive permiserit; illa scilicet causa, quam supra diximus, ut haec eius ludibria inimici libentissime biberent, et ulterius sanguinem non sitirent.

Egreditur ad eos Iesus portans spineam coronam et purpureum vestimentum, non clarus imperio, sed plenus opprobrio; et dicitur eis, Ecce homo: si regi invidetis, iam parcite, quia deiectum videos; flagellatus est, spinis coronatus est, ludibriosa veste amictus est, amaris conviciis illusus est, alapis caesus est; fervet ignominy, frigescat invidia. Sed non frigescit, inardescit potius et increscit. 3. "Cum ergo vidissent eum pontifices et ministri, clamabant dicentes: Crucifige, crucifige eum. Dicit eis Pilatus: Accipite eum vos, et crucifigite; ego enim non invenio in eo causam. Responderunt e¡ Iudaei: Nos Legem habemus, et secundum Legem debent mori, quia Filium Dei se fecit." Ecce alter maior invidia. Parva quippe illa videbatur, velut affectatae illicito ausu, regiae potestatis: et tamen neu-
About the Gospel of Saint John

Jesus usurped falsely, because both are true: he is the only begotten Son of God, and by Him he was made king over Zion, his holy mountain; and with this he gave proof that, the more powerful he was, the more he preferred to be patient. 4. When Pilate heard this, his fear was greater, and, entering again into the praetorium, he said to Jesus: Where are you from? But Jesus does not answer him. Comparing the narratives of the evangelists, it is seen that this silence of Our Lord Jesus Christ did not take place just once: he was silent before the princes of the priests: he was silent before Herod, to whom, according to Saint Luke, Pilate sent him; He remained silent before Pilate himself. And so the prophecy that refers to Him was not in vain: Like a dumb lamb before the shearer, so He did not open his mouth when he did not answer those who questioned him. And, although he answered some questions, he was, however, compared to the lamb in view of those that he did not want to answer, to demonstrate with his silence, not his guilt, but his innocence. When, therefore, when he was judged, he did not open his mouth, he became like a lamb; That is, he did not open it, as if, conscious of his wickedness, he was convicted of his crimes, but rather as a meek lamb, which sacrifices itself for the sake of others. 5. So Pilate said to him: Are you not answering me? Don't you know that I have the power to crucify you and the power to release you? Jesus answered: You would not have any power over me if it had not been given to you from above; For this reason, he who handed me over to you has greater sin. On this occasion he responded; but, when not restrum sibi Iesus mendaciter usurpavit; sed utrumque verum est, et unigenitus est Dei Filius, et rex ab eo constitutus super Sion montem sanctum eius: et utrumque nunc demonstraretur, nisi quanto etat potentior, mucho mallet esse patientior. 4. Cum ergo audisset Pilatus hoc verbum, magis timuit; et ingressus est praetorium iterum, et dicit ad lesum: Unde est tu? Iesus autem responsum non dedit ei. Hoc silentium Domini nostri Iesu Christi non semel factum, collatis omnium Evangelistarum narrationibus reperitur, et apud principes sacerdotum, et apud Herodem, quo eum, sicut Lucas indicat, miserat Pilatus audiendum, et apud ipsum Pilatum (Mt 26,63; 27,14; Mark 14,61; 15,5; Le 23,7-9 et lo 19,9): ut non frustra de illo prophetia praecesserit, Sicut agnus coram tondente se juit sine voce, sic non aperuit os suum (Is 53,7); tune utique quando interrogantibus non responder.

Quamvis enim quibusdam interrogationibus saepe will answer; tamen propter illa in quibus noluit will respond, ad hoc data est de agno similareo, ut in suo silentio non reus, sed innocens haberetur. Cum ergo iudicaretur, ubicumque non aperuit os suum, sicut agnus non aperuit; id est, non sicut male sibi conscius qui de peccatis convincebatur suis, sed sicut mansuetus qui pro peccatis immolabatur alienis. 5. Dicit ergo ei Pilatus: Mihi non loqueris? Nescis quia potestatem habeo crucijigere te, et potestatem habeo dimittere te? Respondit Iesus: Non haberes adversum me potestatem ullam, nisi tibi datum esset desuper: propterea qui me tradidit tibi, maius peccatum habet. Ecce respondit, et tamen ubicumque non responder, non sicut reus sive dolo-
About the Gospel of Saint John

He did it, not as a criminal or as a forger, but as a lamb, that is, as simple and innocent. Consequently, when he did not respond, he was silent like a lamb; but, when he answered, he taught like a shepherd. Let us learn his teaching, also transmitted by the Apostle, that there is no power that does not come from God, and that the sin of one who, out of envy, hands over the innocent to justice, to be sacrificed, is greater than that of justice itself putting him to death for fear of a higher power. Such was the power that God had given to Pilate, leaving him also under the power of Caesar. And thus he says: You would not have any power over me, whatever power you have, if this very power that you have had not been given to you from above. But, because I know its extension, it is not so great that you have absolute freedom; Therefore, he who gave me to you has greater sin. He handed me over to you out of envy, and you exercise it against me out of cowardice. Nor should a man kill another innocent man out of fear; But doing it out of envy is much worse than doing it out of fear. That is why the Teacher of truth does not say that he who handed me over to you has sin, as if Pilate were exempt from it; but he said that he has greater sin, giving him to understand that he also had sin. Well, that is why the sin of the former is greater, because this one also has it. 6. From that moment Pilate tried to give him freedom. What does it mean to say from that moment on, as if you didn't try it before? Read the above and you will see that he was trying to let go of Jesus before. sus, sed sicut agnus, hoc est, sicut simplex atque innocens non aperuit os suum. Proinde ubi non responderbat, sicut ovis silebat; ubi responderbat, sicut pastor twelvebat. Discamus ergo quod dixit, quod et per Apostolum docuit, quia non est potestas nisi a Deo (Rom 13:1); el quia plus peccat qui potestati innocentem occidendum livore tradit, quam potestas ipsa si eum timóte alterius maioris potestatis occidit. Talem quippe Pilate Deus dederat potestatem, ut etiam esset sub Caesaris potestate. Quapropter non haberes, inquit, adversum me potestatem ullam, id est, quantulamcumque habes, nisi hoc ipsum quidquid est, tibi esset datum desuper.

Sed quoniam scio quantum sit; non enim tantum est, ut tibi omni moda libetum sit: propterea qui tradidit me tibi, maius peccatum habet. lile quippe me tuae potestati tradidit invidendo, tu vero eamdem potestatem in me exserturus es metuendo. Nec timendo quidem, praesertim innocentem, homo hominem debent occidere: sed tamen id zelando faceré multo magis malum est, quam timendo. Et ideo non ait verax magister, Qui me tradidit tibi, ipse habet peccatum; tanquam ille non haberet: sed ait, maius habet peccatumut etiam se habere intelligeret. So from that moment it must be understood by this, by this cause, in order not to incur the sin by killing the innocent person placed in his hands, although his sin is less than that of the Jews who had handed him over to take his life. From that moment, then, that is, by not committing that sin, not now for the first time, but from the beginning I was looking for an opportunity to give him freedom. 7. But the Jews cried out, saying, If you let this man go, you are no friend of Caesar; because everyone who becomes king goes against Caesar. They thought that they would instill greater terror in him with the fear of Caesar than with what they had previously said: We have the law, and, according to the law, he must die, because he has become the Son of God. He was not frightened by his law into putting him to death, but by the fear that he was the Son of God. But now he could not show contempt for Caesar, who was the author of his power, as he manifested it by the law of a strange people. 8. And the evangelist continues saying: When Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus outside and sat as a judge in a place called lithostrotos, gabbata in Hebrew. It was on the parasceve of Passover, around the sixth hour. At what hour was the Lord sacrificed, before the testimony of another evangelist, who says: It was the third hour and they crucified Him, usually gives rise to great discussions, which we will deal with, with God's favor, when we reach the passage where the crucifixion is narrated. So when Pilate sat down at the tribunal, he said to the Jews: Here you have your King. But they cried: Take him away, take him away; crucify him, crucify him. Adhuc tamen Evangelista sequitur, et dicit: Pilatus autem eum audisset hos sermones, adduxit foras Iesum, et seedit pro tribunali, in loco qui dicitur Lithostrotos, hebraice autem Gabbatha. Erat autem Parasceve Paschae, almost sixth hour. Qua hora sit Dominus crucifixus, propter evangelistae alterius testimonium qui dixit, Erat autem hora tertia, et crucifixerunt eum (Mark 15:25), quoniam magna disceptatio solet oboriri; eum ad ipsum locum ubi crucifixus narratur ventum fuerit, ut potuerimus, si Dominus voluerit, disseremus. lato: Should I crucify your King? He still tries to overcome the fear of Caesar, which they had instilled in him, wanting to bend them at the sight of their ignominious appearance, saying: Shall I crucify your King?, since he could not bow them before the ignominy of Christ. But then he is overcome by fear. 9. The high priests answered: We have no king but Caesar. Then he handed him over to be crucified. He seemed to go openly against Caesar if, after they had confessed that they had no king but Caesar, he tried to give them another king, releasing the one they had handed over to him for these aspirations to condemn him to death. So he handed him over to be crucified. But did he have other intentions, both when he previously said: Take him and crucify him, and when he also previously said: Take him and judge him according to your Law? Why did they resist so much, saying: It is not lawful for us to kill anyone; showing so much interest in him being killed, not by them, but by the president, and refusing to take him to kill him, if now they take him to kill him? And if this is not so, why does he now say: "Then he was handed over to be crucified"? Is there any difference in this? For it is not written: "Then he handed him over" to be crucified, but: "to be crucified", that is, to be crucified by the sentence and power of the president. But the evangelist said that it was given to them to demonstrate that they were also involved in the crime, of which they tried to appear oblivious; Pilate would not have done this except to satisfy what sedisset Pilatus, Dicit ludaeis; Ecce rex vester. lili autem clabant: Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum. Dixit eis Pilatus: Regem vestrum crucifigam? Adhuc terrorem quem de Caesare ingesserant, superare conatur, de ignominia eorum volens eos frángete saying, Regem vestrum crucifigam? quos de ignominia Christi mitigare non potuit: sed timore mox vincitur. 9. Replyunt enim pontiffs: Non habemus regem nisi Caesarem. Tune ergo tradidit eis illum ut crucifigeretur. Apertissime quippe contra Caesarem vinore videretur, si regem se non habere nisi Caesarem profitentibus, alium regem vellet ingerere resigning impunitum, quem propter hos ausus ei tradiderant occidendum.

Tradidit ergo eis illum ut crucifigeretur. Be numquid aliud et ante cupiebat quando dicebat, Acápite eum vos, et crucifigite; vel etiam superius, Acápite eum vos, et secundum Legem vestram iudicate eum? Cur autem illi tantapere noluerunt, dicentes, Nobis non licet interficere quemquam (lo 28,31); et omni moda moments, ut non ab eis, sed a praeside occideretur, et ideo eum occidendum accipere recusantes, si nunc eum accipiunt occidendum? Aut si hoc non fit, cur dictum est, Tune ergo tradidit eis illum ut crucifigeretur? An liquid interest? Plan interest. Non est enim dictum, Tune ergo tradidit eis illum ut crucifigerent eum; sed, ut crucifigeretur, id est, ut iudicio ac potestate praesidis crucifigeretur. Sed ideo illis traditum dixit Evangelista, ut eos crimini implicatos, a quo alieni esse conabantur, ostenderet: non enim faceret

•I saw, that they wanted so much. What follows: They took Jesus and carried him out, may refer to the soldiers, ministers of the president, as it is stated more clearly later: The soldiers having crucified him; and, although the evangelist attributes everything to the Jews, he does not do so without reason, because they received what they so eagerly asked for, and they did everything they were forced to do. But we will deal with this in another sermon.

Videbat tangebatque hominem, et confitebatur Deum quem non videbat ñeque tangebat; sed per hoc quod videbat atque tangebat, illud iam remote dubitatione credebat. and see how hot it is. In all these cases it is said to see, although we do not deny that sight is typical of the eyes. 1. Post narrationem rei gestae, in qua Thomas discipulus oblatis sibi tangendis in Christi carne vulnerum locis, vidit quod credere nolebat et credidit; interponit haec evangelista Ioannes, et dicit: "Multa quidem et alia signa fecit Iesus in conspectu discipulorum suorum, quae non sunt scripta in libro hoc. Haec autem scripta sunt, ut credatis
About the Gospel of Saint John

book. But all these things have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, so that, believing it, you may have life in his name." This chapter seems to indicate the end of this book, but it still narrates the manifestation of the Lord by the Sea of Tiberias, and how in the capture of the fish the mystery of the Church is recommended, and what the future resurrection of the dead is to be like. I believe that it contributes to giving value to this recommendation that this conclusion serve as a prologue to the following narrative, to leave it, in a certain way, in a more prominent place. This narrative begins like this: "Then Jesus appeared by the sea of Tiberias, and revealed himself in this way: There were together Simon Peter and Thomas, called Didymus, and Nathanael, who was from Cana of Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee and two other of his disciples. Simon Peter tells them: I am going fishing. They replied, "Let us also go with you." 2. On the occasion of this fishing of the disciples, it is often asked why Peter, the two sons of Zebedee, returned to the same occupation they had before being called by the Lord, since they were fishermen, when he said to them: Come after me and I will make you fishers of men. Then they, leaving everything, followed him to devote themselves to his teaching; meanwhile, that rich man who had said: Go, sell as much as he did. You have, give it to the poor and you will have treasure in heaven, and come and follow me; therefore Peter said to him: We have left all things and followed you. Hoc capitulum velut libri huius indicat finem: sed narratur hic deinde quemadmodum se manifestaverit Dominus ad mare Tiberiadis, et in capture piscium commendaverit Ecclesiae sacramentum, qualitative future est ultima resurrectione mortuorum.

Ad hoc itaque commendandum valere arbitror, quod tanquam finis interpositus est libri, quod esset etiam secuturae narrationis quasi prooemium, quod ei quodammodo faceret eminentiorem locum, quae narratio incipit ita: "Postea manifestavit se iterum Iesus ad mare Tiberiadis; manifestavit autem sic: Erant simul Simón Petrus et Thomas qui dicitur Didymus, et Nathanael qui erat a Cana Galilaeae, et filii Zebedaei, et alii ex discipulis eius duo. Dicit eis Simón Petrus: Vado piscari ei: Venimus et nos tecum." 2. Quaeri solet de hac piscatione discipulorum, cur redierint Petrus et filii Zebedaei ad id quod fuerunt priusquam a Domino vocarentur: erant enim piscatores quando eis dixit, Venite post me, et faciam vos piscatores hominum (Mt 4,19). Tune eum quippe illi secuti sunt, ut magisterio eius relictis omnibus adhaererent: in tantum ut cum ab eo dives ille tristis abscederet, cui dixerat, Vade, vende quae babes, et da pauperibus, et habebis thesaurum in cáelo; et veni, sequere me, diceret ei Petrus, Ecce nos dimisimus omnia, et secuti sumus te (ibid. 19,21.22.27). Quid est ergo quod nunc quasi Apostolatu relicto fium

nating the apostolate, they return to what they were and take up again what they had left behind, as if they had forgotten the words they had heard: Is no one who puts his hands on the plow and looks back fit for the kingdom of heaven? If they had done this after Jesus had died and before he had risen from the dead (which they would not have been able to do then, because the day he was crucified kept them in suspense until the hour of burial, which was before vespers, and the next day was Saturday, in which the custom of their parents does not allow them any work; and on the third day the Lord was already resurrected and restored to them the hope, which they had begun to lose), if they had done it then, we would think that they did it by virtue of that desperation that had taken over his spirits. But now, after having him among the living, after the evidence of his flesh, returned to life and offered to their eyes and hands, not only so that they could see it, but also so that they could touch and feel it; after having seen the places of the wounds, until reaching the confession of the apostle Thomas, who had said that otherwise he would not believe; after having received the Holy Spirit by his insufflation; after those words spoken by their mouth in their very ears: As my Father sent me, so I send you: whose sins you forgive, they will be forgiven, and whose sins you retain, they will be retained, suddenly they become fishermen, not of men, but of fish, as they were before. 3. To those who are disturbed by this, we must respond that they were not prohibited from obtaining what was necessary through a

licit and granted art, preserving the integrity of their apostolate, if they had no other recourse to obtain what was necessary to live. Unless it occurs to someone to think or say that Saint Paul did not have the perfection of those who, leaving all things, followed Christ, because, in order not to burden any of those to whom he preached the Gospel, he himself provided for their maintenance with his own hands, and thus in him what was said was fulfilled: I have worked more than all of them; adding: But not I, but the grace of God with me; In such a way that he attributes to the grace of God the ability to dedicate himself body and soul more than all of them to work, to the point of not ceasing in the preaching of the Gospel, and, nevertheless, not having need of the Gospel to sustain his life, when he sowed it with greater extension and fruit in so many nations that had not heard the name of Christ. There he demonstrates that the obligation to live, that is, to draw sustenance from the Gospel, was not imposed on the apostles, but that they were given that power. The Apostle mentions this faculty when he says: "If we have sown spiritual goods in you, will it be too much for us to reap your material goods? If others share in your property, do we not have a greater right? I have never used this right." And shortly after he adds: "Those who serve at the altar have their part at the altar; and thus the Lord commanded the preachers of the Gospel to live by the Gospel: I have not made use of these faculties." It is, therefore, very clear that it was not a precept, but a faculty granted to the apostles not to live by anything other than the Gospel; and of those in whom

quod fuerunt, et quod dimiserant repetunt, tanquam obliti quod audierant, Nenio ponens manum super aratrum, et respiciens retro, aptus est regno caelorum? (Luke 9:62). Quod si fecissent defuncto Iesu, priusquam resurrexisset a mortuis: quod quidem non poterant, quoniam dies quo crucifixus est, totos eos tenebat attentos, usque ad eius sepulturam, quae ante vesperam facta est; Sequens autem dies erat sabbati, quando eis morem patrium servantibus, operari utique non licebat; tertio vero die Dominus resurrexit, eosque revocavit ad spem quam de lio non habere iam coeperant: tamen si tune fecissent, putaremus eos illa quae spirits eorum oceupaverat, desperatione fecisse. Nunc vero post eum sibi de sepulcro redditum vivum, post oblatam suis oculis et manibus, non solum videndam, verum etiam tangendam atque palpandam redivivae carnis evidentissimam veritatem; post inspecta vulnerum loca, usque ad apostoli Thomae confessionem, qui se aliter crediturum non esse praedixerat; post acceptum eius insufflatione Spiritum sanctum, post verba in suas aures eius ore prolata, Sicut misit me Pater, et ego mitto vos: quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis, et quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt (lo 20,21-23): súbito fiunt sicut fuerant, non hominum, sed piscium piscators. 3- His ergo quos hoc movet responderdum est, non eos fueisse prohibitos arte sua, licita scilicet atque concessa, victum necessarium

quaerere, sui Apostolatus integrate setvata, si quando unde viverent aliud non haberent. Nisi forte quispiam putare audebit aut dicere, apostolum Paulum non pertinuisse ad eorum perfectionem qui relictis omnibus Christum secuti sunt, quoniam ne quemquam eorum tumbaret quibus Evangelium praedicabat, suum victum suis manibus transigebat (2 Thess 3,8): ubi magis impletum est quod ait, Plus bus My jobsavi; et adiunxit, Non autem ego, sed gratia Dei mecum (1 Cor 15:10): ut hoc quoque appareat Dei gratiae deputandum, quod et animo et corpore poterat usque adeo plus illis ómnibus laborare, ut ñeque cessaret ab Gospel praedicando, ñeque tamen ex Gospel, sicut lili, sustainret hanc vitam; cum id per all gentes in quibus Chtisti nomen non fuet prophetatum, multo latius atque fertilius seminaret. Ubi otendit ex Evangelio vivirdi, hoc est victum habendi, non necessitatem Apostolis impositam, sed potestatem datam. Quam potestatem commemorat idem apostolus say: "Si nos vobis spiritualia seminavimus, magnum est si vestra carnalia metamus? Si alii potestatis vesttae participant, non magis nos? Sed non sumus," he inquited, "usi hac potestate." Et paulo post: "Qui altari serviunt", inquit, "altari compattiuntur; sic et Dominus otdinavit his qui Evangelium annuntiant, de Evangelio livere: ego autem nullo horum usus sum." With the preaching of the Gospel they sowed spiritual goods, collected the materials, that is, what was necessary for their bodily sustenance, and, as soldiers of Christ, received the soldiery from their suppliers. For this reason, this same soldier of Christ had said a little earlier about this: Who serves in the military at his own expense? And this is what he did, because he worked harder than everyone. If, then, Saint Paul, not making use, like them, of that faculty that was common to him with the other preachers of the Gospel, except to do battle at his own expense and not to scandalize the Gentiles, so foreign to the name of Christ, his doctrine seeming venal to them and having another education, he learned trades that he did not know so as not to be burdensome to his listeners and to live off the work of his hands, how much better would Saint Peter, who had previously been a fisherman, return to exercise what he already knew, if on that occasion he found no other way to provide for himself? 4. Perhaps someone might object: How is it that he did not have it, if the Lord had promised it, when he said: Seek ye first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you in addition? On this occasion God fulfilled his promise. Because; Who gathered there the fish they caught? And it can be thought that He reduced them to that hardship that forced them to fish, because He wanted to perform in their sight that miracle, with which, while giving food to the preachers of His Gospel, He recommended the same Gospel with the mystery enclosed in the number viverent nisi ex Gospel, et ab eis quibus Evangelium praedicando spiritualia seminabant, carnalia meterent; hoc est, carnis huius sustainculum sumerent, et tanquara milites Christi stipendium debitum acciperent, sicut a provincialibus Christi. Unde idem ipse miles egregius paulo superius de hac re dixerat, Quis militat suis stipendiis unquam? (1 Cor 9,11-15.7). Quod tamen ipse faciebat, quia plus illis omnibus laborabat.

Si ergo beatus Paulus ut ea potestate, quam prefect cum caeteris Evangelii praedicatoribus habebat, non cum caeteris uteretur, sed suo stipendio militaret, ne gentes a nomine Christi penitus alienas doctrina eius quasi venalis offenderet, aliter educatus, artem quam non noverat didicit, ut dum suis manibus transigitur doctor, nullus auditor graveretur; quanto magis beatus Petrus, qui iam piscator fuet, quod noverat fecit, si ad praesens illud tempus, aliud unde viveret, non invenit? 4. Sed responderbit quispiam: Et cur non invenit, cum Dominus promiserit dices, Quaerite primum regnum et iustitiam Dei, et haec omnia apponentur vobis? (Mt 6,33). Prorsus etiam sic Dominus quod promisit implevit. Nam quis alius pisces qui caperentut apposuit? qui non ob aliud credendus est eis ingessisse penufiam qua compellerentur iré piscatum, nisi dispositum volens exhibite miraculum: ut simul et praedicatores Evangelii sui pasceret, et ipsum Evangelium both sacra-

of the fish. And now, with the favor of God, I am going to tell you something about this fishing. 5. Simon Peter says: I'm going fishing. Those who were with him say to him: Let us also go with you. They went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing. When it was morning, Jesus appeared on the beach, without the disciples knowing who Jesus was. So Jesus said to them: Boys, do you have anything to eat? They answered him: No. He said to them: Cast the net on the right side of the boat and you will find it. They cast it, and could not drag the net because of the number of fish. Then that disciple whom Jesus loved says to Peter: It is the Lord. Peter, having heard that it was the Lord, put on his tunic, because he was naked, and jumped into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat (because they were not far from the land, about two hundred cubits) dragging the net with the fish. After they landed, they saw some hot coals prepared and on them a fish and a loaf of bread. Jesus says to them: Bring some of the fish that you have caught now. Simon Peter went up and dragged the net to land with one hundred and fifty-three large fish. And, even though there were so many, the network did not break. 6. This is the great mystery in the great Gospel of Saint John, and to further emphasize it, written in the last place. The fact that there were seven disciples who took part in this fishing: Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the two sons of Zebedee and two others whose names he kept silent, with their septenary number, indicate the end of time. All time circles in the seven days. To this it was mentioned quod erat de numero piscium commendaturus augeret. De qua re etiam nos quod ipse apposuerit, dicere iam debenmus. 5. Dicit ergo Simón Petrus: Vado piscari. Dicunt ei qui cum illo weret: Venimus et nos tecum. And exierunt and ascenderunt in navem: et illa nocte nihil apprehenderunt. Mane autem iam jacto stetit Iesus in littore; non tamen cognoverunt discipuli quia Iesus est. Dicit ergo eis Iesus: Pueri, numquid pulmentarium habetis? Replyunt ei: Non. Dicit eis: Mittite in dexteram navigii rete, et invenietis. Miserunt ergo, et iam non valebant illud trahere a multitudine piscium. Dicit ergo discipulus Ule quem diligebat Iesus, Petro: Dominus est. Simon Petrus cum audisset quia Dominus est, tunica succinxit se, erat enim nudus, et misit se in mare. Alli autem discipuli navigio venerunt (non enim longe erant a terra, sed quasi cubitis ducentis), trahentes rete piscium.

Ut ergo descenderunt in terram, viderunt prunas positas, et piscem superpositum, et panem. Dicit eis Iesus: Afferte de piscibus quos apprehendistis nunc. Ascendit Simón Petrus, et traxit rete in terram plenum magnis piscibus centum quinquaginta tribus. Et cum tanti essent, non est scissum rete. 6. Hoc est magnum sacramentum in magno Ioannis Gospel; et ut vehementius commendaretur, loco ultimo scriptum. Quod ergo septem discipuli fuerunt in ista piscatione, Petrus, et Thomas, et Nathanael, et duo filii Zebedaei, et alii duo quorum nomina tacentur, isti suo septenario numero finem significant temporis. Universum quippe septem
About the Gospel of Saint John

refers to Jesus being on the beach in the early morning, because the beach is the end of the sea, and thus means the end of time, also represented by the extraction of the net towards the land, that is, towards the beach by Peter. Which the Lord himself explained when he explained the parable of the net thrown into the sea, and they brought it, he says, to the coast. And expounding the meaning of the coastline, he says: This is how the end of time will be. 7. But that was a parable by way of example: it was not a fact. With this fact the Lord wanted to imply what the Church will be like at the end of time; and with that parable, what the Church is like in the present time. Because he had said this at the beginning of his preaching and this fishing had been carried out after his resurrection, he implied that this capture of fish meant the good and the bad that are now in the Church, and this represents only the good, which it will always have at the end of the world and after the resurrection of the dead. In that one, finally, Jesus was not standing on the beach, as in this one, when he ordered fishing, but, getting into one of the ships, which was Simon Peter's, he asked him to remove it a little from the land, and, sitting in it, he taught the crowds. When he had stopped speaking, he said to Simon, Row in and let down the nets for a catch. What they caught then was collected in the ships, not like now, when the net was pulled to land. By these signs and others that may perhaps be found, the former represented the Church in this world, and the latter the Church at the end of the world. That is why that one took place before and this one diebus volvitur tempus. Ad hoc pertinet quod mane facto lesus stetit in littore; quia etiam littus finís est maris, et ideo finem significat saeculi. Eumdem finem saeculi otendit et quod Petrus rete extraxit in terram, hoc est in littus. Quod ipse Dominus aperuit, ubi alio quodam loco de sagena in mare missa similarityinem dedit: Et eam trahunt, inquit, ad littus. Quod littus quid esset exponens, ait: Sic erit in consummatione saeculi (Mt 13,48.49). 7. Sed illa verbi est, non rei gestae parabola: re autem gesta, sicut hoc loco qualiter in saeculi fine Future sit, ita Dominus alia piscatione significavit Ecclesiam qualiter nunc sit.

Quod autem illud fecit in initio praedicationis suae, hoc vero post resurrectionem suam, hinc otendit illam captutam piscium, bonds et mals significare, quos nunc habet Ecclesia; istam vero tantummodo bonds, quos habebit in aeternum, complete in fine huius saeculi resurrectione mortuotum. Denique ibi lesus non sicut hic in littore stabat, quando iussit pisces capi; sed ascendens in unam navim quae erat Simonis, rogavit eum ut a terra reduceret pusillum; et in ea sedens twelvebat turbas. Ut cessavit autem toqui, say ad Simonem: Duc in altum, et láxate relia vestra in capturem. Et illic quod captum est piscium in naviculis Fuit, non sicut hic rete extraxerunt in terram. His signis et si qua allia potuerint reperiri, ibi Ecclesia in hoc saeculo, hic vero in fine saeculi figurata est: ideo illud ante, hoc autem post resurrectionem Domini factum est; quia ibi nos Christus
About the Gospel of Saint John

after the resurrection of the Lord, because in the former Christ represented our vocation, and in this our resurrection. There the net is not cast, neither to the right, so as not to mean only the good, nor to the left, so as not to only understand the bad; but in a general way: Cast, he says, the nets to catch fish, implying that the good are mixed with the bad; but here it says: Cast the net to the right of the ship, to signify that only the good were on the right. There the network was broken, remembering the schisms; But here, since then there will be no schisms in that supreme peace of the saints, the evangelist was careful to note that, being so many, that is, so great, the network was not broken; as if remembering when it was broken, and making this good more expensive in comparison to that evil. In that one the multitude of fish was so great that, when the two ships were full, they were submerged, that is, they threatened to submerge; They did not sink, but they were in danger. Why are there so many evils in the Church, if not because it is not possible to face the avalanche that, to sink discipline, enters its customs, entirely opposed to the path of the saints? In this one they threw the net to the right of the ship and could not drag it due to the number of fish. What does it mean that they could not drag it but that those who belong to the resurrection of life, that is, to the right, and end their life within the networks of the Christian name, will not appear except on the beach, that is, when they have risen at the end of the world? That's why they were not able to drag the nets and unload the caught fish into the boat, as they did with the others, they broke the nets and put meanings, they resurrected them. Ibi retia non mittuntur in dexteram, ne solos significant bonds, nec in sinistram, ne solos malo; sed indifferenter, Laxate, inquit, retia vestra in capturem, ut permixtos intelligamus bonds et mals: hic autem, inquit, Mittite in dexteram navigii rete, ut significare! eos qui stabant ad dexteram, only bonds.

Ibi rete propter significanda schismata rumpebatur: hic vero quoniam tune iam in illa summa pace sanctorum nulla erunt schismata, pertinuit ad Evangelistam dicere, Et cum tanti essent, id est, tam magni, non est scissum rete; tanquam illud respiceret ubi scissum est, et in illius mali comparatione commendaret hoc bonum. Ibi capture this multitude piscium tanta, ut impleta duo navigia mergerentur (Lk 5,3-7), id est, in submetsionem premerentur: non enim mersa sunt, sed tamen periclitata. Unde enim existunt in Ecclesia, tanta quae gemimus; nisi cum tantae multitudini obsisti non potest, quae ad submetgendam ptopemodum disciplinam intrat cum moribus suis a sanctorum itinere penitus alienis? Hic autem miserunt rete in dexteram partem, et iam non valebant illud trahere a multitudine piscium. Quid est, iam non valebant illud trahere, nisi quia illi qui pettinent ad resurrectionem vitae, id est ad dexteram, et intra christiani nominis retia defunguntur, nonnisi in littore, id est in fine saeculi cum resurrexerint, apparebunt? in danger to ships. The Church keeps those who come out from the right in the dream of peace, after leaving this mortal life, as if hidden in the depths, until they reach the beach where they are dragged about two hundred steps away. What was represented there by the two naves, that is, the circumcision and the foreskin, I believe is represented here by the two hundred cubits in attention to the two classes of elect, one hundred for the circumcision and one hundred for the foreskin, because the number, added to the hundreds, passes to the right. Finally, in that fishing the number of the fish is not expressed, as if what the prophet says was verified there: I preached and spoke and they multiplied without number; but here none exceeds the number, which is fixed at one hundred and fifty-three. With the help of the Lord I will give you the reason for this number. 8. If we wanted to represent the Law by a number, what would it be but ten? We know very well that the decalogue of the Law, that is, those ten well-known commandments, were first written by the finger of God on two tables of stone. The Law, without the help of grace, gives rise to prevaricators, and remains only in the letter. For this reason mainly the Apostle says: The letter kills, but the spirit gives life. Let the spirit join the letter so that the letter does not kill those whom the spirit does not give life. Let us fulfill the precepts of the Law, supported not by our merits, but by the grace of the Savior. When grace is joined to the Law, that is, the spirit to the letter, seven are added to the number ten. And none of those who were lying down dared to ask him: Who are you?, knowing that it was the Lord. If they knew, what need did they have to ask? Seek my glory in them, and not yours; my domain, and not yours; my interests, and not yours; Do not join with those who belong to dangerous times, lovers of themselves, and other sectarians attached to the beginning of this misfortune? For the Apostle having said: "There will be men who love themselves," he then added: "Lovers of money, boasters, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, criminals, impious, shameless detractors, dishonest, cruel, lacking in kindness, traitors, ribald, obstinate, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, with appearances of piety, but lacking in his spirit." As from a source, all these evils come from the principle stated above: love of self. Rightly, then, it is said to Peter: Do you love me?, and he answers: I love you; and this is what it refers to: A-feed my lambs; and so on for the second and third time. This shows that love and affection are one thing, since the Lord in the last time does not say: Do you love me?, but: Do you love me? Let us not love ourselves, then, but Him; and in the feeding of his sheep let us not seek our interests, but his. I do not know for what inexplicable reason, whoever loves himself and does not love God does not love himself; and, on the other hand, whoever loves God and does not love himself, loves himself. He who cannot live for himself, dies loving himself; Well, you don't love someone who loves me so as not to live. But when you love Him for whom you live, not loving yourself, you love more, because you do not love yourself by loving Him Who is your life. Those who feed Christ's sheep do not love themselves.

All these things and other similar vices, whether they are all gathered in one person, or some in some and others in others, come from self-love, just as the stems all come from the same root. Your spiritual love for Him must grow, so much so that it overcomes the natural fear of death, despising death, when we want to live in Christ. The Apostle says that he desires to be loosed to be with Christ; He groans under his bonds, but he does not want to be stripped of them, but rather to put on another garment so that what is mortal can be absorbed by life. And thus says the Lord to this lover of his: When you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and take you where you do not want to go. This he told him, showing what kind of death he would glorify God with. You will stretch out your hands, he says; that is, you will be crucified. And for you to come to this, another will gird you and lead you, not where you want, but where you do not want. First he said what would happen, and then how it would happen. Well, not when he was crucified, but when he was going to be crucified, he was taken where he did not want to be; because, once crucified, he went, not where he did not want to go, but where he wanted to go. Unbound from the body, he wanted to be with Christ; but, if it were possible, he desired eternal life without passing through those mortal discomforts to which he was led against his will, and from which he emerged according to his wishes. Without wanting it, he reached them, and willingly, he conquered them and got rid of this affection of weakness with which everyone flees from death, so natural that not even old age can take it away from the blessed Peter, to whom it was said: When you are old you will be taken where you do not want. And, for our consolation, the Savior took upon Himself this affection, saying: Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; being thus that He had come precisely to lem crescere ardorem, ut vincat etiam mortis naturalem timorem, quo mori nolumus, et quando cum Christo vívere volumus. Nam et apostolus Paulus dicit se habere concupiscentiam dissolve et esse cum Christo (Phil 1,23): ingemiscit tamengravatus, et non vult exspoliari, sed supervestiri, ut absorbatur mortale a vita (2 Cor 5,4). Et huic Dominus dilectori suo, Cum senueris, inquit, extendes manus tuas, et alius te cinget, et ducet quo tu non vis. Hoc enim ei dixit, significans qua morte clarificaturus etat Deum. Extendes, inquit, manus tuas, hoc est crucifigeris. Ad hoc autem ut venias, alius te cinget, et ducet, non quo vis, sed quo non vis. Prius said quod ieront, et deinde quomodo íieret. Non enim crucifixus, sed utique crucifigendus quo nollet est ductus: nam crucifixus non quo nolebat abiit, sed potius quo volebat.

Solutus quippe a corpore volebat esse cum Christo, sed si fieti posset, praeter mortis molestam vitam concupiscebat aeternam: ad quam molestam nolens ductus est, sed ab ea volens eductus est: nolens ad eam venit, sed volens eam vicit; et reliquit hunc infirmitatis affectum quo nemo vult mori, usque adeo naturalem, ut eum beatato Petro nec senectus auferre potuerit, cui dictum est, Cum senueris, duceris quo non vis. Propter nos consolandos hunc etiam in se transfiguravit ipse Salvator, they say, Pater, si fieri potest, transeat a me calix iste (Mt 26,39): qui utique mori venerat, nec habebat mortis necessitatem, sed voluntatem,

die without needing to die, but by his will, having the power to give his life and to take it up again. But the annoyances of death, however great they may be, must be overcome by the strength of love for Him who, being our life, wanted to suffer even death for us. Because, if there were no discomfort in death, even if small, the glory of the martyrs would not be so great. And if the Good Shepherd, who gave his life for his sheep, made so many of his sheep his martyrs, how much more must those to whom he entrusts the feeding of his sheep, that is, his teaching and government, fight for the truth and against sin, until blood is shed? For this reason, and given the example of his passion, who does not see that shepherds should imitate the Shepherd more, when so many sheep have imitated him, under whose staff and in a single flock the shepherds themselves are also sheep? He made them all his sheep; He suffered for all of them, because, to suffer for them, He Himself became a sheep.

1. Non parva quaestio est, cur apostólo Petro, quando se tertio manifestavit discipulis, dixerit Dominus, Sequere me; de apostólo autem Ioanne, Sk eum vola manere doñee veniam; quid ad te? Huic quaestio-

stay until I come; what to you? To the discussion or solution of this difficulty we will dedicate, with the help of the Lord, the last treatise of this work. Having already announced to Peter the type of death with which he was to glorify God, he said to him: Follow me. And Peter, turning, saw that the disciple whom Jesus loved was following him, who at the Supper was also reclining on his chest, and he asked the Lord: Who will betray you? Peter, seeing this man, said to Jesus: Lord, and what about this man? Jesus answers him: I want this one to remain like this until I come; to you what? You follow me. A rumor began to spread among the brothers that this disciple did not die. And Jesus did not say to him: He does not die, but: I want him to remain like this until I come; what does it matter to you? You see the extent of the difficulty of this passage of the Gospel, the depth of which not a little tortures the intelligence of those who consider it. Why does he only say to Peter: Follow me, and not to all those present together? Because there is no doubt that they also, as disciples, followed the Master. And if we take this for martyrdom, was it only Peter who suffered for Christian truth? Was not among those seven the other son of Zebedee and brother of John, whom Herod killed after the Ascension? Some will say, and they are right, that James was not crucified, and that it was rightly said to Peter: Follow me, for he not only suffered death, but, like Christ, the death of a cross. Let us accept this interpretation if no other more convenient one is found. Why then is it said of Saint John: I want it to remain so until I come; to you what?, and then repeats: Tú ni, quantum Dominus ipse donaverit, sive pertractandae, sive solvendae sermonem novissimum huius operis impendimus. Cum ergo praenuntiasset Dominus Petro, qua morte clarificaturus esset Deum, dicit ei: Sequere me. Conversas Petrus vidit illum discipulum quem diligebat lesus, sequentem: qui et recubuit in coena super pectus eius, et dixit, Domine, quis est qui tradet te? Hunc ergo cum vidisset Petrus, dicit lesu: Domine, hic autem quid? Dicit ei lesus: Sic eum voló manere doñee veniam; quid ad te? You dry me up. Exiit ergo sermo iste inter fratres, quia discipulus Ule non moritur. Et non dixit ei lesus, Non moritur; thirst, Sic eum flew manere doñee veniam; quid ad te? Ecce quousque in hoc Gospel extenditur quaestio, quae sua profunditate non mediocriter mentem scrutantis exercet.

Cur enim dicitur Petro, Sequere me, nec dicitur caeteris qui simul aderant? Et profecto eum sicut magistrum discipuli sequebantur. Sed si ad passionem intelligendum est, numquid solus pro christiana veritate passus est Petrus? Tender says that Jesus loved him, as if he alone were loved, to distinguish him by this sign from the others, whom he undoubtedly loved. What does he mean by this if not that he was the most loved? And we cannot doubt that this is the truth. Because what greater proof of his deepest love for him could Jesus give him than, being a man, companion of the other fellow disciples in the work of salvation, he alone rested on the breast of the Savior himself? And that the apostle Peter loved Christ more can be proven with a multitude of testimonies; But in order not to go further in search, in the same narration of the third appearance of the Lord, read shortly before, and preceding this one, it appears with evidence, when, questioning him, the Lord said to him: Do you love me more than these? The Lord knew this well, and yet he questioned him, so that we, who read the Gospel, might also know Peter's love through the Lord's question and through his response. As for Peter in his answer not adding: More than these, it is because he only answered what he knew about himself. For he could not know how much each of the others loved him, because he did not see their hearts. Even so, by saying earlier: That's right, Lord, you know, he clearly implied that the Lord knew what he was asking. Therefore, the Lord knew that not only did he love him, but that he loved him more than the others. However, if we propose to inquire which of the two was the better, the one who loved more or the one who loved Christ less, who will hesitate to answer that the one who loved more? And if we ask which of the two is better, the one that is more or the one that is diligebat Iesus, quasi solum diligeret, ut hoc signo discerneretur a caeteris, quos utique omnes diligebat: quid ergo, nisi amplius se dilectum, cum hoc diceret, volebat intelligi? quod absit ut mendaciter diceret. Quod autem maius daré potuit Iesus maioris erga eum suae dilectionis indicium, quam ut homo cum caeteris condiscipulis suis socius tantae salutis, solus tamen discubuerit super pectus ipsius Salvatoris?

Quod utique sciebat, et tamen interrogabat, ut etiam nos qui legimus Evangelium, amorem Petri erga Dominum, et illo interrogante et isto respondeme nossemus. In the first of the proposed comparisons, Peter is placed before Juan; but in the second Juan surpasses Pedro. That is why I propose a third: which of the two is the better, the one who loves Christ less than his fellow disciple, but is more loved by Christ, or the one who loves Christ more, but is loved less by Christ? Here the response stops and the difficulty increases. For my part, I would easily give this answer: that he who loves Christ more is better, and he who is more loved by Christ is happier, and I would see a way to defend the justice of our Liberator, who loves less those who love him more and loves more those who love him less. 5. Supported and adored by the manifest mercy of Him whose judgments are hidden, I am going to try to resolve this tremendous question according to the strength that He deigns to grant us. Until now I have proposed it, I have not exposed it. Let this be the preamble to your presentation; Let us remember that we live a miserable life in this mortal body that weighs on the soul. But those of us who have already been redeemed by the Mediator and have received the Holy Spirit as a pledge, have the blessed life in hope, although we do not have it in possession. The hope you see is not hope. Because who expects what they see? And if we wait for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience. Patience is necessary to endure the evils that each one suffers, not in the goods that one enjoys. And, although the first cause of the miseries of this life has been sin, all men are forced, even after pergitur a Christo, meliorem procul dubio responderimus. In illa ergo comparisone quam prius posui, Petrus Ioanni; in hac vero altera, Ioannes anteponitur Petro. Proinde tertiam sic proponimus: quis est duorum discipulorum melior, qui minus quam condiscipulus eius diligit Christum, et plus quam condiscipulus eius diligitur a Christo? an ille quem minus quam condiscipulum eius diligit Christus, cum plus ipse quam suus condiscipulus diligat Christum? Hic planned cunctatur responsio, et augetur quaestio.

Quantum autem ipse sapio, meliorem qui plus diligit Christum, feliciorem vero quem plus diligit Christus, facile responderem; si iustitiam liberatoris nostri minus eum diligentis a quo plus diligitur, et eum plus a quo minus diligitur, quemadmodum defendem, perviderem. 5. The penalty is longer than the guilt, so that the guilt would not be considered small if the penalty ended with it. And for this reason, whether to demonstrate the misery owed, whether to amend a laudable life, or to exercise the necessary patience, punishment temporarily retains the man whose guilt does not hold him as a punishment or eternal damnation. This is the condition, worthy of being mourned, but not of being rebuked, of these bad days that we spend in this mortal life, although we long to see good days in it. For the righteous wrath of God comes, of which the Scripture says: Man, born of a woman, is short-lived and full of wrath, the wrath of God not being like that of man, that is, a disturbance of the excited spirit, but a calm determination of just punishment. In the midst of his wrath, God, who, as it is written, does not stop the course of his mercies, in addition to other consolations that he never ceases to provide to the human race, in the fullness of the time in which he knew that he must be executed, sent his only begotten Son, through whom he created all things, so that, remaining God, he would become man and be the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; and as many as believe in Him, freed by the laver of regeneration from the guilt of all sins, that is, from the original, contracted by generation, and against which it was mainly

And because, even though they are on that path, they are not exempt from sins, born of the weakness of this life, he granted them the healthy remedy of alms, with which they could help their prayers, when he taught us to say: Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. This makes the Church happy with that hope during this laborious life. Of this Church, by the primacy of his apostolate, Peter carried the representation in all its universality. As to his personal properties, by nature he was a man, by grace a Christian, by greater grace an apostle, and the first of them; but when it was said to him, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; What you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and what you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven, represented the entire Church, which in this mortal life is shaken by various temptations, such as rains, rivers and storms, but does not fall, because it is founded on a firm rock, from which comes the name Peter. For the stone is not derived from Peter, but Peter from the stone, just as Christ does not come from a Christian, but a Christian from Christ. Ac per hoc vel ad demonstrationem debitae miseriae, vel ad emendationem labilis vitae, vel ad exercitationem necessariae patientiae, temporaliter hominem detinet poena et quem iam ad damnationem sempiternam reum non detinet culpa. In hac ira sua Deus non continens, sicut scriptum est, miserationes suas (Ps 76,10), praeter alia solaría miserorum quae generi humano praebere non cessat, in plenitudine temporis, quo ipse sciebat hoc esse faciendum, misit Filium suum unigenitum (Gal 4,4), per quem creavit universa, ut manens Deus ieront homo, et esset mediator Dei ét hominum homo Christus Iesus (1 Tim 2,5): in quem credentes, per lavactum regenerationis soluto reatu orntiium peccatorum, et originalis

Et quia in ipso quoque ambulantes non sunt sine peccatis, quae de huius vitae infirmitate subrepunt, dedit eleemosynarum remedia salutaria, quibus eorum adiuvaretur orado, ubi eos dicere docuit, dimitte nobis debita riostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris (Mt 6,12). Quod enim ad ipsum proprie pertinet, natura unus homo erat, gratia unus christianus, abundantiore gratia unus idemque primus apostolus: sed quando ei dictum est, Tibi dabo keys regni caelorum, et quodcumque ligaveris super terram, erit ligatum et in caelis; et quodcumque solveris super terram, erit solutum et in caelis, universam significat Ecclesiam, quae in hoc saeculo divetsis tentationibus velut imbtibus, fluminibus, tempestatibus quatitur, et non cadit, quoniam fundata est super petram, unde Petrus nomen accepit. Non enim a Petto petra, sed Petrus a petra; sicut non Christus a christiano, sed christianus a Christo vocatur. Christ, Son of the living God. On this rock that he confessed, I will build my Church. The stone was Christ, and on that foundation Peter was also built. No one can lay another foundation than the one that is laid, which is Christ Jesus. And so the Church, founded on Christ, received from Him, in the person of Peter, the keys of the kingdom of heaven, that is, the power to bind and loose sins. What properly is the Church in Christ, that is figuratively Peter in the stone; and in this figure, Christ is the stone, and Peter is the Church. But this Church, represented by Peter, while living among evils, loving Christ, is freed from the same evils. And it follows most closely in the person of those who fight for the truth to the death. Thus, to that universal group it is said: Follow me, because Christ suffered for him, of whom Peter himself says: Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we follow in his footsteps. For this reason it was said to him: Follow me. But there is another immortal life, in which there are no evils; There we will see face to face what we see here in a mirror and in figures when much progress has been made in the truth. Thus, then, the Church is aware of two lives that have been preached and entrusted to her by divine inspiration, of which one lives in faith and the other in contemplation; one in the time of pilgrimage, the other in the eternity of the mansion; one at work, the other at rest; one on the road, the other in the homeland; one in the work of activity, the other in the reward of contemplation; the one turns away from evil to do good, the Filias Dei vivi (ibid. 16,16-19). Super hanc ergo, inquít, petram quam confessus es, aedificabo Ecclesiam meam. Petra enim erat Christus (1 Cor 10:4): super quod fundamentum etiam ipse aedificatus est Petrus. Fundamentum quippe aliud nemo potest will put praeter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus (ibid. 3,11). Ecclesia ergo quae fundatur in Christo, keys ab eo regni caelorum accepit in Petro, id est potestatem ligandi solvendique peccata. Quod est enim per proprietatem in Christo Ecclesia, hoc est per significationem Petrus in petra; qua significatione intelligitur Christus petra, Petrus Ecclesia. Haec igitur Ecclesia quam significat Petrus, quamdiu degit in malis, loving et sequendo Christum liberatur a malis.

Magis autem sequitur in eis qui certant pro veritate usque ad mortem. Sed universitati dicitur, Sequete me, pro qua universitate passus est Christus: de quo dicit idem Petrus, Christus pro nobis passus est, relinquens nobis exemplum, ut sequamur vestigia eius (1 Petr 2,21). Ecce propter quod ei dictum est, Sequere me. Est autem alia vita immortalis, quae non est in malis: ibi facie ad faciem videbimus, quod hic per speculum et in aenigmate videtur (1 Cor 13:12), quando multum in conspicienda veritate proficitur. Duas itaque vitas sibi divinitus praedicatas et commendatas novit Ecclesia, quarum est una in fide, altera in specie; una in tempore peregrinationis, altera in aeternitate mansionis; una in labore, alters in requie; una via, alters in patria; una in opere actionis, altera in mercede

another has no evil to avoid and has a great good to enjoy; one fights with the enemy, the other reigns without an enemy; One becomes strong in adversity, the other does not feel anything adverse; the one restrains carnal lusts, the other indulges in spiritual delights; one strives to achieve victory, the other lives securely in the peace of victory; One needs help in temptations, the other without any temptation rejoices in her protector; one helps the needy, the other is where there are no needs; The one forgives the sins of others so that his own sins may be forgiven, the other does not have to forgive nor be forgiven; the one is shaken by evils so that it does not take pride in good things, the other, through the fullness of grace, is devoid of all evil so that without any danger of pride it is adhered to the supreme Good; The one must discern between evil and good, the other only contemplates the good; In conclusion, one is good, but still full of miseries; the other is better and blessed. This is figured by the apostle Peter; that one, for Juan. This develops completely here until the end of the world and there it finds its end; that will be complete after this life, but in the next life it will have no end. Therefore it is said to this one: Follow me; of that one, on the other hand: I want it to remain like this until I come; what to you? You follow me. What does this mean? What should it mean, according to my scope and understanding, but: You follow me by imitation, suffering temporal evils, and he stays until he comes to give you the everlasting gifts?

More clearly it can be said in this way: Follow me a perfect activity, informed by the example of my contemplationis; una declinat a malo et facit bonum, alter nullum habet a quo declinet malum, et magnum habet quo fruatur bonum; una cum hoste pugnat, alter sine hoste regnat; una fortis est in adversis, alter nihil sentit adversi; a carnal libido frenat, alters spiritualibus delectationibus vacat; una es vincendi cura sollicita, alter victoriae pace secura; una in tentationibus adiuvatur, alter sine ulla tentatione in ipso adiutore laetatur; una subvenit indigenti, altera ibi est ubi nullum invenit indigentem; una aliena peccata ut sua sibi ignoscantur ignoscit, alter nec patitur quod ignoscat, nec facit quod sibi poscat ignosci; una flagellatur malis, ne extollatur in bonis, altera tanta plenitudine gratiae caret omni malo, ut sine ulla temptatione superbiae cohaereat summo bono; una bona et mala discernit, altera quae sola bona sunt cernit: ergo una bona est, sed adhuc misera; Altera melior et beata. This meaning is per apostolum Petrum, illa per Ioannem. Tota hic agitur ista usque in huius saeculi finem, et illic invenit finem: differtur illa complenda post huius saeculi finem, sed in future saeculo non habet finem. Ideo dicitur huic, Sequere me: de illo autem, Sic eum voló manere doñee veniam; quid ad te? You dry me up. Quid enim est hoc? For not because Christ loves us in the future life, in which we will live endlessly with Him, more than in this, from which we are taken to live always in that, will we love Him less there, when we will be better, since we cannot become better except by loving Him more. Why, then, did John love him less than Peter, if he represented that life in which he is to be loved much more, but because it was said: I want him to remain, that is, wait until I come, to indicate that we still do not have that same love, which will then be much greater, but we hope to have it in the future, when He has come? And that is why the same apostle says in his Epistle: What we will be has not yet appeared, because we know that when this appears, we will be like Him, because we will see Him as He is. Then we will love more what we see. But the Lord, knowing what our future life will be in us, loves it more in his predestination, to lead us to it with his love for us. Therefore, since all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, we recognize our present misery, because we feel it; And that is why we love more the mercy of the Lord, which we desire to be granted to us to see us free from our misery, and daily we ask it mainly for the remission of sins, being granted to us by Him. And this is what the apostle Peter meant, that he loves more, but is loved less, because Christ loves us less in our misery than in our blessedness. We too love the contemplation of truth less, as

Follow Christ the pious fullness of patience reaching even death; but the fullness of wisdom, which is then to be manifested, remains in this state until the coming of Christ. Here, in the land of mortals, the evils of this world are tolerated; There, in the land of the living, the Lord's goods are contemplated. But as soon as he says: I want him to remain until I come, it is not to be understood in the sense of staying or remaining, but in the sense of waiting; because what is meant by it will not be verified now, but when Christ comes. But as for what is meant by the one to whom it was said: You follow me, if it is not realized during this life, the life expected will not be reached. In this active life, the more we love Christ, the more easily we free ourselves from evil; He, however, loves us less in this state, and takes us out of this state so that we are not always like this. There he loves us more, because there will no longer be anything in us that displeases him and that he has to tear out; but here He does not love us except in order to heal us and separate us from the things that He does not love. Then he loves us here, where he does not want us to remain, and he loves us more there, where he wants us to pass and from where he does not want us to ever fall. But no one separates these two distinguished apostles. Both were in what Peter represented and both were to be in what John represented. In figure he followed that one and this one remained; but by faith both tolerated the evils of this misery, and both hoped for the goods of that beatitude. And not only them, but the entire Church, Bride of Christ, does this to be free from these temptations and to preserve herself for that happiness. These two lives were figured by Peter and John, one each; but both temporarily walked in the latter by faith, and both enjoyed the former by contemplation. Peter, the first of the apostles, received the keys of the kingdom of heaven to bind and loose the sins of all the righteous belonging inseparably to the body of Christ, to sustain the governance of this tempestuous life. And representing those same righteous people, destined for the most peaceful bosom of that most secret life, John the Evangelist was reclining on the chest of Christ. Because not only Peter binds and looses sins, but the entire Church; nor did only John drink from the fountains of the divine breast that in the beginning the Word of God was in God and all other sublime things amat us Christus miseros quam blessed. Nec ipsi soli, sed universala hoc facit sancta Ecclesia sponsa Christi, ab istis tentationibus eruenda, in illa congratulate yourself servanda. Quas duas vitas Petrus et Ioannes figuraverunt, singuli singulas: verum et in hac temporaliter ambulaverunt both per fidem, et illa in aeternum fruentur both per speciem. Omnibus igitur sanctis ad Christi corpus inseparabiliter pertinentibus, propter huius vitae procellosissimae gubernaculum, ad liganda et solvenda peccata keys regni caelorum primus Apostolorum Petrus accepit: eisdemque omnibus sanctis propter vitae illius secretissimae quietissimum sinum, super pectus Christi Ioannes evangelist discubuit. This is that disciple who testifies to these things and has written them, and we know that his testimony is true. There are many other things that Jesus did that, if they were written one by one, I believe that the world itself could not contain the books that were to be written. It should not be understood that the world could not contain them spatially, because how could writing be done in the world, if the world were not capable of containing writings? But perhaps they could not be understood by the capacity of the readers; because, even if the veracity of things is preserved, words often seem to exceed that reality. But this does not happen when doubtful or obscure things are exposed, adding causes and reasons, but when what is clear and open is increased or decreased without Deum apud Deum, et caetera de Christi divinitate, et de totius divinitatis trinitate atque unitate sublimia, quae in illo regno facie ad faciem contemplanda, nunc autem doñee veniat Dominus, in speculo atque in aenigmate contuenda sunt, quae praedicando ructaret, de fonte Dominici pectoris solus bibit; sed ipse Dominus ipsum Evangelium pro sua cuiusque capacítate omnibus suis bibendum toto terratum orbe diffudit. Sunt qui senserint, et hi quidem non contemptibiles sacri eloquii ttactatotes, a Christo loannem apostolum propterea plus amatum, quod ñeque uxorem duxeiit, et ab ineunte pueritia castissimus vixerit (HlERON. 1.1 Contra lovinianum).

Because then the words so exceed the loyalty of the things they indicate that the will of the speaker appears clear without the intention of falsifying them, and the listener knows well to what extent they should be believed. This way of speaking is called hyperbole by the masters of Greek letters, as well as by the masters of Latin letters. And this way of saying is found not only in this passage, but in many others of the Divine Letters, such as: They put their mouths in heaven; The tip of the hair of those who walk in their crimes, and many others, which are not scarce in the Holy Scriptures, as well as other tropes, that is, ways of saying. I would speak at greater length about them if I were not forced to conclude this sermon at the same time as the evangelist concludes his gospel. significandae veritatis erratur; quoniam sic verba rem quae indicatur excedunt, ut voluntas loquentis nec fallentis appareat, qui novit quousque credatur, a quo ultra quam credendum est vel minuitur loquendo aliquid, vel augetur. Hunc loquendi modum graeco nomine, non solum graecarum, verum etiam latinarum litterarum magistri hyperbolen vocant.
